steps.title: 줄 서는 맛집
steps.title_en: Is it really worth the wait?
steps.scene_desc: 3월 첫 토요일 점심, 소문난 국숫집 앞 긴 줄. 아직 쌀쌀한 날씨에 지우가 목도리를 두르고 손을 비비며 반신반의하는 얼굴이고, 마야는 신이 나서 줄 앞쪽을 가리키며 웃음. 줄 선 사람들 몇몇이 휴대폰으로 사진을 찍음(간판·메뉴판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Is it really worth the wait?" (줄 서는 맛집). Goal: 기다릴 가치가 있는지 따져 말하기. Today's scene: 3월 첫 토요일 점심, 소문난 국숫집 앞 긴 줄. 아직 쌀쌀한 날씨에 지우가 목도리를 두르고 손을 비비며 반신반의하는 얼굴이고, 마야는 신이 나서 줄 앞쪽을 가리키며 웃음. 줄 선 사람들 몇몇이 휴대폰으로 사진을 찍음(간판·메뉴판에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Is it really worth waiting ___?".

steps.when: 들이는 시간만큼 가치가 있는지 물어요. worth 뒤에는 *-ing* 동사.
steps.extra: Is it really worth waiting an hour for noodles?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Is it really worth waiting ___?" (정말 ~ 기다릴 만해요?). When to use it: 들이는 시간만큼 가치가 있는지 물어요. worth 뒤에는 -ing 동사. Note: Is it really worth waiting an hour for noodles?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I don’t see the point of ___.".

steps.en: I don’t see the point of ___.
steps.when: 어떤 일이 내겐 별 의미 없어 보인다고 부드럽게 말해요. of 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: I don’t see the point of standing in a queue.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I don’t see the point of ___." (~하는 게 무슨 의미인지 모르겠어요.). When to use it: 어떤 일이 내겐 별 의미 없어 보인다고 부드럽게 말해요. of 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: I don’t see the point of standing in a queue.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "To me, it’s all about ___.".

steps.when: 나에게 가장 중요한 것을 말해요. 내 생각이니까 *To me*로 시작해요.
steps.extra: To me, it’s all about the atmosphere.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "To me, it’s all about ___." (저한테는 ~가 제일 중요해요.). When to use it: 나에게 가장 중요한 것을 말해요. 내 생각이니까 To me로 시작해요. Note: To me, it’s all about the atmosphere.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("An Hour in Line · 3월 첫 토요일 점심, 소문난 국숫집 앞에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: An Hour in Line · 3월 첫 토요일 점심, 소문난 국숫집 앞에서

lines.en: Wow, look at that line. I reckon it’s about an hour’s wait.
lines.ko: 와, 저 줄 좀 봐요. 한 시간쯤 기다려야 할 것 같아요.

lines.en: An hour? {{Is it really worth waiting}} that long for a bowl of noodles?
lines.ko: 한 시간이요? 국수 한 그릇 먹자고 정말 그렇게 오래 기다릴 만해요?

lines.en: Trust me. Their signature dish is literally made by hand while you watch.
lines.ko: 날 믿어요. 이 집 대표 메뉴는 보는 앞에서 말 그대로 손으로 만들어요.

lines.en: Honestly, {{I don’t see the point of}} standing in a queue in the cold. Life’s too short to wait in line.
lines.ko: 솔직히 추운 데서 줄 서는 게 무슨 의미인지 모르겠어요. 줄 서서 기다리기엔 인생이 너무 짧아요.

lines.en: But half the fun is the wait! We can chat, and we get really hungry.
lines.ko: 그래도 기다리는 게 재미의 반이에요! 수다도 떨고, 배도 엄청 고파지고요.

lines.en: I can barely feel my fingers. Isn’t it mostly hype? People just want to post photos.
lines.ko: 손가락 감각이 거의 없어요. 대부분 과장된 소문 아니에요? 다들 그냥 사진 올리고 싶은 거고요.

lines.en: Some do. {{To me, it’s all about}} the experience. The smell, the noise, the atmosphere.
lines.ko: 그런 사람도 있죠. 저한테는 경험이 제일 중요해요. 냄새, 북적이는 소리, 분위기요.

lines.en: I guess. But popular doesn’t always mean good. Maybe it’s… a little overrated?
lines.ko: 그렇긴 하죠. 그래도 인기 있다고 늘 좋은 건 아니에요. 어쩌면… 좀 과대평가된 거 아닐까요?

lines.en: Say it like you mean it!
lines.ko: 진심이면 자신 있게 말해요!

lines.en: Okay. It’s overrated! It sounds silly, but that’s what I think.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 과대평가됐어요! 좀 우습게 들리겠지만 그게 제 생각이에요.

lines.en: (Later, inside the shop) So? Was it worth the wait?
lines.ko: (나중에, 가게 안에서) 그래서요? 기다린 보람이 있었어요?

lines.en: The noodles are great. But for me, it’s a once-in-a-while thing. Each to their own!
lines.ko: 국수는 정말 맛있어요. 그래도 저한테는 어쩌다 한 번이면 되는 일이에요. 사람마다 다른 거죠!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "An Hour in Line · 3월 첫 토요일 점심, 소문난 국숫집 앞에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "Wow, look at that line. I reckon it’s about an hour’s wait." (와, 저 줄 좀 봐요. 한 시간쯤 기다려야 할 것 같아요.)
2. Jiwoo: "An hour? Is it really worth waiting that long for a bowl of noodles?" (한 시간이요? 국수 한 그릇 먹자고 정말 그렇게 오래 기다릴 만해요?)
3. Maya: "Trust me. Their signature dish is literally made by hand while you watch." (날 믿어요. 이 집 대표 메뉴는 보는 앞에서 말 그대로 손으로 만들어요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Honestly, I don’t see the point of standing in a queue in the cold. Life’s too short to wait in line." (솔직히 추운 데서 줄 서는 게 무슨 의미인지 모르겠어요. 줄 서서 기다리기엔 인생이 너무 짧아요.)
5. Maya: "But half the fun is the wait! We can chat, and we get really hungry." (그래도 기다리는 게 재미의 반이에요! 수다도 떨고, 배도 엄청 고파지고요.)
6. Jiwoo: "I can barely feel my fingers. Isn’t it mostly hype? People just want to post photos." (손가락 감각이 거의 없어요. 대부분 과장된 소문 아니에요? 다들 그냥 사진 올리고 싶은 거고요.)
7. Maya: "Some do. To me, it’s all about the experience. The smell, the noise, the atmosphere." (그런 사람도 있죠. 저한테는 경험이 제일 중요해요. 냄새, 북적이는 소리, 분위기요.)
8. Jiwoo: "I guess. But popular doesn’t always mean good. Maybe it’s… a little overrated?" (그렇긴 하죠. 그래도 인기 있다고 늘 좋은 건 아니에요. 어쩌면… 좀 과대평가된 거 아닐까요?)
9. Maya: "Say it like you mean it!" (진심이면 자신 있게 말해요!)
10. Jiwoo: "Okay. It’s overrated! It sounds silly, but that’s what I think." (좋아요. 과대평가됐어요! 좀 우습게 들리겠지만 그게 제 생각이에요.)
11. Maya: "(Later, inside the shop) So? Was it worth the wait?" ((나중에, 가게 안에서) 그래서요? 기다린 보람이 있었어요?)
12. Jiwoo: "The noodles are great. But for me, it’s a once-in-a-while thing. Each to their own!" (국수는 정말 맛있어요. 그래도 저한테는 어쩌다 한 번이면 되는 일이에요. 사람마다 다른 거죠!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

frame: Is it really worth waiting ___? / Was it worth the wait?
I don’t see the point of ___. — To me, it’s all about ___.
head: 장소나 물건
할 만해요? (Is it really worth …?)
제일 중요한 것 (To me, it’s all about …)
rows: paying that much for a ticket
buying it on the first day
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Is it really worth waiting ___? / Was it worth the wait? / I don’t see the point of ___. — To me, it’s all about ___. Table (장소나 물건 → 할 만해요? (Is it really worth …?)):
- a famous bakery → waiting 40 minutes for bread
- a new café → going there on a weekend
- a concert → paying that much for a ticket
- a new phone → buying it on the first day
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Is it really *worth waiting* an hour? 정말 한 시간 기다릴 만해요? · It’s *worth the wait*. 기다릴 만해요. 
worth 뒤에는 -ing 동사나 명사. 짧게 답할 때는 It’s (not) worth it.

I don’t see *the point of* standing in line. 줄 서는 게 무슨 의미인지 모르겠어요. 
To me, it’s *all about* the food. 저한테는 음식이 제일 중요해요.
errors: I don’t see the point to wait.
I don’t see the point of waiting.
이 표현은 the point 뒤에 of + -ing.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- worth + -ing — 시간을 들일 만한가: Is it really worth waiting an hour? 정말 한 시간 기다릴 만해요? · It’s worth the wait. 기다릴 만해요. / worth 뒤에는 -ing 동사나 명사. 짧게 답할 때는 It’s (not) worth it.
- the point of · all about: I don’t see the point of standing in line. 줄 서는 게 무슨 의미인지 모르겠어요. / To me, it’s all about the food. 저한테는 음식이 제일 중요해요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Is it worth to wait? → Is it worth waiting? (worth 뒤에는 to + 동사가 아니라 -ing.)
- I don’t see the point to wait. → I don’t see the point of waiting. (이 표현은 the point 뒤에 of + -ing.)
- It doesn’t worth it. → It isn’t worth it. (worth는 동사가 아니에요. be + worth.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: worth + -ing — 시간을 들일 만한가: Is it really worth waiting an hour? 정말 한 시간 기다릴 만해요? · It’s worth the wait. 기다릴 만해요. worth 뒤에는 -ing 동사나 명사. 짧게 답할 때는 It’s (not) worth it.
the point of · all about: I don’t see the point of standing in line. 줄 서는 게 무슨 의미인지 모르겠어요. To me, it’s all about the food. 저한테는 음식이 제일 중요해요.
mistakes: Is it worth to wait? → Is it worth waiting?
I don’t see the point to wait. → I don’t see the point of waiting.
It doesn’t worth it. → It isn’t worth it.

steps.note: 예) wait an hour for a table / the food → A: Is it really worth waiting an hour for a table? B: Maybe. To me, it’s all about the food. 또는 I don’t see the point of …
items: wait an hour for a table
pay extra for a window seat

drive two hours to a famous café
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) wait an hour for a table / the food → A: Is it really worth waiting an hour for a table? B: Maybe. To me, it’s all about the food. 또는 I don’t see the point of …. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: wait an hour for a table → the food | pay extra for a window seat → the view | get up early for concert tickets → the live experience | drive two hours to a famous café → the atmosphere.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Is it really worth the wait?" (줄 서는 맛집); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Is it really worth waiting ___?" / "I don’t see the point of ___." / "To me, it’s all about ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Half the fun is the wait.
Life’s too short to wait in line.
줄 서서 기다리기엔 인생이 너무 짧아요.
인기 있다고 늘 좋은 건 아니에요.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 기다림에 대해: "Half the fun is the wait." (기다리는 것도 재미의 반이에요., 친근); "It’s a once-in-a-while thing." (어쩌다 한 번 하는 일이에요., 보통)
- 유행을 의심할 때: "Life’s too short to wait in line." (줄 서서 기다리기엔 인생이 너무 짧아요., 친근); "It’s mostly hype." (대부분 과장된 소문이에요., 친근); "Popular doesn’t always mean good." (인기 있다고 늘 좋은 건 아니에요., 보통); "People just want to post photos." (다들 그냥 사진 올리고 싶은 거예요., 보통)
- 솔직한 생각: "The food was good, but not that good." (음식은 괜찮았지만 그 정도는 아니었어요., 보통); "I’d rather go somewhere quiet." (차라리 조용한 데 갈래요., 보통); "Each to their own." (사람마다 취향이 다른 거죠., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

*queue* = line, 줄(영국에서 더 흔함) 
*ambience* = atmosphere, 분위기(조금 격식)

steps.blank:
A: Is it really worth ___ an hour?   B: Sure. Half the fun is the ___.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 일상의 느낌 낱말: hunger 배고픔 · thirst 목마름, 갈증 / joy 큰 기쁨 · silly 우스운, 바보 같은 / literally 말 그대로, 정말로 · barely 거의 ~ 않다 / reckon ~라고 생각하다(친근한 말)
- 맛집 낱말 (참고): queue = line, 줄(영국에서 더 흔함) / ambience = atmosphere, 분위기(조금 격식) / foodie 맛있는 음식을 즐겨 찾는 사람 / a frequent customer 자주 오는 손님, 단골 / 이 과의 국숫집은 수업을 위해 지어낸 곳이에요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Is it really worth ___ an hour? B: Sure. Half the fun is the ___. / A: I don’t see the ___ of standing in line. B: Well, each to their ___. / 낱말 상자: waiting · wait · point · own
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: queue (줄, 대기 줄), crowd (군중, 많은 사람), signature dish ((가게의) 대표 메뉴), foodie (미식가, 맛집을 즐겨 찾는 사람), reservation (예약), post ((사진·글을) 올리다), wait time (대기 시간), grin (활짝 웃음; 활짝 웃다), sigh (한숨; 한숨 쉬다), wander (천천히 거닐다, 돌아다니다), bunch (다발, 송이; 무리), golden (황금빛의).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: She posts on social media a lot.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: hype (과장된 소문, 지나친 떠들썩함) — "It’s mostly hype."; overrated (과대평가된) — "I think it’s overrated."; underrated (과소평가된) — "That café is underrated."; atmosphere (분위기) — "I love the atmosphere here."; ambience ((장소의) 분위기(조금 격식)) — "a quiet ambience"; social (사회의, 사교의(social media 소셜 미디어)) — "She posts on social media a lot."; trend (유행, 추세) — "a new food trend"; quality (질, 품질) — "high-quality noodles"; popular (인기 있는) — "a popular place"; worth ((시간·돈을) 들일 가치가 있는) — "It’s worth the wait.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Would you wait an hour at a popular restaurant? Why or why not?
Yes. To me, it’s all about ___. / No. I don’t see the point of ___.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Would you wait an hour at a popular restaurant? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: Yes. To me, it’s all about ___. / No. I don’t see the point of ___.)
- "Is there something you think is overrated?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is a bit overrated. Popular doesn’t always mean good.)
- "What is worth waiting for, in your opinion?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is worth waiting for, because ___.)
- "A reservation or a line, which do you prefer?" (hint on screen: I’d rather ___. Each to their own!)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Was It Worth It?
steps.text: That evening, Jiwoo thought about the day. She and Maya had spent a full hour’s *worth of* time in line, and they made it inside just after one. Was it worth it? To be fair, the golden broth was rich, and Maya now calls herself a fan *for life*. Still, Jiwoo thinks a lot of it is hype. Some people wander up, take photos of the crowd, and leave. Trends change fast, and even busy places can *close down*. On the *way out*, Jiwoo saw a quiet little noodle shop next door with no line at all. Maybe she’ll try it next time. But she understands Maya. For her, the wait is part of the joy. Then Jiwoo remembered: Daniel’s first debate group is next Thursday. Maybe this could be a topic!
steps.gloss: worth of ~어치, ~ 분량 · for life 평생 · close down 문을 닫다, 폐업하다 · way out 나가는 길, 출구 · to be fair 공정하게 말하면 · wander up 천천히 다가오다
questions: How long did Jiwoo and Maya wait in line?
What did Jiwoo see on the way out?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Was It Worth It?". Text: "That evening, Jiwoo thought about the day. She and Maya had spent a full hour’s worth of time in line, and they made it inside just after one. Was it worth it? To be fair, the golden broth was rich, and Maya now calls herself a fan for life. Still, Jiwoo thinks a lot of it is hype. Some people wander up, take photos of the crowd, and leave. Trends change fast, and even busy places can close down. On the way out, Jiwoo saw a quiet little noodle shop next door with no line at all. Maybe she’ll try it next time. But she understands Maya. For her, the wait is part of the joy. Then Jiwoo remembered: Daniel’s first debate group is next Thursday. Maybe this could be a topic!" Words: worth of ~어치, ~ 분량 · for life 평생 · close down 문을 닫다, 폐업하다 · way out 나가는 길, 출구 · to be fair 공정하게 말하면 · wander up 천천히 다가오다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "How long did Jiwoo and Maya wait in line?" / "What did Jiwoo see on the way out?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

‘I don’t see the point of ___.’로 별 의미 없어 보인다고 부드럽게 말할 수 있어요.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Is it really worth waiting ___?’로 들일 만한 가치가 있는지 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I don’t see the point of ___.’로 별 의미 없어 보인다고 부드럽게 말할 수 있어요.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 온라인 리뷰
steps.title_en: Can you trust online reviews?
steps.scene_desc: 3월 둘째 목요일 저녁 7시 반, 동네 카페 안쪽 방. 이웃 여덟아홉 명이 둥글게 앉아 있고 대니얼이 앞에서 모임을 열며 손짓함. 지우와 클로이가 나란히 앉아 휴대폰 화면의 별점을 보며 소곤소곤 이야기함(화면·벽에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Can you trust online reviews?" (온라인 리뷰). Goal: 경험에 비춰 믿을 만한지 따지기. Today's scene: 3월 둘째 목요일 저녁 7시 반, 동네 카페 안쪽 방. 이웃 여덟아홉 명이 둥글게 앉아 있고 대니얼이 앞에서 모임을 열며 손짓함. 지우와 클로이가 나란히 앉아 휴대폰 화면의 별점을 보며 소곤소곤 이야기함(화면·벽에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "You can’t always trust ___.".

steps.when: 늘 믿을 만한 건 아니라고 말해요. ‘You can’t trust …’보다 부드러워요.
steps.extra: You can’t always trust star ratings.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "You can’t always trust ___." (~를 늘 믿을 수는 없어요.). When to use it: 늘 믿을 만한 건 아니라고 말해요. ‘You can’t trust …’보다 부드러워요. Note: You can’t always trust star ratings.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "In my experience, ___.".

steps.when: 모두에게 맞는 사실이 아니라 내가 겪은 일에서 나온 의견을 말해요.
steps.extra: In my experience, photos tell you more than stars.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "In my experience, ___." (제 경험으로는 ~.). When to use it: 모두에게 맞는 사실이 아니라 내가 겪은 일에서 나온 의견을 말해요. Note: In my experience, photos tell you more than stars.

The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s hard to tell whether ___.".

steps.when: 예·아니요로 답할 일이 확실하지 않을 때 써요. *whether* 뒤에는 완전한 문장.

steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s hard to tell whether ___." (~인지 아닌지 알기 어려워요.). When to use it: 예·아니요로 답할 일이 확실하지 않을 때 써요. whether 뒤에는 완전한 문장. Note: It’s hard to tell whether a review is real.

Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). steps.title: The First Meeting · 3월 둘째 목요일 저녁, 동네 카페 안쪽 방에서

lines.en: Welcome, everyone! Tonight’s question is simple. Can we trust online reviews?
lines.ko: 여러분, 환영합니다! 오늘 질문은 간단해요. 온라인 리뷰, 믿을 수 있을까요?

lines.en: (quietly) Jiwoo, you read reviews before you buy anything, right?
lines.ko: (작은 목소리로) 지우 씨는 뭐 사기 전에 리뷰 읽죠?

lines.en: I do. But {{you can’t always trust}} them. Some reviews are fake.
lines.ko: 읽어요. 그런데 늘 믿을 수는 없어요. 가짜 리뷰도 있거든요.

lines.en: True. {{In my experience}}, angry customers write more reviews than happy ones.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 제 경험으로는 화난 손님이 만족한 손님보다 리뷰를 더 많이 써요.

lines.en: That’s why I read the bad reviews first. But a few bad reviews don’t mean much.

lines.en: And some five-star reviews are sponsored. {{It’s hard to tell whether}} the writer is giving an honest opinion or just promoting the product.

frame: You can’t always trust ___. / It’s hard to tell whether ___.
head: 대상
늘 믿을 순 없는 것 (You can’t always trust …)
알기 어려운 것 (It’s hard to tell whether …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: You can’t always trust ___. / It’s hard to tell whether ___. / In my experience, ___. Table (대상 → 늘 믿을 순 없는 것 (You can’t always trust …)):
- hotel photos → hotel photos.
- food blogs → free-meal blogs.
- star ratings → perfect ratings.
- online ads → ads that sound too good.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It’s hard to tell *whether* it’s real (or not). 진짜인지 아닌지 알기 어려워요. 
whether(= if)는 예·아니요 질문을 문장 안에 넣어요.

You can’t *always* trust ratings. 별점을 늘 믿진 못해요. 
*In my experience*, photos help. 제 경험상 사진이 도움돼요.
errors: It’s hard to tell whether is it real.
It’s hard to tell whether it’s real.
whether 뒤에는 보통 문장 순서(it is).
You can’t always trust to reviews.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- whether — 예일까, 아니요일까: It’s hard to tell whether it’s real (or not). 진짜인지 아닌지 알기 어려워요. / whether(= if)는 예·아니요 질문을 문장 안에 넣어요.
- can’t always · in my experience: You can’t always trust ratings. 별점을 늘 믿진 못해요. / In my experience, photos help. 제 경험상 사진이 도움돼요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s hard to tell whether is it real. → It’s hard to tell whether it’s real. (whether 뒤에는 보통 문장 순서(it is).)
- In my experiences, photos help. → In my experience, photos help. (이 표현에서 experience에는 -s를 붙이지 않아요.)
- You can’t always trust to reviews. → You can’t always trust reviews. (trust 뒤에 to를 쓰지 않아요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) a review with no photos / the buyer used it → A: You can’t always trust a review with no photos. B: True. It’s hard to tell whether …
items: a blog post on a new café
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) a review with no photos / the buyer used it → A: You can’t always trust a review with no photos. B: True. It’s hard to tell whether …. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: a review with no photos → the buyer used it | a perfect 5.0 rating → the reviews are real | a blog post on a new café → it’s sponsored | a hotel’s own photos → the room is that big.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Can you trust online reviews?" (온라인 리뷰); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "You can’t always trust ___." / "In my experience, ___." / "It’s hard to tell whether ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 의심스러운 점: "Some reviews are fake." (가짜 리뷰도 있어요., 보통); "Angry customers write more reviews." (화난 손님이 리뷰를 더 많이 써요., 보통); "A few bad reviews don’t mean much." (나쁜 리뷰 몇 개는 별 의미 없어요., 보통)
- 나만의 방법: "I only trust reviews with photos." (사진 있는 리뷰만 믿어요., 보통); "I read the bad reviews first." (나쁜 리뷰부터 읽어요., 보통); "I check several sites." (여러 사이트를 확인해요., 보통); "Look for patterns." (여러 사람이 되풀이하는 말을 찾아봐요., 보통)
- 균형 잡힌 생각: "It’s better than nothing." (없는 것보다는 나아요., 친근); "Take them with a grain of salt." (다 믿지 말고 걸러서 들어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: star (별), rating (평점, 별점), review (리뷰, 후기), comment (댓글, 의견), blog (블로그), advertisement (광고), buyer (구매자, 산 사람), customer (손님, 고객), fake (가짜의; 가짜), platform ((온라인) 플랫폼), pattern (패턴, 되풀이되는 모습), verify ((사실인지) 확인하다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The shop has a good reputation.
I’m not sure whether it’s true.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: bias (편견, 한쪽으로 치우침) — "Every writer has some bias."; sponsored (협찬받은, 후원받은) — "a sponsored post"; influence (영향을 주다; 영향) — "Ratings influence what we buy."; reputation (평판) — "The shop has a good reputation."; trust (믿다, 신뢰하다) — "I trust my friends’ advice."; reliable (믿을 만한) — "a reliable source"; opinion (의견) — "In my opinion, it’s fine."; honest (정직한, 솔직한) — "an honest review"; whether (~인지 아닌지) — "I’m not sure whether it’s true.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Do you read online reviews before you buy something?

What makes a review easy to trust?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Do you read online reviews before you buy something?" (hint on screen: Yes, always. / Not really. In my experience, ___.)
- "What makes a review easy to trust?" (hint on screen: I only trust reviews with ___. / I look for ___.)
- "Should we believe a perfect five-star rating?" (hint on screen: You can’t always trust ___. It’s hard to tell whether ___.)
- "Have you ever been fooled by a review or an ad?" (hint on screen: Yes. It said ___, but ___. / Not that I remember.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The First Debate
steps.text: Nine neighbors came to the first meeting. Daniel opened it. “*First of all*, there are no wrong answers here.” One neighbor said reviews save her time. Another said we *take for granted* that reviews are true and forget they can be wrong. Chloe trusts reviews only *to the extent* that they match each other. “One random comment means little,” she said, “but a pattern means a lot.” Some people dismiss all reviews as fake, but nobody in the room went that far. Most agreed that reviews are an adequate starting point, not the absolute truth. On the way home, Jiwoo said, “That was a lot to *take in*.” Chloe laughed. “Presumably, next time will be even longer!”
steps.gloss: first of all 우선, 무엇보다 먼저 · take for granted 당연하게 여기다 · to the extent that ~하는 정도까지만 · random 무작위의 · dismiss 무시하다, 일축하다 · take in 받아들이다, 이해하다
questions: How many neighbors came to the first meeting?
When does Chloe trust reviews?

steps.title: 선물 대신 현금
steps.title_en: It’s the thought that counts
steps.scene_desc: 3월 말 저녁, 아파트 1층 우편함 앞. 벤이 한 손에 빈 선물 상자, 다른 손에 흰 봉투를 들고 고민하는 얼굴이고, 퇴근한 지우가 가방을 멘 채 웃으며 의견을 말함(봉투·상자에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s the thought that counts" (선물 대신 현금). Goal: 실용과 마음 사이에서 의견 말하기. Today's scene: 3월 말 저녁, 아파트 1층 우편함 앞. 벤이 한 손에 빈 선물 상자, 다른 손에 흰 봉투를 들고 고민하는 얼굴이고, 퇴근한 지우가 가방을 멘 채 웃으며 의견을 말함(봉투·상자에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s the thought that counts.".

steps.when: 작고 소박한 선물도 특별하다고 말해요. 선물을 받고 고마움을 전할 때도 써요.
steps.extra: It’s just a card, but it’s the thought that counts.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It’s the thought that counts." (마음이 중요한 거죠.). When to use it: 작고 소박한 선물도 특별하다고 말해요. 선물을 받고 고마움을 전할 때도 써요. Note: It’s just a card, but it’s the thought that counts.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "From a practical point of view, ___.".

steps.en: From a practical point of view, ___.
steps.when: 기분보다 쓸모, 곧 현실적인 면에서 본 생각을 말해요.
steps.extra: From a practical point of view, cash is easier.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "From a practical point of view, ___." (실용적으로 보면 ~.). When to use it: 기분보다 쓸모, 곧 현실적인 면에서 본 생각을 말해요. Note: From a practical point of view, cash is easier.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’d rather ___ than ___.".

steps.when: 두 행동 중 더 좋은 쪽을 말해요. *rather*와 *than* 뒤에는 동사원형.
steps.extra: I’d rather choose a gift than send cash.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’d rather ___ than ___." ((~보다) 차라리 ~할래요.). When to use it: 두 행동 중 더 좋은 쪽을 말해요. rather와 than 뒤에는 동사원형. Note: I’d rather choose a gift than send cash.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Cash or a Gift? · 3월 말 저녁, 지우네 아파트 우편함 앞에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Cash or a Gift? · 3월 말 저녁, 지우네 아파트 우편함 앞에서

lines.en: Hey, Jiwoo. Can I ask you something? My nephew in Boston turns twelve next week.
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? 보스턴에 사는 조카가 다음 주에 열두 살이 돼요.

lines.en: Oh, nice! What are you getting him?
lines.ko: 와, 좋네요! 뭐 사 줄 거예요?

lines.en: That’s the problem. I can’t decide between cash and a real gift.
lines.ko: 그게 문제예요. 현금이냐 진짜 선물이냐 못 정하겠어요.

lines.en: Well, {{from a practical point of view}}, cash is more useful. He can buy what he wants.
lines.ko: 음, 실용적으로 보면 현금이 더 쓸모 있어요. 원하는 걸 살 수 있잖아요.

lines.en: True. But it can feel a bit cold. A gift shows you know the person.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그런데 좀 정 없게 느껴질 수 있어요. 선물은 그 사람을 잘 안다는 걸 보여 주잖아요.

lines.en: Then why not a gift card? Gift cards are a good compromise.
lines.ko: 그럼 기프트 카드는 어때요? 기프트 카드가 좋은 절충안이에요.

lines.en: Maybe. Last year I sent him a wooden puzzle with a little magic trick inside. He loved it.
lines.ko: 그럴까요. 작년엔 작은 마술 장치가 든 나무 퍼즐을 보냈는데, 아주 좋아했어요.

lines.en: See? {{It’s the thought that counts}}.
lines.ko: 봐요. 마음이 중요한 거죠.

lines.en: Exactly. Honestly, {{I’d rather}} spend an hour choosing something {{than}} just send money.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 솔직히 그냥 돈을 보내느니 한 시간 들여서 뭘 고르는 게 나아요.

lines.en: But what if he has a wish list?
lines.ko: 그런데 조카한테 갖고 싶은 것 목록이 있으면요?

lines.en: Then I’ll pretend I never saw it. Kidding! I’ll read it… very carefully.
lines.ko: 그럼 못 본 척할 거예요. 농담이에요! 읽을 거예요… 아주 꼼꼼히.

lines.en: (laughs) In Korea, cash gifts are common at weddings. But for a kid’s birthday, I’d pick something personal.
lines.ko: (웃으며) 한국에선 결혼식에 현금 선물이 흔해요. 그래도 아이 생일이면 그 아이에게 맞는 걸 고를래요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Cash or a Gift? · 3월 말 저녁, 지우네 아파트 우편함 앞에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Ben: "Hey, Jiwoo. Can I ask you something? My nephew in Boston turns twelve next week." (지우 씨, 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? 보스턴에 사는 조카가 다음 주에 열두 살이 돼요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Oh, nice! What are you getting him?" (와, 좋네요! 뭐 사 줄 거예요?)
3. Ben: "That’s the problem. I can’t decide between cash and a real gift." (그게 문제예요. 현금이냐 진짜 선물이냐 못 정하겠어요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Well, from a practical point of view, cash is more useful. He can buy what he wants." (음, 실용적으로 보면 현금이 더 쓸모 있어요. 원하는 걸 살 수 있잖아요.)
5. Ben: "True. But it can feel a bit cold. A gift shows you know the person." (맞아요. 그런데 좀 정 없게 느껴질 수 있어요. 선물은 그 사람을 잘 안다는 걸 보여 주잖아요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Then why not a gift card? Gift cards are a good compromise." (그럼 기프트 카드는 어때요? 기프트 카드가 좋은 절충안이에요.)
7. Ben: "Maybe. Last year I sent him a wooden puzzle with a little magic trick inside. He loved it." (그럴까요. 작년엔 작은 마술 장치가 든 나무 퍼즐을 보냈는데, 아주 좋아했어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "See? It’s the thought that counts." (봐요. 마음이 중요한 거죠.)
9. Ben: "Exactly. Honestly, I’d rather spend an hour choosing something than just send money." (바로 그거예요. 솔직히 그냥 돈을 보내느니 한 시간 들여서 뭘 고르는 게 나아요.)
10. Jiwoo: "But what if he has a wish list?" (그런데 조카한테 갖고 싶은 것 목록이 있으면요?)
11. Ben: "Then I’ll pretend I never saw it. Kidding! I’ll read it… very carefully." (그럼 못 본 척할 거예요. 농담이에요! 읽을 거예요… 아주 꼼꼼히.)
12. Jiwoo: "(laughs) In Korea, cash gifts are common at weddings. But for a kid’s birthday, I’d pick something personal." ((웃으며) 한국에선 결혼식에 현금 선물이 흔해요. 그래도 아이 생일이면 그 아이에게 맞는 걸 고를래요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Ben exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Ben (you): "Hey, Jiwoo. Can I ask you something? My nephew in Boston turns twelve next week." (지우 씨, 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? 보스턴에 사는 조카가 다음 주에 열두 살이 돼요.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Oh, nice! What are you getting him?" (와, 좋네요! 뭐 사 줄 거예요?)
3. Ben (you): "That’s the problem. I can’t decide between cash and a real gift." (그게 문제예요. 현금이냐 진짜 선물이냐 못 정하겠어요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Well, from a practical point of view, cash is more useful. He can buy what he wants." (음, 실용적으로 보면 현금이 더 쓸모 있어요. 원하는 걸 살 수 있잖아요.)
5. Ben (you): "True. But it can feel a bit cold. A gift shows you know the person." (맞아요. 그런데 좀 정 없게 느껴질 수 있어요. 선물은 그 사람을 잘 안다는 걸 보여 주잖아요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Then why not a gift card? Gift cards are a good compromise." (그럼 기프트 카드는 어때요? 기프트 카드가 좋은 절충안이에요.)
7. Ben (you): "Maybe. Last year I sent him a wooden puzzle with a little magic trick inside. He loved it." (그럴까요. 작년엔 작은 마술 장치가 든 나무 퍼즐을 보냈는데, 아주 좋아했어요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "See? It’s the thought that counts." (봐요. 마음이 중요한 거죠.)
9. Ben (you): "Exactly. Honestly, I’d rather spend an hour choosing something than just send money." (바로 그거예요. 솔직히 그냥 돈을 보내느니 한 시간 들여서 뭘 고르는 게 나아요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "But what if he has a wish list?" (그런데 조카한테 갖고 싶은 것 목록이 있으면요?)
11. Ben (you): "Then I’ll pretend I never saw it. Kidding! I’ll read it… very carefully." (그럼 못 본 척할 거예요. 농담이에요! 읽을 거예요… 아주 꼼꼼히.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "(laughs) In Korea, cash gifts are common at weddings. But for a kid’s birthday, I’d pick something personal." ((웃으며) 한국에선 결혼식에 현금 선물이 흔해요. 그래도 아이 생일이면 그 아이에게 맞는 걸 고를래요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Ben. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Last year, Ben sent his nephew cash.
Ben would rather choose a gift than just send money.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: From a practical point of view, ___.
It’s the thought that counts. — I’d rather ___ than ___.
head: 경우
실용적으로 보면 …
차라리 (I’d rather … than …)
rows: give cash than buy a vase.
buy a book than send money.
write a card than buy a mug.
bring food than bring a plant.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: From a practical point of view, ___. / It’s the thought that counts. — I’d rather ___ than ___. Table (경우 → 실용적으로 보면 …):
- a friend’s wedding → cash helps the couple.
- a child’s birthday → toys can be a waste.
- a teacher’s last class → a gift card is easy.
- a housewarming → plants need care.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It’s small, but *it’s the thought that counts*. 작지만 마음이 중요한 거죠. 
선물에 담긴 마음이 가장 중요하다는 뜻. counts = 중요하다(matters).

*I’d rather* choose a gift *than* send cash. 현금을 보내느니 차라리 선물을 고를래요. 
두 곳 모두 동사원형. I’d = I would. 짧게 사양할 때는 I’d rather not.
errors: I’d rather to choose a gift.
I’d rather 뒤에 to를 쓰지 않아요.
I’d rather choose a gift than sending cash.
I’d rather choose a gift than send cash.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- It’s the thought that counts.: It’s small, but it’s the thought that counts. 작지만 마음이 중요한 거죠. / 선물에 담긴 마음이 가장 중요하다는 뜻. counts = 중요하다(matters).
- I’d rather A than B: I’d rather choose a gift than send cash. 현금을 보내느니 차라리 선물을 고를래요. / 두 곳 모두 동사원형. I’d = I would. 짧게 사양할 때는 I’d rather not.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d rather to choose a gift. → I’d rather choose a gift. (I’d rather 뒤에 to를 쓰지 않아요.)
- I’d rather choose a gift than sending cash. → I’d rather choose a gift than send cash. (than 뒤에도 동사원형.)
- It’s the thought that count. → It’s the thought that counts. (주어 the thought가 단수라 counts.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: It’s the thought that counts.: It’s small, but it’s the thought that counts. 작지만 마음이 중요한 거죠. 선물에 담긴 마음이 가장 중요하다는 뜻. counts = 중요하다(matters).
I’d rather A than B: I’d rather choose a gift than send cash. 현금을 보내느니 차라리 선물을 고를래요. 두 곳 모두 동사원형. I’d = I would. 짧게 사양할 때는 I’d rather not.
mistakes: I’d rather to choose a gift. → I’d rather choose a gift.
I’d rather choose a gift than sending cash. → I’d rather choose a gift than send cash.
It’s the thought that count. → It’s the thought that counts.

steps.note: 예) choose a gift / send cash → A: Cash or a gift? B: I’d rather choose a gift than send cash. It’s the thought that counts.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) choose a gift / send cash → A: Cash or a gift? B: I’d rather choose a gift than send cash. It’s the thought that counts. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: choose a gift → send cash | make a card → buy a fancy one | give a gift card → wrap a present | give to charity → buy another mug.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: From a practical point of view, ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It’s the thought that counts" (선물 대신 현금); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s the thought that counts." / "From a practical point of view, ___." / "I’d rather ___ than ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: 머그잔을 또 받고 싶은 사람은 없어요.
Gift cards are a good compromise.
A gift shows you know the person.
선물은 그 사람을 잘 안다는 걸 보여 줘요.
It can feel a bit cold.
좀 정 없게 느껴질 수 있어요.
In Korea, cash gifts are common at weddings.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 실용적인 면: "Cash is more useful." (현금이 더 쓸모 있어요., 보통); "Nobody wants another mug." (머그잔을 또 받고 싶은 사람은 없어요., 친근); "Gift cards are a good compromise." (기프트 카드가 좋은 절충안이에요., 보통)
- 마음의 면: "A gift shows you know the person." (선물은 그 사람을 잘 안다는 걸 보여 줘요., 보통); "It can feel a bit cold." (좀 정 없게 느껴질 수 있어요., 보통); "Some people find it rude." (무례하다고 여기는 사람도 있어요., 보통)
- 경우에 따라 달라요: "In Korea, cash gifts are common at weddings." (한국에서는 결혼식에 현금 선물이 흔해요., 보통); "It depends on the occasion." (어떤 자리냐에 따라 달라요., 보통); "There’s no right or wrong." (정답은 없어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 돈에 관한 낱말

*wealthy* 부유한 · a *privilege* 특권, 특별한 기회 
*expenditure* 지출(격식) · a *deficit* 부족액, 적자 
a *margin* (만일에 대비한) 여유분 · *insure* 보험에 들다
선물 낱말 (참고)

*dedicate* a book *to* someone 책 첫머리에 이름을 적어 바치다 
*tender* 다정한, 부드러운 · a tender note 다정한 쪽지 
풍습은 집집마다 달라요. 정답은 없어요.
steps.blank:
A: Cash or a gift?   B: I’d ___ choose a gift ___ send cash. 
A: It’s just a small card.   B: Still, it’s the ___ that counts. 
A: From a practical point of ___, cash is easier. 
낱말 상자: rather · than · thought · view
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 돈에 관한 낱말: wealthy 부유한 · a privilege 특권, 특별한 기회 / expenditure 지출(격식) · a deficit 부족액, 적자 / a margin (만일에 대비한) 여유분 · insure 보험에 들다
- 선물 낱말 (참고): dedicate a book to someone 책 첫머리에 이름을 적어 바치다 / tender 다정한, 부드러운 · a tender note 다정한 쪽지 / 풍습은 집집마다 달라요. 정답은 없어요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Cash or a gift? B: I’d ___ choose a gift ___ send cash. / A: It’s just a small card. B: Still, it’s the ___ that counts. / A: From a practical point of ___, cash is easier. / 낱말 상자: rather · than · thought · view
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 빨간 봉투(음력 설에 돈을 넣어 줌)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: envelope (봉투), red envelope (빨간 봉투(음력 설에 돈을 넣어 줌)), gift card (기프트 카드, 상품권), wish list (갖고 싶은 것 목록), gift (선물), card (카드), wedding (결혼식), charity (자선 단체), rose (장미), stamp (우표), wooden (나무로 된), magic (마술).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: practical (실용적인) — "a practical gift"; thoughtful (사려 깊은, 배려하는) — "What a thoughtful gift!"; occasion ((특별한) 행사, 경우) — "It depends on the occasion."; useful (쓸모 있는, 유용한) — "Cash is useful."; personal (개인의, 그 사람에게 맞춘) — "a personal note"; rude (무례한) — "Some find cash rude."; value (가치) — "the value of a gift"; valuable (귀중한, 값진) — "a valuable lesson"; waste (낭비) — "It’s a waste of money."; compromise (절충안, 타협) — "a good compromise".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: For a friend’s birthday, would you give cash or a gift?
What’s a gift you think is often a waste?
Is a gift card a good compromise?
From a practical point of view, ___. / It depends on the occasion.
Tell me about a small gift that meant a lot.
Someone gave me ___. It wasn’t expensive, but it’s the thought that counts.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "For a friend’s birthday, would you give cash or a gift?" (hint on screen: I’d rather ___ than ___, because ___.)
- "What’s a gift you think is often a waste?" (hint on screen: Honestly, ___. Nobody wants another ___.)
- "Is a gift card a good compromise?" (hint on screen: From a practical point of view, ___. / It depends on the occasion.)
- "Tell me about a small gift that meant a lot." (hint on screen: Someone gave me ___. It wasn’t expensive, but it’s the thought that counts.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: For a friend’s birthday, would you give cash or a gift?

Tell me about a small gift that meant a lot.

steps.title: A Box Full of Meaning
steps.text: In the end, Ben made his choice. He filled a small wooden box with *quite a lot* of little things: a new magic trick, a bookmark with a pressed rose, and a postcard with Korean stamps. In money, it was worth *little more than* a gift card, but he spent an evening writing a tender note. Jiwoo still thinks cash is fine. “Every family has its own custom,” she said. “For some people, the meaning is in the envelope.” Then Thursday came, and Daniel brought it up at the debate group. Should gifts be *limited to* things on a wish list? Some neighbors said yes. Others didn’t *go along* with that. One neighbor said it’s also about tradition. They agreed on one thing: there’s no right or wrong.
steps.gloss: quite a lot 꽤 많이 · little more than ~ 정도에 불과한, 겨우 · tender 다정한 · custom 풍습, 관습 · limited to ~로 한정된 · go along with ~에 동의하다, 따르다
questions: What did Ben put in the wooden box?
What did the neighbors agree on?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A Box Full of Meaning". Text: "In the end, Ben made his choice. He filled a small wooden box with quite a lot of little things: a new magic trick, a bookmark with a pressed rose, and a postcard with Korean stamps. In money, it was worth little more than a gift card, but he spent an evening writing a tender note. Jiwoo still thinks cash is fine. “Every family has its own custom,” she said. “For some people, the meaning is in the envelope.” Then Thursday came, and Daniel brought it up at the debate group. Should gifts be limited to things on a wish list? Some neighbors said yes. Others didn’t go along with that. One neighbor said it’s also about tradition. They agreed on one thing: there’s no right or wrong." Words: quite a lot 꽤 많이 · little more than ~ 정도에 불과한, 겨우 · tender 다정한 · custom 풍습, 관습 · limited to ~로 한정된 · go along with ~에 동의하다, 따르다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Ben put in the wooden box?" / "What did the neighbors agree on?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘It’s the thought that counts.’로 선물은 마음이 중요하다고 말할 수 있어요.
‘From a practical point of view, ___.’로 실용적인 면을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’d rather ___ than ___.’로 두 가지 중 더 좋은 쪽을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘It’s the thought that counts.’로 선물은 마음이 중요하다고 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘From a practical point of view, ___.’로 실용적인 면을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’d rather ___ than ___.’로 두 가지 중 더 좋은 쪽을 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.goal: 생활 습관에 대한 통념에 맞서 의견 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 초 토요일 아침 7시 반, 한강 근처 작은 카페 창가. 새벽 촬영을 막 마친 클로이가 카메라 가방을 옆에 두고 따뜻한 차를 마시며 웃고, 아직 졸린 얼굴의 지우가 커피를 두 손으로 감싸 쥠. 창밖으로 옅은 아침 햇살과 강변 산책로(간판·컵에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s a myth that…" (아침형 인간). Goal: 생활 습관에 대한 통념에 맞서 의견 말하기. Today's scene: 4월 초 토요일 아침 7시 반, 한강 근처 작은 카페 창가. 새벽 촬영을 막 마친 클로이가 카메라 가방을 옆에 두고 따뜻한 차를 마시며 웃고, 아직 졸린 얼굴의 지우가 커피를 두 손으로 감싸 쥠. 창밖으로 옅은 아침 햇살과 강변 산책로(간판·컵에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s a myth that ___.".

steps.when: 많은 사람이 믿는 생각에 반론을 펴요. *that* 뒤에는 완전한 문장.
steps.extra: It’s a myth that night owls are lazy.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It’s a myth that ___." (~라는 건 근거 없는 통념이에요.). When to use it: 많은 사람이 믿는 생각에 반론을 펴요. that 뒤에는 완전한 문장. Note: It’s a myth that night owls are lazy.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "What works for one person might not work for another.".

steps.en: What works for one person might not work for another.
steps.ko: 한 사람에게 맞는 방법이 다른 사람에게는 안 맞을 수도 있어요.
steps.when: 사람마다 다르다는 걸 인정하며 토론을 부드럽게 마무리해요.

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Studies suggest that ___.".

steps.when: 연구에서 나온 일반적인 생각을 조심스럽게 전해요. suggest는 prove(증명하다)보다 약한 말.

steps.title: Early Bird, Night Owl · 4월 초 토요일 이른 아침, 강 근처 카페에서

lines.en: You made it! I’ve been up since four. The sunrise shoot by the river just finished.
lines.ko: 왔네요! 저는 4시부터 깨어 있었어요. 강가 해돋이 촬영이 방금 끝났어요.

lines.en: Since four? You must be a real morning person.
lines.ko: 4시부터요? 진짜 아침형 인간인가 봐요.

lines.en: Not at all. I’m a night owl. I’m most creative at night. Today was just for work.
lines.ko: 전혀요. 저는 올빼미형이에요. 밤에 아이디어가 제일 잘 나와요. 오늘은 그냥 일 때문이에요.

lines.en: Really? But everyone says early birds get more done.
lines.ko: 정말요? 그래도 다들 아침형 인간이 일을 더 많이 한다잖아요.

lines.en: Well, {{it’s a myth that}} everyone works best in the morning.
lines.ko: 글쎄요, 누구나 아침에 일이 제일 잘된다는 건 근거 없는 통념이에요.

lines.en: My old boss got up at five every day, and she was so productive.
lines.ko: 예전 상사는 매일 5시에 일어났는데, 일을 정말 많이 해냈어요.

lines.en: Good for her! But {{what works for one person might not work for another}}.
lines.ko: 그분한테는 잘된 일이죠! 그래도 한 사람에게 맞는 방법이 다른 사람에겐 안 맞을 수도 있어요.

lines.en: Fair point. I always thought I was just lazy in the morning.
lines.ko: 일리 있네요. 저는 늘 제가 그냥 아침에 게으른 줄 알았어요.

lines.en: You’re not lazy. {{Studies suggest that}} people’s sleep timing can differ. That’s just what I’ve read, though.
lines.ko: 게으른 게 아니에요. 연구에 따르면 사람마다 잠드는 시간대가 다를 수 있대요. 제가 읽은 것일 뿐이지만요.

lines.en: So I should just find my own rhythm?
lines.ko: 그럼 저한테 맞는 리듬을 찾으면 되는 거예요?

lines.en: Yes! You can train yourself a little, but it’s about getting enough sleep. And nice “rhythm”! Your “th” was perfect.
lines.ko: 네! 조금은 몸을 길들일 수 있지만, 핵심은 충분히 자는 거예요. 그리고 rhythm 좋았어요! th 소리가 완벽했어요.

9. Chloe: "You’re not lazy. Studies suggest that people’s sleep timing can differ. That’s just what I’ve read, though." (게으른 게 아니에요. 연구에 따르면 사람마다 잠드는 시간대가 다를 수 있대요. 제가 읽은 것일 뿐이지만요.)
10. Jiwoo: "So I should just find my own rhythm?" (그럼 저한테 맞는 리듬을 찾으면 되는 거예요?)
11. Chloe: "Yes! You can train yourself a little, but it’s about getting enough sleep. And nice “rhythm”! Your “th” was perfect." (네! 조금은 몸을 길들일 수 있지만, 핵심은 충분히 자는 거예요. 그리고 rhythm 좋았어요! th 소리가 완벽했어요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). frame: It’s a myth that ___. / Studies suggest that ___.
What works for one person might not work for another.
head: 흔한 믿음
근거 없는 통념 (It’s a myth that …)
연구에 따르면 (Studies suggest that …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It’s a myth that ___. / Studies suggest that ___. / What works for one person might not work for another. Table (흔한 믿음 → 근거 없는 통념 (It’s a myth that …)):
- Night owls are lazy. → night owls are lazy.
- Everyone needs 8 hours. → we all need the same.
- Morning people try harder. → it’s all about effort.
- Kids need less sleep. → kids need less sleep.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: It’s a myth that … — 잘못 알려진 생각

*It’s a myth that* night owls are lazy. 올빼미형이 게으르다는 건 근거 없는 통념이에요. 
많은 사람이 믿지만 사실이 아니라는 뜻.

*Studies suggest that* needs differ. 연구에 따르면 필요한 잠이 사람마다 다를 수 있대요. 
suggest = ~일 수 있다고 보여 주다(증명은 아님).
errors: It’s a myth that night owls lazy.
It’s a myth that night owls are lazy.
that 뒤 문장에 동사가 있어야 해요(are).
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- It’s a myth that … — 잘못 알려진 생각: It’s a myth that night owls are lazy. 올빼미형이 게으르다는 건 근거 없는 통념이에요. / 많은 사람이 믿지만 사실이 아니라는 뜻.
- Studies suggest that … — 조심스러운 근거: Studies suggest that needs differ. 연구에 따르면 필요한 잠이 사람마다 다를 수 있대요. / suggest = ~일 수 있다고 보여 주다(증명은 아님).
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s a myth that night owls lazy. → It’s a myth that night owls are lazy. (that 뒤 문장에 동사가 있어야 해요(are).)
- Studies suggest that sleep help. → Studies suggest that sleep helps. (여기서 sleep은 단수라 -s를 붙여요.)
- I’m creative in night. → I’m creative at night. (‘밤에’는 at night.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: It’s a myth that … — 잘못 알려진 생각: It’s a myth that night owls are lazy. 올빼미형이 게으르다는 건 근거 없는 통념이에요. 많은 사람이 믿지만 사실이 아니라는 뜻.
Studies suggest that … — 조심스러운 근거: Studies suggest that needs differ. 연구에 따르면 필요한 잠이 사람마다 다를 수 있대요. suggest = ~일 수 있다고 보여 주다(증명은 아님).

steps.note: 예) night owls are lazy / some people work better late → A: Night owls are lazy, right? B: It’s a myth that … Some people …
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) night owls are lazy / some people work better late → A: Night owls are lazy, right? B: It’s a myth that … Some people …. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: night owls are lazy → some people work better late | early birds are happier → it depends on the person | everyone needs eight hours → sleep needs are different | habits never change → you can train yourself.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: What works for one person might not work for another.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It’s a myth that…" (아침형 인간); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s a myth that ___." / "What works for one person might not work for another." / "Studies suggest that ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: 아침형 인간이 일을 더 많이 해요.
저는 밤에 아이디어가 제일 잘 나와요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 흔한 믿음: "Early birds get more done." (아침형 인간이 일을 더 많이 해요., 보통); "Society favors morning people." (사회는 아침형 인간에게 유리하게 돌아가요., 보통); "Schools start too early." (학교는 너무 일찍 시작해요., 보통); "It’s in your genes." (타고나는 거예요(유전이에요)., 친근)
- 나에 대해: "I’m a night owl." (저는 올빼미형이에요., 친근); "I’m most creative at night." (저는 밤에 아이디어가 제일 잘 나와요., 보통)
- 다정한 조언: "It’s about getting enough sleep." (중요한 건 충분히 자는 거예요., 보통); "You can train yourself." (조금씩 몸을 길들일 수 있어요., 보통); "Find your own rhythm." (나에게 맞는 리듬을 찾아요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 과학 낱말

a *hypothesis* 가설 · *theoretical* 이론적인

*nerve* 용기 · get up the nerve 용기를 내다 · *firmly* 단호하게 
*depress* (격식) 누르다 · depress a button 버튼을 누르다 
연구 — 아침형·저녁형에는 유전 요인도 있어요(Jones 외, 2019). 나이별 권장 수면 시간도 범위가 있어요(Hirshkowitz 외, 2015). 의학적 조언이 아니에요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 과학 낱말: a hypothesis 가설 · theoretical 이론적인 / experimental 실험적인, 시험 중인 / measurement 측정 · stimulate 자극하다, 활발하게 하다 / psychological 심리적인

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: It’s a ___ that night owls are lazy. B: Right. Studies ___ that needs differ. / A: What works for one person might not work for ___. B: So find your own ___. / 낱말 상자: myth · suggest · another · rhythm
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: owl (올빼미, 부엉이), bird (새), alarm (알람, 자명종), gene (유전자), schedule (일정, 시간표), laboratory (실험실), darkness (어둠), sleep (잠; 자다), energy (에너지, 활력), focus (집중), rhythm (리듬, 규칙적인 흐름), research (연구, 조사).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: myth (근거 없는 통념) — "It’s a myth."; study ((한 편의) 연구) — "a sleep study"; productive (생산적인, 일을 많이 해내는) — "a productive morning"; creative (창의적인) — "I’m creative at night."; scientific (과학적인) — "scientific evidence"; habit (습관) — "a good habit"; society (사회) — "Society favors morning people."; early bird (아침형 인간, 일찍 일어나는 사람) — "I’m not an early bird.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Are you a morning person or a night owl?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Are you a morning person or a night owl?" (hint on screen: I’m a ___. I’m most ___ in the ___.)
- "Some say early birds get more done. Do you agree?" (hint on screen: Partly. / It’s a myth that ___.)
- "Should schools or offices start later? Why?" (hint on screen: I think ___, because ___.)
- "What’s one habit that works for you but maybe not for others?" (hint on screen: ___ works for me. But what works for one person might not work for another.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Finding My Rhythm
steps.text: For years, Jiwoo set her alarm for 6 a.m. and felt tired all morning. *Given that* her best design ideas come after dinner, maybe the early alarm was the problem. She read a few articles, but she knew they were general ideas, not rules for her. Still, she decided to *act on* Chloe’s advice and give a new schedule *a go*: wake up at 7:30, do easy tasks in the morning, and save creative work for the evening. Two weeks later, she had more energy and better focus. Of course, many people love early mornings, and that’s fine too. “It’s not magic,” Jiwoo texted Chloe, “but it works for me.” Chloe sent back a sunrise photo and one line: “What works for one person …” Jiwoo smiled and typed the rest.
steps.gloss: given that ~라는 점을 생각하면 · act on ~에 따라 행동하다 · give it a go 한번 해 보다 · focus 집중 · energy 활력
questions: When do Jiwoo’s best design ideas come?
What time does Jiwoo wake up now?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Finding My Rhythm". Text: "For years, Jiwoo set her alarm for 6 a.m. and felt tired all morning. Two weeks later, she had more energy and better focus. Words: given that ~라는 점을 생각하면 · act on ~에 따라 행동하다 · give it a go 한번 해 보다 · focus 집중 · energy 활력.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "When do Jiwoo’s best design ideas come?" / "What time does Jiwoo wake up now?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye.
