steps.title: 혼자 하는 여행
steps.title_en: It’s not for everyone.
steps.goal: 혼자 하는 일의 좋고 나쁨을 경험과 함께 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당 창가 자리. 마야가 휴대폰 속 제주 바닷가 사진(글자 없이)을 신나게 보여 주고, 지우는 젓가락을 든 채 고개를 갸웃함. 마야 의자 옆에 작은 배낭이 놓여 있음(간판·글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s not for everyone." (혼자 하는 여행). Goal: 혼자 하는 일의 좋고 나쁨을 경험과 함께 말하기. Today's scene: 4월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당 창가 자리. 마야가 휴대폰 속 제주 바닷가 사진(글자 없이)을 신나게 보여 주고, 지우는 젓가락을 든 채 고개를 갸웃함. 마야 의자 옆에 작은 배낭이 놓여 있음(간판·글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "There’s something special about ___ on your own.".

steps.en: There’s something special about ___ on your own.
steps.ko: 혼자 ~하는 데는 뭔가 특별한 게 있어요.
steps.when: 혼자 하는 일의 좋은 점을 말해요. *about* 뒤에는 *-ing*.
steps.extra: There’s something special about traveling on your own.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "There’s something special about ___ on your own." (혼자 ~하는 데는 뭔가 특별한 게 있어요.). When to use it: 혼자 하는 일의 좋은 점을 말해요. about 뒤에는 -ing. Note: There’s something special about traveling on your own.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "The best part is ___.".

steps.when: 가장 큰 장점을 짚어요. 뒤에는 명사나 *(that) + 문장*.
steps.extra: The best part is the people you meet.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "The best part is ___." (제일 좋은 점은 ~예요.). When to use it: 가장 큰 장점을 짚어요. 뒤에는 명사나 (that) + 문장. Note: The best part is the people you meet.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s not for everyone.".

steps.when: 나와 다른 생각을 존중하며 말해요. ‘It’s bad.’보다 부드러워요.
steps.extra: Solo travel is great, but it’s not for everyone.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s not for everyone." (모든 사람에게 맞는 건 아니에요.). When to use it: 나와 다른 생각을 존중하며 말해요. ‘It’s bad.’보다 부드러워요. Note: Solo travel is great, but it’s not for everyone.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Trip for One · 4월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Trip for One · 4월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서

lines.en: I finally booked it. Five days in Jeju in May, all on my own.
lines.ko: 드디어 예약했어요. 5월에 제주에서 5일, 완전히 혼자서요.

lines.en: On your own? Won’t you feel lonely?
lines.ko: 혼자서요? 외롭지 않겠어요?

lines.en: Not really. {{There’s something special about}} traveling on your own. You can do whatever you want, like reading in the shade for hours.
lines.ko: 별로요. 혼자 여행하는 데는 뭔가 특별한 게 있어요. 그늘에서 몇 시간씩 책을 읽든, 하고 싶은 건 뭐든 할 수 있죠.

lines.en: I get the freedom part. But eating alone in a restaurant feels awkward to me.
lines.ko: 자유로운 건 알겠어요. 그래도 식당에서 혼자 먹는 건 저한텐 어색해요.

lines.en: That’s fair. But {{the best part is}} the people you meet. You end up talking to strangers.
lines.ko: 그럴 수 있죠. 그래도 제일 좋은 점은 만나는 사람들이에요. 어느새 낯선 사람들과 이야기하게 돼요.

lines.en: On my Busan work trip, I ate on my own every night. It got lonely at dinner.
lines.ko: 부산 출장 때 매일 밤 혼자 먹었어요. 저녁 먹을 때 외롭더라고요.

lines.en: True. Solo travel is great, but {{it’s not for everyone}}.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 혼자 여행은 좋지만 모든 사람에게 맞는 건 아니에요.

lines.en: Also, safety is a big concern for me.
lines.ko: 그리고 저는 안전이 크게 걱정돼요.

lines.en: Tell me more. What exactly worries you?
lines.ko: 더 얘기해 봐요. 정확히 뭐가 걱정돼요?

lines.en: Getting lost at night, I guess. Nobody would know where I was.
lines.ko: 밤에 길을 잃는 거요. 제가 어디 있는지 아무도 모를 테니까요.

lines.en: That’s why I text my plans to a friend every evening.
lines.ko: 그래서 저는 매일 저녁 친구한테 일정을 문자로 보내요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Trip for One · 4월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "I finally booked it. Five days in Jeju in May, all on my own." (드디어 예약했어요. 5월에 제주에서 5일, 완전히 혼자서요.)

frame: There’s something special about ___ on your own.
The best part is ___. But it’s not for everyone.
head: 혼자 하면 특별한 것
제일 좋은 점 (The best part is …)
하지만 (But …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: There’s something special about ___ on your own. / The best part is ___. But it’s not for everyone. Table (혼자 하면 특별한 것 → 제일 좋은 점 (The best part is …)):
- traveling on your own. → the freedom.
- eating out alone. → the quiet time.
- going to movies alone. → you pick the film.
- hiking on your own. → the peace.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I’m going to Jeju *on my own*. 제주에 혼자 가요. 
She traveled *on her own*. 그녀는 혼자 여행했어요. (my · your · her · their + own)
on my own = 남의 도움 없이

I planned it all *on my own*. 제가 혼자 다 계획했어요. 
Can you fix it *on your own*? 혼자 고칠 수 있어요?
errors: The best part are the people.
The best part is the people.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- on my own = 혼자서: I’m going to Jeju on my own. 제주에 혼자 가요. / She traveled on her own. 그녀는 혼자 여행했어요. (my · your · her · their + own)
- on my own = 남의 도움 없이: I planned it all on my own. 제가 혼자 다 계획했어요. / Can you fix it on your own? 혼자 고칠 수 있어요?
Common mistakes on screen:
- I traveled on myself. → I traveled on my own. (on my own이나 by myself로 말해요.)
- The best part are the people. → The best part is the people. (주어가 part(단수)라 is.)
- Safety is a big concerned. → Safety is a big concern. (여기에는 명사 concern(걱정)이 와야 해요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: on my own = 혼자서: I’m going to Jeju on my own. 제주에 혼자 가요. She traveled on her own. 그녀는 혼자 여행했어요. (my · your · her · their + own)
on my own = 남의 도움 없이: I planned it all on my own. 제가 혼자 다 계획했어요. Can you fix it on your own? 혼자 고칠 수 있어요?
mistakes: I traveled on myself. → I traveled on my own.
The best part are the people. → The best part is the people.
Safety is a big concerned. → Safety is a big concern.

steps.note: 예) traveling / the freedom → A: There’s something special about traveling on your own. B: Why? A: The best part is the freedom.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) traveling / the freedom → A: There’s something special about traveling on your own. B: Why? A: The best part is the freedom. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: traveling → the freedom | eating out → the quiet time | hiking → the peace | studying → the focus.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: There’s something special about ___ on your own.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It’s not for everyone." (혼자 하는 여행); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "There’s something special about ___ on your own." / "The best part is ___." / "It’s not for everyone.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: You can do whatever you want.
하고 싶은 건 뭐든 할 수 있어요.
It can get lonely at dinner.
저녁 먹을 때 외로울 수 있어요.
You end up talking to strangers.
I’d recommend it at least once.
적어도 한 번은 해 보길 권해요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 좋은 점: "You can do whatever you want." (하고 싶은 건 뭐든 할 수 있어요., 친근); "You get to know yourself." (나 자신을 알게 돼요., 보통); "It’s about freedom." (핵심은 자유예요., 친근); "It made me more confident." (덕분에 자신감이 생겼어요., 보통)
- 힘든 점: "It can get lonely at dinner." (저녁 먹을 때 외로울 수 있어요., 친근); "Safety is a big concern." (안전이 큰 걱정이에요., 보통); "Some people feel awkward." (어색해하는 사람도 있어요., 보통)
- 권하기: "You end up talking to strangers." (어느새 낯선 사람들과 이야기하게 돼요., 친근); "I’d recommend it at least once." (적어도 한 번은 해 보길 권해요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 혼자 여행 낱말

*venture* out 새로운 곳에 나서 보다 · take a *leap* 과감하게 해 보다

Share your plans with a friend. 친구에게 일정을 알려 둬요. · Keep copies of important papers. 중요한 서류는 사본을 챙겨요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 혼자 여행 낱말: a distant island 먼 섬 · wherever you like 원하는 곳 어디든 / venture out 새로운 곳에 나서 보다 · take a leap 과감하게 해 보다 / gaze at the sea 바다를 오래 바라보다 · glance at a map 지도를 힐끗 보다 / in a flash 순식간에 · in the shade 그늘에서

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: I’m going to Jeju ___ my own. B: Really? Won’t you feel lonely? / A: Not really. The best ___ is the freedom. B: Hmm, I think it’s not for ___. / 낱말 상자: on · part · everyone (everybody도 돼요)
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 호스텔(여럿이 방을 같이 쓰는 싼 숙소)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: solo (혼자 하는, 단독의), hostel (호스텔(여럿이 방을 같이 쓰는 싼 숙소)), backpack (배낭), journal (일기장), stranger (낯선 사람), explore (탐험하다, 둘러보다), adventure (모험), awkward (어색한, 불편한), safety (안전), confidence (자신감), freedom (자유), wanderlust (여행을 떠나고 싶은 마음, 방랑벽).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: A trip alone gives you time for reflection.
My budget for the trip is small.
I text my plans to a friend.
I’d recommend it at least once.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: independence (독립, 자립) — "Solo travel gives you independence."; reflection ((자신을) 돌아봄, 성찰) — "A trip alone gives you time for reflection."; individual (개인, 한 사람) — "Every individual travels differently."; alone (혼자) — "I ate alone every night."; concern (걱정, 우려) — "Safety is a big concern."; budget (예산) — "My budget for the trip is small."; plan (계획, 일정) — "I text my plans to a friend."; recommend (추천하다, 권하다) — "I’d recommend it at least once."; experience (경험) — "It was a great experience.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Would you like to travel on your own? Why or why not?
There’s something special about ___. / It’s not for me because ___.
What’s something you like doing on your own?
I like ___ on my own. The best part is ___.
What could be hard about a solo trip?
It can get lonely at dinner. / Safety is a big concern.
Ask me about something I do on my own.
Do you ever ___ on your own?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Would you like to travel on your own? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: There’s something special about ___. / It’s not for me because ___.)
- "What’s something you like doing on your own?" (hint on screen: I like ___ on my own. The best part is ___.)
- "What could be hard about a solo trip?" (hint on screen: It can get lonely at dinner. / Safety is a big concern.)

steps.title: Maya’s Old Journal
steps.text: Before her Jeju trip, Maya found her old travel journal. At twenty-five, she backpacked on her own for a month. “I was *something of a* nervous traveler,” she says. “I had never eaten alone, *let alone* traveled alone.” On day one, she booked a hostel through a *third party*, and the room looked nothing like the photos. But she sorted it out on her own, and that felt great. Her journal is full of tales about strangers who became friends and a lazy afternoon floating in the sea. “Solo travel isn’t a survival test,” she says. “It’s about freedom, and you get to know yourself. It made me more confident.” This time, she plans to write one page every night in Jeju.

steps.title: Two Ways to Travel · 5월 어느 오후, 그레이스네 집에서

lines.en: My parents are visiting Korea in the fall, and I’m planning their trip. Package tour or independent travel?
lines.ko: 가을에 부모님이 한국에 오셔서 제가 여행을 짜고 있어요. 패키지여행이 나을까요, 자유 여행이 나을까요?

lines.en: How did this trip come about?
lines.ko: 이번 여행은 어떻게 하게 된 거예요?

lines.en: My mom saw my photos and said, “We’re coming!” So far as I can tell, they just miss me.
lines.ko: 엄마가 제 사진을 보시더니 “우리 간다!” 하셨어요. 제가 보기엔 그냥 제가 보고 싶으신 것 같아요.

lines.en: You used to work in travel. Which is better?
lines.ko: 그레이스 씨는 예전에 여행 일을 했잖아요. 어느 쪽이 나아요?

lines.en: Well, {{whereas}} package tours save a lot of hassle, independent travel is more flexible.
lines.ko: 글쎄요, 패키지여행은 번거로운 일을 많이 덜어 주는 반면, 자유 여행은 더 융통성이 있어요.

lines.en: With a package, you don’t have to plan anything. That sounds nice for them.
lines.ko: 패키지면 아무것도 계획할 필요가 없잖아요. 부모님께는 그게 좋을 것 같은데요.

lines.en: True, but you’re stuck with the group. My dad hates early buses.
lines.ko: 맞아요, 그런데 단체에 꼼짝없이 묶여 있어야 해요. 아빠는 아침 일찍 버스 타는 걸 질색하세요.

lines.en: But it can be stressful to plan everything on your own.
lines.ko: 하지만 혼자서 다 계획하려면 스트레스받을 수 있어요.

lines.en: So, you mean they need a bit of both?
lines.ko: 그러니까 둘 다 조금씩 필요하다는 말이에요?

lines.en: Exactly. It’s convenience versus freedom.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 편리함이냐 자유냐의 문제죠.

lines.en: And {{it all comes down to}} what they enjoy. They love history and markets, and they hate rushing.
lines.ko: 그리고 결국 부모님이 뭘 즐기시느냐에 달렸어요. 역사랑 시장을 정말 좋아하시고, 서두르는 건 싫어하세요.

lines.en: Then for a first trip, {{I’d go for}} a short tour with lots of free time.
lines.ko: 그럼 첫 여행이니까, 저라면 자유 시간이 많은 짧은 투어로 하겠어요.

6. Jiwoo: "With a package, you don’t have to plan anything. That sounds nice for them." (패키지면 아무것도 계획할 필요가 없잖아요. 부모님께는 그게 좋을 것 같은데요.)
7. Grace: "True, but you’re stuck with the group. My dad hates early buses." (맞아요, 그런데 단체에 꼼짝없이 묶여 있어야 해요. 아빠는 아침 일찍 버스 타는 걸 질색하세요.)
8. Jiwoo: "But it can be stressful to plan everything on your own." (하지만 혼자서 다 계획하려면 스트레스받을 수 있어요.)
9. Grace: "So, you mean they need a bit of both?" (그러니까 둘 다 조금씩 필요하다는 말이에요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Exactly. It’s convenience versus freedom." (바로 그거예요. 편리함이냐 자유냐의 문제죠.)
11. Grace: "And it all comes down to what they enjoy. They love history and markets, and they hate rushing." (그리고 결국 부모님이 뭘 즐기시느냐에 달렸어요. 역사랑 시장을 정말 좋아하시고, 서두르는 건 싫어하세요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Then for a first trip, I’d go for a short tour with lots of free time." (그럼 첫 여행이니까, 저라면 자유 시간이 많은 짧은 투어로 하겠어요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

4. Jiwoo: "You used to work in travel. Which is better?" (그레이스 씨는 예전에 여행 일을 했잖아요. 어느 쪽이 나아요?)
5. Grace: "Well, whereas package tours save a lot of hassle, independent travel is more flexible." (글쎄요, 패키지여행은 번거로운 일을 많이 덜어 주는 반면, 자유 여행은 더 융통성이 있어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "With a package, you don’t have to plan anything. That sounds nice for them." (패키지면 아무것도 계획할 필요가 없잖아요. 부모님께는 그게 좋을 것 같은데요.)
7. Grace: "True, but you’re stuck with the group. My dad hates early buses." (맞아요, 그런데 단체에 꼼짝없이 묶여 있어야 해요. 아빠는 아침 일찍 버스 타는 걸 질색하세요.)
8. Jiwoo: "But it can be stressful to plan everything on your own." (하지만 혼자서 다 계획하려면 스트레스받을 수 있어요.)
9. Grace: "So, you mean they need a bit of both?" (그러니까 둘 다 조금씩 필요하다는 말이에요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Exactly. It’s convenience versus freedom." (바로 그거예요. 편리함이냐 자유냐의 문제죠.)
11. Grace: "And it all comes down to what they enjoy. They love history and markets, and they hate rushing." (그리고 결국 부모님이 뭘 즐기시느냐에 달렸어요. 역사랑 시장을 정말 좋아하시고, 서두르는 건 싫어하세요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Then for a first trip, I’d go for a short tour with lots of free time." (그럼 첫 여행이니까, 저라면 자유 시간이 많은 짧은 투어로 하겠어요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It all comes down to ___. I’d go for ___.
head: 한쪽 (Whereas …)
다른 쪽
고르기 (I’d go for …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Whereas ___, ___. / It all comes down to ___. I’d go for ___. Table (한쪽 (Whereas …) → 다른 쪽):
- package tours are easy → independent travel is flexible.
- hotels are comfortable → hostels are cheap.
- trains are relaxing → planes are fast.
- big cities are exciting → small towns are calm.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Whereas* tours are easy, independent travel is flexible. 투어는 편한 반면, 자유 여행은 융통성이 있어요. 
Tours are easy, *whereas* independent travel is flexible. whereas 부분이 뒤에 와도 돼요.

It’s easy, *while* the other is flexible. while도 ‘~인 반면’ 
*whilst* = while(영국식) · We travel *differently*. 우리는 여행 방식이 달라요.
errors: Whereas it’s easy, but it’s slow.
whereas 부분 뒤에 but을 또 쓰지 않아요.
It all comes down on the price.
It all comes down to the price.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Whereas A, B — ~인 반면: Whereas tours are easy, independent travel is flexible. 투어는 편한 반면, 자유 여행은 융통성이 있어요. / Tours are easy, whereas independent travel is flexible. whereas 부분이 뒤에 와도 돼요.
- 대조하는 다른 말: It’s easy, while the other is flexible. while도 ‘~인 반면’ / whilst = while(영국식) · We travel differently. 우리는 여행 방식이 달라요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Whereas it’s easy, but it’s slow. → Whereas it’s easy, it’s slow. (whereas 부분 뒤에 but을 또 쓰지 않아요.)
- It all comes down on the price. → It all comes down to the price. (comes down 뒤에는 to.)
- I’d go to a package. → I’d go for a package. (‘~를 고르다’는 go for.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) hotels / comfortable · hostels / cheap → Whereas hotels are comfortable, hostels are cheap.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) hotels / comfortable · hostels / cheap → Whereas hotels are comfortable, hostels are cheap. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: tours / easy → independent travel / flexible | hotels / comfortable → hostels / cheap | trains / relaxing → planes / fast | cities / exciting → towns / calm.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "It all comes down to this." (패키지 vs 자유 여행); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Whereas ___, ___." / "It all comes down to ___." / "I’d go for ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Package tours save a lot of hassle.
You don’t have to plan anything.
It can be stressful to plan everything.
It depends on where you’re going.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 패키지여행: "Package tours save a lot of hassle." (번거로운 일을 많이 덜어 줘요., 보통); "You don’t have to plan anything." (아무것도 계획할 필요가 없어요., 친근); "You’re stuck with the group." (단체에 꼼짝없이 묶여 있어요., 친근)
- 자유 여행: "Traveling independently is more flexible." (자유 여행이 더 융통성 있어요., 보통); "You meet more locals." (현지 사람들을 더 많이 만나요., 보통); "It can be stressful to plan everything." (다 계획하려면 스트레스받을 수 있어요., 보통)
- 고르기: "It depends on where you’re going." (어디 가느냐에 따라 달라요., 보통); "For a first trip, ___." (첫 여행이라면 ~., 보통); "Each has its own charm." (둘 다 나름의 매력이 있어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

Picture words on screen. New: tour guide (여행 가이드, 관광 안내원), itinerary (여행 일정(표)), backpacker (배낭여행자), destination (목적지, 여행지), group (단체, 무리), peak (절정, 한창(peak season 성수기)), free time (자유 시간), package (패키지여행(앞에서는 ‘포장 상자’)), tour (여행, 관광, 투어), local (현지 사람, 주민). Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

items: Package tours save a lot of hassle.
I love the freedom of a solo trip.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: guide (안내원, 가이드; 안내서) — "The guide knows every market."; hassle (번거로운 일, 귀찮은 일) — "Package tours save a lot of hassle."; independent (독립적인, 남에게 기대지 않는) — "Independent travel is more flexible."; convenience (편리함, 편의) — "It’s convenience versus freedom."; charm (매력) — "Each has its own charm."; flexible (융통성 있는, 바꾸기 쉬운) — "Independent travel is more flexible."; freedom (자유) — "I love the freedom of a solo trip."; adventure (모험) — "Backpacking is an adventure.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Package tour or independent travel? Which do you prefer?" (hint on screen: Whereas ___, ___. I’d go for ___.)
- "What’s the most important thing when you choose a trip?" (hint on screen: It all comes down to ___.)
- "What’s a good trip for a first visit to your country?" (hint on screen: For a first trip, I’d go for ___.)
- "Ask me about my travel style." (hint on screen: Do you prefer ___ or ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Grace’s Plan
steps.text: Grace compared two made-up tours. The first was a comprehensive ten-day package with a guide who is also a historian. Whereas it covers every famous place, the schedule starts at seven every morning. The second was a three-day trip to the eastern coast, followed by free time in Seoul. “In my old job, I learned to *allow for* rest days,” Grace says. “A busy plan can *come off* as a race.” Her parents don’t want a fancy hotel *or anything*. They just want good food, a few markets and time with their daughter. Consequently, Grace went for the short trip. “Each has its own charm,” she says. “But for my parents, it all comes down to comfort.”
steps.gloss: comprehensive 빠짐없는, 종합적인 · allow for ~을 감안해 두다 · come off as ~처럼 보이다 · or anything 뭐 그런 것 · consequently 그래서, 그 결과
questions: Why didn’t Grace choose the ten-day package?
What do her parents want on their trip?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Grace’s Plan". Text: "Grace compared two made-up tours. The first was a comprehensive ten-day package with a guide who is also a historian. They just want good food, a few markets and time with their daughter. Consequently, Grace went for the short trip. “Each has its own charm,” she says. “But for my parents, it all comes down to comfort.”" Words: comprehensive 빠짐없는, 종합적인 · allow for ~을 감안해 두다 · come off as ~처럼 보이다 · or anything 뭐 그런 것 · consequently 그래서, 그 결과.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why didn’t Grace choose the ten-day package?" / "What do her parents want on their trip?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 반려동물
steps.title_en: It’s a big responsibility.
steps.scene_desc: 5월 말 저녁, 동네 공원 산책길. 벤치에 앉은 벤과 지우가 잔디밭에서 꼬리를 흔드는 개를 바라보며 이야기함. 멀리 개를 산책시키는 이웃 몇 명(글자·간판 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s a big responsibility." (반려동물). Goal: 책임을 말하고 결론으로 잇기. Today's scene: 5월 말 저녁, 동네 공원 산책길. 벤치에 앉은 벤과 지우가 잔디밭에서 꼬리를 흔드는 개를 바라보며 이야기함. 멀리 개를 산책시키는 이웃 몇 명(글자·간판 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s a big responsibility to ___.".

steps.when: 가볍게 정할 수 없는 일을 말해요. 뒤에는 *to + 동사원형*.
steps.extra: It’s a big responsibility to adopt a dog.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It’s a big responsibility to ___." (~하는 건 큰 책임이에요.). When to use it: 가볍게 정할 수 없는 일을 말해요. 뒤에는 to + 동사원형. Note: It’s a big responsibility to adopt a dog.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Not everyone can ___.".

steps.when: 모든 사람에게 맞지는 않는다고 부드럽게 말해요.
steps.extra: Not everyone can walk a dog twice a day.
steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That’s why ___.".

steps.when: 앞에서 말한 이유에 결과나 결론을 이어요.
steps.extra: That’s why you have to think long-term.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That’s why ___." (그래서 ~예요.). When to use it: 앞에서 말한 이유에 결과나 결론을 이어요. Note: That’s why you have to think long-term.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Thinking About Adoption · 5월 말 저녁, 동네 공원에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Thinking About Adoption · 5월 말 저녁, 동네 공원에서

lines.en: See that dog wagging its tail? I’ve been thinking about adopting one from a shelter.
lines.ko: 저기 꼬리 흔드는 개 보여요? 보호소에서 한 마리 입양할까 생각 중이에요.

lines.en: Really? That’s a big step. Pets are like family.
lines.ko: 정말요? 큰 결심이네요. 반려동물은 가족 같잖아요.

lines.en: I know. {{It’s a big responsibility to}} look after another living creature.
lines.ko: 그러게요. 다른 생명을 돌보는 건 큰 책임이죠.

lines.en: And they need a lot of time. You teach until six.
lines.ko: 게다가 시간도 많이 들어요. 벤 씨는 여섯 시까지 수업하잖아요.

lines.en: True. Plus, vet bills can be expensive. {{Not everyone can}} handle that.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 동물 병원비도 비쌀 수 있고요. 누구나 감당할 수 있는 건 아니죠.

head: 책임 (It’s a big responsibility to …)
어려운 점 (Not everyone can …)
결론 (That’s why …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It’s a big responsibility to ___. / Not everyone can ___. That’s why ___. Table (책임 (It’s a big responsibility to …) → 어려운 점 (Not everyone can …)):
- adopt a dog. → walk it every day.
- raise a cat. → pay the vet bills.
- care for a pet. → stay home a lot.
- train a puppy. → be that patient.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*It’s* a big responsibility *to adopt* a dog. 개를 입양하는 건 큰 책임이에요. 
*It* takes time *to train* a puppy. 강아지를 훈련하려면 시간이 걸려요.

*To adopt* a dog is a big responsibility. 
보통은 *It*으로 시작해요.
errors: It’s hard to train a dog.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- It + be + 명사·형용사 + to 동사: It’s a big responsibility to adopt a dog. 개를 입양하는 건 큰 책임이에요. / It takes time to train a puppy. 강아지를 훈련하려면 시간이 걸려요.
- 뜻은 같지만 덜 쓰는 꼴: To adopt a dog is a big responsibility. / 보통은 It으로 시작해요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s hard train a dog. → It’s hard to train a dog. (동사 앞에 to를 넣어요.)
- Not everyone can affords it. → Not everyone can afford it. (can 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- It’s a big responsible. → It’s a big responsibility. (a big 뒤에는 명사 responsibility.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: It + be + 명사·형용사 + to 동사: It’s a big responsibility to adopt a dog. 개를 입양하는 건 큰 책임이에요. It takes time to train a puppy. 강아지를 훈련하려면 시간이 걸려요.
뜻은 같지만 덜 쓰는 꼴: To adopt a dog is a big responsibility. 보통은 It으로 시작해요.

Not everyone can affords it. → Not everyone can afford it.
It’s a big responsible. → It’s a big responsibility.

steps.note: 예) adopt a dog / walk it twice a day → It’s a big responsibility to adopt a dog. Not everyone can walk it twice a day.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) adopt a dog / walk it twice a day → It’s a big responsibility to adopt a dog. Not everyone can walk it twice a day. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: adopt a dog → walk it twice a day | raise a cat → pay the vet bills | train a puppy → be patient every day | keep a pet rat → clean its cage often.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "It’s a big responsibility." (반려동물); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s a big responsibility to ___." / "Not everyone can ___." / "That’s why ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

- 반려동물이 좋은 이유: "Pets are like family." (반려동물은 가족 같아요., 친근); "A pet can be good company when you live alone." (혼자 살면 반려동물이 좋은 벗이 돼요., 보통); "It changes your life." (삶이 달라져요., 친근)
- 어려운 점: "They need a lot of time." (시간이 많이 들어요., 보통); "Vet bills can be expensive." (동물 병원비가 비쌀 수 있어요., 보통); "Small apartments aren’t ideal for big dogs." (작은 아파트는 큰 개에게 알맞지 않아요., 보통)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:

steps.title: Pets Night at the Café
steps.text: At Thursday’s meeting, Daniel asked, “Should everyone have a pet?” A neighbor who volunteers at a shelter spoke first. “Some animals come to us because people got them on impulse,” she said. “Adopt, don’t shop.” Another neighbor said pets bring joy, and for people who live alone, they’re good company. *With respect to* money, most people agreed: food, vet bills, training, *things like that* add up fast. One man added that every species has its own needs. Ben listened carefully and asked about older dogs. In the end, Daniel said, “We all agree on one thing: a pet is a long-term commitment.” Walking home, Ben told Jiwoo, “I’m not ready yet. I’ll think about it some more.”
steps.gloss: with respect to ~에 관해서는 · things like that 그런 것들 · add up (조금씩) 불어나다 · commitment (오래 책임지겠다는) 약속
questions: What did the shelter volunteer say?
What did Ben decide after the meeting?

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "I could see myself living there." (시골에서 노후). Goal: 조건을 달아 내 모습을 그려 보기. Today's scene: 6월 목요일 밤, 토론 모임이 끝난 뒤 동네 카페에서 아파트로 걸어가는 골목길. 가로등 아래 그레이스와 지우가 나란히 걸으며 이야기하고, 그레이스가 손으로 먼 곳을 가리킴. 조용한 밤거리(간판·글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "The thing is, ___.".

steps.when: 진짜 문제나 핵심을 꺼낼 때 써요.
steps.extra: The thing is, hospitals are too far away.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "The thing is, ___." (문제는 ~예요. 실은 ~거든요.). When to use it: 진짜 문제나 핵심을 꺼낼 때 써요. Note: The thing is, hospitals are too far away.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "As long as ___, ___.".

steps.when: 조건을 달아요. 앞날 일이라도 as long as 뒤에는 *현재형*.
steps.extra: As long as there’s a clinic nearby, I’d be fine.

steps.when: 앞으로의 내 모습을 상상해요. 뒤에는 *-ing*.

steps.title: The Walk Home · 6월 토론 모임이 끝나고, 조용한 골목에서

lines.en: That was a fun debate. So, would you ever retire to the countryside?
lines.ko: 재미있는 토론이었어요. 그럼 지우 씨는 은퇴하면 시골에 가서 살 생각 있어요?

lines.en: Maybe. The air is cleaner, and it’s so peaceful.
lines.ko: 어쩌면요. 공기도 더 깨끗하고 정말 평화롭잖아요.

lines.en: {{The thing is}}, hospitals are too far away. That matters more as we get older.
lines.ko: 문제는 병원이 너무 멀다는 거예요. 나이가 들수록 그게 더 중요해지잖아요.

lines.en: True. And you’d need a car. I don’t even drive!
lines.ko: 맞아요. 차도 있어야 하고요. 저는 운전도 안 하는걸요!

lines.en: Me neither! And it might get lonely.
lines.ko: 저도요! 그리고 외로울 수도 있어요.

lines.en: {{As long as}} there’s a clinic and a grocery store nearby, I’d be fine.
lines.ko: 근처에 의원이랑 식료품 가게만 있으면 저는 괜찮을 거예요.

lines.en: So, you mean a small town, not a farm in the middle of nowhere?
lines.ko: 그러니까 외딴 곳의 농장이 아니라 작은 읍내 같은 데요?

lines.en: Exactly. {{I could see myself}} growing vegetables in a little garden.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 작은 텃밭에서 채소를 기르는 제 모습이 그려져요.

lines.en: Not me. I’d miss the city. Cafés, concerts, people!
lines.ko: 저는 아니에요. 도시가 그리울 거예요. 카페, 공연, 사람들!

lines.en: But housing is much cheaper out there.
lines.ko: 그래도 거기는 집값이 훨씬 싸잖아요.

lines.en: Fair enough. Maybe somewhere in between? A quiet town an hour from Seoul?
lines.ko: 그건 그래요. 그 중간 어디쯤은 어때요? 서울에서 한 시간 거리의 조용한 동네요?

lines.en: Perfect. Let’s keep talking about it for the next thirty years!
lines.ko: 완벽해요. 앞으로 삼십 년 동안 계속 얘기해 봐요!

9. Grace: "Not me. I’d miss the city. Cafés, concerts, people!" (저는 아니에요. 도시가 그리울 거예요. 카페, 공연, 사람들!)
10. Jiwoo: "But housing is much cheaper out there." (그래도 거기는 집값이 훨씬 싸잖아요.)
11. Grace: "Fair enough. Maybe somewhere in between? A quiet town an hour from Seoul?" (그건 그래요. 그 중간 어디쯤은 어때요? 서울에서 한 시간 거리의 조용한 동네요?)
12. Jiwoo: "Perfect. Let’s keep talking about it for the next thirty years!" (완벽해요. 앞으로 삼십 년 동안 계속 얘기해 봐요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

1. Grace: "That was a fun debate. So, would you ever retire to the countryside?" (재미있는 토론이었어요. 그럼 지우 씨는 은퇴하면 시골에 가서 살 생각 있어요?)

3. Grace: "The thing is, hospitals are too far away. That matters more as we get older." (문제는 병원이 너무 멀다는 거예요. 나이가 들수록 그게 더 중요해지잖아요.)
4. Jiwoo: "True. And you’d need a car. I don’t even drive!" (맞아요. 차도 있어야 하고요. 저는 운전도 안 하는걸요!)
5. Grace: "Me neither! And it might get lonely." (저도요! 그리고 외로울 수도 있어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "As long as there’s a clinic and a grocery store nearby, I’d be fine." (근처에 의원이랑 식료품 가게만 있으면 저는 괜찮을 거예요.)
7. Grace: "So, you mean a small town, not a farm in the middle of nowhere?" (그러니까 외딴 곳의 농장이 아니라 작은 읍내 같은 데요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Exactly. I could see myself growing vegetables in a little garden." (바로 그거예요. 작은 텃밭에서 채소를 기르는 제 모습이 그려져요.)
9. Grace: "Not me. I’d miss the city. Cafés, concerts, people!" (저는 아니에요. 도시가 그리울 거예요. 카페, 공연, 사람들!)
10. Jiwoo: "But housing is much cheaper out there." (그래도 거기는 집값이 훨씬 싸잖아요.)
11. Grace: "Fair enough. Maybe somewhere in between? A quiet town an hour from Seoul?" (그건 그래요. 그 중간 어디쯤은 어때요? 서울에서 한 시간 거리의 조용한 동네요?)
12. Jiwoo: "Perfect. Let’s keep talking about it for the next thirty years!" (완벽해요. 앞으로 삼십 년 동안 계속 얘기해 봐요!)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: As long as ___, I could see myself ___ing.
head: 조건 (As long as …)
내 모습 (I could see myself …)
문제 (The thing is, …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: The thing is, ___. / As long as ___, I could see myself ___ing. Table (조건 (As long as …) → 내 모습 (I could see myself …)):
- there’s a bus, → living in the country.
- I have Wi-Fi, → working from a farm.
- my friends visit, → living by the sea.
- there’s a clinic, → retiring to a village.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*As long as* there’s a bus, I can live anywhere. 버스만 있으면 어디서든 살 수 있어요. 
I’d be fine, *as long as* there’s a clinic. 조건이 뒤에 와도 돼요.

I could *see myself growing* vegetables. 채소 기르는 제 모습이 그려져요. 
I can’t *see myself living* on a farm. 농장에서 사는 건 상상이 안 돼요.
errors: As long as there will be a bus, I’ll go.
As long as there’s a bus, I’ll go.
as long as 뒤에는 앞날 일도 현재형.
I could see myself grow vegetables.
I could see myself growing vegetables.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- As long as + 현재형: As long as there’s a bus, I can live anywhere. 버스만 있으면 어디서든 살 수 있어요. / I’d be fine, as long as there’s a clinic. 조건이 뒤에 와도 돼요.
- see myself + -ing: I could see myself growing vegetables. 채소 기르는 제 모습이 그려져요. / I can’t see myself living on a farm. 농장에서 사는 건 상상이 안 돼요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- As long as there will be a bus, I’ll go. → As long as there’s a bus, I’ll go. (as long as 뒤에는 앞날 일도 현재형.)
- I could see myself grow vegetables. → I could see myself growing vegetables. (see myself 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I’d miss city. → I’d miss the city. (the city, the countryside처럼 the를 붙여요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: As long as + 현재형: As long as there’s a bus, I can live anywhere. 버스만 있으면 어디서든 살 수 있어요. I’d be fine, as long as there’s a clinic. 조건이 뒤에 와도 돼요.
see myself + -ing: I could see myself growing vegetables. 채소 기르는 제 모습이 그려져요. I can’t see myself living on a farm. 농장에서 사는 건 상상이 안 돼요.
mistakes: As long as there will be a bus, I’ll go. → As long as there’s a bus, I’ll go.
I could see myself grow vegetables. → I could see myself growing vegetables.
I’d miss city. → I’d miss the city.

steps.note: 예) there’s a bus / living in the country → As long as there’s a bus, I could see myself living in the country.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) there’s a bus / living in the country → As long as there’s a bus, I could see myself living in the country. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: there’s a bus → living in the country | I have Wi-Fi → working from a farm | my friends visit → living by the sea | there’s a clinic → retiring to a village.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "I could see myself living there." (시골에서 노후); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "The thing is, ___." / "As long as ___, ___." / "I could see myself ___ing.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’d like to grow my own food.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 좋은 점: "The air is cleaner." (공기가 더 깨끗해요., 친근); "It’s so peaceful." (정말 평화로워요., 친근); "Housing is much cheaper." (집값이 훨씬 싸요., 보통); "I’d like to grow my own food." (먹을거리를 직접 길러 보고 싶어요., 보통)
- 힘든 점: "Hospitals are too far away." (병원이 너무 멀어요., 보통); "You’d need a car." (차가 있어야 할 거예요., 친근); "It might get lonely." (외로울 수도 있어요., 친근); "I’d miss the city." (도시가 그리울 거예요., 친근)
- 중간 찾기: "Maybe somewhere in between." (그 중간 어디쯤이 좋겠어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 조용한 삶 낱말

walk *quietly* 조용히 걷다 
*bury* seeds 씨앗을 땅에 묻다 
The noise *fades*. 소리가 점점 사라져요. 
a *veteran* farmer 경험 많은 농부 
a fishing *vessel* 고깃배, 어선
(참고) 앞날 이야기

I can’t live there *forever*. 거기서 영원히 살 수는 없어요. 
a *wise* choice 현명한 선택 
의견을 나누는 연습이에요. 돈·건강 조언이 아니에요.
steps.blank:
A: Would you live in the countryside?   B: The ___ is, I can’t drive. 
A: But as ___ as there’s a bus, you’d be fine.   B: True. I could see myself ___ there. 
낱말 상자: thing · long · living
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 조용한 삶 낱말: walk quietly 조용히 걷다 / bury seeds 씨앗을 땅에 묻다 / The noise fades. 소리가 점점 사라져요. / a veteran farmer 경험 많은 농부 / a fishing vessel 고깃배, 어선
- (참고) 앞날 이야기: I can’t live there forever. 거기서 영원히 살 수는 없어요. / a wise choice 현명한 선택 / 의견을 나누는 연습이에요. 돈·건강 조언이 아니에요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Would you live in the countryside? B: The ___ is, I can’t drive. / A: But as ___ as there’s a bus, you’d be fine. B: True. I could see myself ___ there. / 낱말 상자: thing · long · living
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: farm (농장), grocery store (식료품 가게), clinic (의원, 작은 병원), retiree (은퇴한 사람), countryside (시골, 전원), hospital ((큰) 병원), garden (정원, 텃밭), housing (주택, 집), nature (자연), transport (교통(수단)), rural (시골의, 농촌의), urban (도시의).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The village has a warm community.
Isolation can be hard for retirees.
She wants a quiet life by the sea.
Where would you spend your retirement?
I love the convenience of city life.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: peaceful (평화로운, 조용한) — "It’s so peaceful here."; community ((한 지역의) 공동체, 주민) — "The village has a warm community."; isolation (고립, 외따로 떨어짐) — "Isolation can be hard for retirees."; quiet life (조용한 삶) — "She wants a quiet life by the sea."; retire (은퇴하다) — "My uncle retired at sixty."; retirement (은퇴, 은퇴 후의 시기) — "Where would you spend your retirement?"; convenience (편리함, 편의) — "I love the convenience of city life."; aging (나이 듦, 노화) — "Aging changes what we need.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Could you see yourself living in the countryside? Why or why not?
I could see myself ___ing. / The thing is, ___.
What would you need to live happily in a small town?
As long as ___, I’d be fine.
City life or country life? Which suits you better?
The thing is, ___. Maybe somewhere in between.
Ask me about my dream place to live.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Could you see yourself living in the countryside? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: I could see myself ___ing. / The thing is, ___.)
- "What would you need to live happily in a small town?" (hint on screen: As long as ___, I’d be fine.)
- "City life or country life? Which suits you better?" (hint on screen: The thing is, ___. Maybe somewhere in between.)
- "Ask me about my dream place to live." (hint on screen: Could you see yourself ___ing?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Tonight’s Debate
steps.text: At tonight’s meeting, the topic was rural life. A neighbor shared her parents’ story. *Long ago*, they moved to a small farm village to *get away* from the busy city. “*Contrary to* what people think, it wasn’t silent,” she said. “Birds, frogs, tractors. Never quiet!” Her parents grew vegetables and gave piles of them to their neighbors. But the village slowly changed. Young people left, and the bus came less often. Isolation became a real worry. Daniel asked, “Is rural life better for retirees?” Some said yes, as long as there’s good transport and a strong community. Others said they couldn’t leave the city forever. Grace whispered to Jiwoo, “Maybe the wise answer is: it depends.”
steps.gloss: long ago 오래전에 · get away (쉬러) 떠나다, 벗어나다 · contrary to ~와 달리 · silent 아무 소리 없는 · pile 더미 · whisper 속삭이다
questions: Why did the neighbor’s parents move to the village?
What became a real worry in the village?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Tonight’s Debate". Text: "At tonight’s meeting, the topic was rural life. A neighbor shared her parents’ story. Long ago, they moved to a small farm village to get away from the busy city. “Contrary to what people think, it wasn’t silent,” she said. “Birds, frogs, tractors. Never quiet!” Her parents grew vegetables and gave piles of them to their neighbors. But the village slowly changed. Young people left, and the bus came less often. Isolation became a real worry. Daniel asked, “Is rural life better for retirees?” Some said yes, as long as there’s good transport and a strong community. Others said they couldn’t leave the city forever. Grace whispered to Jiwoo, “Maybe the wise answer is: it depends.”" Words: long ago 오래전에 · get away (쉬러) 떠나다, 벗어나다 · contrary to ~와 달리 · silent 아무 소리 없는 · pile 더미 · whisper 속삭이다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why did the neighbor’s parents move to the village?" / "What became a real worry in the village?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘The thing is, ___.’로 핵심 문제를 짚을 수 있어요.
‘As long as ___, ___.’로 조건을 달아 말할 수 있어요.
‘I could see myself ___ing.’로 앞으로의 내 모습을 그려 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘The thing is, ___.’로 핵심 문제를 짚을 수 있어요.
- ‘As long as ___, ___.’로 조건을 달아 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I could see myself ___ing.’로 앞으로의 내 모습을 그려 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 재택근무
steps.title_en: Personally, I prefer working from home.
steps.scene_desc: 6월 말 토요일 오후, 클로이 집 근처 작은 카페 창가 자리. 클로이가 노트북을 옆에 덮어 두고 아이스커피를 든 채 신나게 이야기하고, 지우가 조금 지친 얼굴로 턱을 괴고 듣고 있음. 창밖은 초여름 햇빛이 비치는 골목(간판·화면에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Personally, I prefer working from home." (재택근무). Goal: 선호를 말하고 양보하며 반박하기. Today's scene: 6월 말 토요일 오후, 클로이 집 근처 작은 카페 창가 자리. 클로이가 노트북을 옆에 덮어 두고 아이스커피를 든 채 신나게 이야기하고, 지우가 조금 지친 얼굴로 턱을 괴고 듣고 있음. 창밖은 초여름 햇빛이 비치는 골목(간판·화면에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Personally, I prefer ___.".

steps.when: 내 선택을 말해요. *Personally*를 붙이면 ‘제 생각일 뿐’이라는 느낌이에요.
steps.extra: Personally, I prefer working from home.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Personally, I prefer ___." (저는 개인적으로 ~가 더 좋아요.). When to use it: 내 선택을 말해요. Personally를 붙이면 ‘제 생각일 뿐’이라는 느낌이에요. Note: Personally, I prefer working from home.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Even though ___, ___.".

steps.when: 한 가지 사실은 인정하고, 그래도 다른 결과나 의견을 말해요.
steps.extra: Even though my commute is long, I like the office.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Even though ___, ___." (~이긴 하지만, ~.). When to use it: 한 가지 사실은 인정하고, 그래도 다른 결과나 의견을 말해요. Note: Even though my commute is long, I like the office.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That’s a fair point.".

steps.when: 생각이 달라도 상대의 좋은 지적은 인정해요.
steps.extra: That’s a fair point. Even so, I need my team around me.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That’s a fair point." (일리 있는 말이에요.). When to use it: 생각이 달라도 상대의 좋은 지적은 인정해요. Note: That’s a fair point. Even so, I need my team around me.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Home or Office? · 6월 말, 클로이 집 근처 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Home or Office? · 6월 말, 클로이 집 근처 카페에서

lines.en: You look tired. Long week?

lines.en: The subway had delays all week. It took over an hour each way instead of the usual thirty minutes. Even so, I still like going to the office.

lines.en: Really? {{Personally, I prefer}} working from home. It saves so much commuting time, and it’s easier to focus at home.

lines.en: {{Even though}} my commute is long, I like seeing my team. Collaboration is easier in person, and I learn a lot just by listening.

frame: Even though ___, ___. / That’s a fair point, but ___.
head: 인정 (Even though …,)
그래도 (I still prefer …)
대답
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Personally, I prefer ___. / Even though ___, ___. / That’s a fair point, but ___. Table (인정 (Even though …,) → 그래도 (I still prefer …)):
- my commute is long, → working at the office.
- it can get lonely, → working from home.
- the office is noisy, → meeting in person.
- home is more flexible, → a mix of both.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Even though* my commute is long, I like the office. 출퇴근길이 길긴 하지만 회사가 좋아요. 
뒤에 와도 돼요. I like the office *even though* my commute is long.

*Even though* + 주어 + 동사 → 두 생각을 한 문장으로 이어요. 
My commute is long. *Even so*, I like the office. (새 문장을 시작해요) 
despite + 명사도 돼요. despite the long commute
errors: Even though it’s far, but I go.
Even though it’s far, I go.
even though 부분 뒤에 *but*을 또 쓰지 않아요.
Even though it’s far, I go.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- even though — 사실 인정하기: Even though my commute is long, I like the office. 출퇴근길이 길긴 하지만 회사가 좋아요. / 뒤에 와도 돼요. I like the office even though my commute is long.
- even though와 even so: Even though + 주어 + 동사 → 두 생각을 한 문장으로 이어요. / My commute is long. Even so, I like the office. (새 문장을 시작해요) / despite + 명사도 돼요. despite the long commute
Common mistakes on screen:
- Even though it’s far, but I go. → Even though it’s far, I go. (even though 부분 뒤에 but을 또 쓰지 않아요.)
- Even it’s far, I go. → Even though it’s far, I go. (주어 + 동사 앞에는 even though.)
- I prefer work from home. → I prefer working from home. (prefer 뒤에는 -ing(또는 to + 동사원형).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

mistakes: Even though it’s far, but I go. → Even though it’s far, I go.
Even it’s far, I go. → Even though it’s far, I go.
I prefer work from home. → I prefer working from home.

items: I’d go for a mix of both
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) → Even though it can get lonely, I prefer working from home. — That’s a fair point. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: it can get lonely → I prefer working from home | my commute is long → I like the office | the café is noisy → I can focus there | home is comfortable → I’d go for a mix of both.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Personally, I prefer working from home." (재택근무); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Personally, I prefer ___." / "Even though ___, ___." / "That’s a fair point.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:

- 힘든 점: "It can get lonely." (외로울 수 있어요., 보통); "It’s hard to switch off." (일에서 마음을 끄기가 어려워요., 친근); "The line between work and home gets blurry." (일과 집의 경계가 흐려져요., 보통)

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Where do you prefer to work or study? Why?" (hint on screen: Personally, I prefer ___ because ___.)
- "Give one downside, but keep your opinion." (hint on screen: Even though ___, I still ___.)
- "Your friend says, “Working from home is lonely.” Answer politely." (hint on screen: That’s a fair point, but ___.)
- "What helps you concentrate?" (hint on screen: I can concentrate better when ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s Notes
steps.text: That night, Jiwoo wrote down her thoughts. Chloe’s team works alongside people in three cities, and her team lead is *on the road* most weeks. *Even so*, they finish their projects successfully. Their tools are functional: one shared calendar, one file format, and prompt replies in the team chat. For Jiwoo, remote work has one big constraint: it’s hard to read faces on a screen, and continuous online meetings hurt her concentration. She enjoys *the odd* coffee break with coworkers, too, because it strengthens mutual trust. This summer, the personnel team at her company is asking about new ways to work. Jiwoo’s answer is clear: a mix of both.
steps.gloss: on the road 출장 중인 · even so 그래도 · alongside ~와 함께 · functional 실용적인, 제 기능을 하는 · prompt 즉각적인 · constraint 제약 · continuous 끊임없는 · the odd 가끔 있는 · personnel team 인사팀

steps.scene_desc: 7월 오후, 회사 작은 회의실. 마야가 화이트보드 앞에서 펜을 들고 서 있고, 지우가 노트북을 앞에 두고 앉아 웃으며 손가락 네 개를 펴 보임. 화이트보드에는 네모 칸 네 개와 빈 칸 하나만 그려져 있음(글자·숫자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It would be great if we had Fridays off." (주 4일 근무). Goal: 좋은 점을 가정하고 단점·조건 말하기. Today's scene: 7월 오후, 회사 작은 회의실. 마야가 화이트보드 앞에서 펜을 들고 서 있고, 지우가 노트북을 앞에 두고 앉아 웃으며 손가락 네 개를 펴 보임. 화이트보드에는 네모 칸 네 개와 빈 칸 하나만 그려져 있음(글자·숫자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It would be great if ___.".

steps.title: Four Days a Week? · 7월, 회사의 작은 회의실에서

lines.en: Did you see the survey? The company might try a four-day week as a pilot program in August.
lines.ko: 설문 봤어요? 회사가 8월에 시범 프로그램으로 주 4일 근무를 해 볼 수도 있대요.

lines.en: I did! {{It would be great if}} we had Fridays off. People would be happier, and productivity might go up.
lines.ko: 봤어요! 금요일마다 쉬면 정말 좋겠어요. 사람들도 더 행복하고, 생산성도 오를지 몰라요.

lines.en: In theory, yes. But it’s a compressed schedule — four ten-hour days. {{The downside is that}} workers might have to work longer days.
lines.ko: 이론상으론요. 근데 하루 10시간씩 나흘인 압축 근무예요. 단점은 하루 근무가 길어질 수 있다는 거예요.

lines.en: Ten hours a day? Hmm. I’d be tired by Thursday.
lines.ko: 하루 열 시간이요? 음. 목요일쯤엔 지칠 것 같아요.

lines.en: So would you vote yes or no? Tell me your real reasons.
lines.ko: 그래서 찬성할 거예요, 반대할 거예요? 진짜 이유를 말해 줘요.

lines.en: Yes, I think. It’s worth trying. With a three-day weekend, I’d rest properly and come back with more energy. Honestly, the five-day week feels a little old-fashioned.
lines.ko: 찬성할래요. 해 볼 만해요. 주말이 사흘이면 푹 쉬고 힘내서 올 거예요. 솔직히 주 5일은 좀 구식 같아요.

lines.en: {{It depends on the type of}} business, though. Some businesses can’t afford it, and hospitals can’t just close on Fridays.
lines.ko: 그래도 업종에 따라 달라요. 그럴 여유가 없는 회사도 있고, 병원은 금요일에 그냥 문을 닫을 수 없잖아요.

lines.en: True. There’s no one-size-fits-all answer. I’ve heard it works well in some countries, but our team is different.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 모두에게 맞는 정답은 없죠. 어떤 나라에서는 잘된다고 들었지만, 우리 팀은 사정이 달라요.

lines.en: Exactly. We’d need to test it first. That’s why it’s only a two-month trial.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 먼저 시험해 봐야 해요. 그래서 두 달짜리 시범 운영인 거고요.

lines.en: Well, if it’s only a trial, we might as well try it.
lines.ko: 음, 시범 운영일 뿐이라면 해 보는 게 낫겠네요.

lines.en: Good answer. Now write that in the survey!
lines.ko: 좋은 대답이에요. 이제 그걸 설문에 쓰세요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Four Days a Week? · 7월, 회사의 작은 회의실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:

8. Jiwoo: "True. There’s no one-size-fits-all answer. I’ve heard it works well in some countries, but our team is different." (맞아요. 모두에게 맞는 정답은 없죠. 어떤 나라에서는 잘된다고 들었지만, 우리 팀은 사정이 달라요.)

10. Jiwoo: "Well, if it’s only a trial, we might as well try it." (음, 시범 운영일 뿐이라면 해 보는 게 낫겠네요.)
11. Maya: "Good answer. Now write that in the survey!" (좋은 대답이에요. 이제 그걸 설문에 쓰세요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
