steps.title: Four Days a Week? · 7월, 회사의 작은 회의실에서

lines.en: Did you see the survey? The company might try a four-day week as a pilot program in August.
lines.ko: 설문 봤어요? 회사가 8월에 시범 프로그램으로 주 4일 근무를 해 볼 수도 있대요.

lines.en: I did! {{It would be great if}} we had Fridays off. People would be happier, and productivity might go up.
lines.ko: 봤어요! 금요일마다 쉬면 정말 좋겠어요. 사람들도 더 행복하고, 생산성도 오를지 몰라요.

lines.en: In theory, yes. But it’s a compressed schedule — four ten-hour days. {{The downside is that}} workers might have to work longer days.
lines.ko: 이론상으론요. 근데 하루 10시간씩 나흘인 압축 근무예요. 단점은 하루 근무가 길어질 수 있다는 거예요.

lines.en: Ten hours a day? Hmm. I’d be tired by Thursday.
lines.ko: 하루 열 시간이요? 음. 목요일쯤엔 지칠 것 같아요.

lines.en: So would you vote yes or no? Tell me your real reasons.
lines.ko: 그래서 찬성할 거예요, 반대할 거예요? 진짜 이유를 말해 줘요.

lines.en: Yes, I think. It’s worth trying. With a three-day weekend, I’d rest properly and come back with more energy. Honestly, the five-day week feels a little old-fashioned.
lines.ko: 찬성할래요. 해 볼 만해요. 주말이 사흘이면 푹 쉬고 힘내서 올 거예요. 솔직히 주 5일은 좀 구식 같아요.

lines.en: {{It depends on the type of}} business, though. Some businesses can’t afford it, and hospitals can’t just close on Fridays.
lines.ko: 그래도 업종에 따라 달라요. 그럴 여유가 없는 회사도 있고, 병원은 금요일에 그냥 문을 닫을 수 없잖아요.

lines.en: True. There’s no one-size-fits-all answer. I’ve heard it works well in some countries, but our team is different.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 모두에게 맞는 정답은 없죠. 어떤 나라에서는 잘된다고 들었지만, 우리 팀은 사정이 달라요.

lines.en: Exactly. We’d need to test it first. That’s why it’s only a two-month trial.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 먼저 시험해 봐야 해요. 그래서 두 달짜리 시범 운영인 거고요.

lines.en: Well, if it’s only a trial, we might as well try it.
lines.ko: 음, 시범 운영일 뿐이라면 해 보는 게 낫겠네요.

lines.en: Good answer. Now write that in the survey!
lines.ko: 좋은 대답이에요. 이제 그걸 설문에 쓰세요!

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Maya exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Maya (you): "Did you see the survey? The company might try a four-day week as a pilot program in August." (설문 봤어요? 회사가 8월에 시범 프로그램으로 주 4일 근무를 해 볼 수도 있대요.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "I did! It would be great if we had Fridays off. People would be happier, and productivity might go up." (봤어요! 금요일마다 쉬면 정말 좋겠어요. 사람들도 더 행복하고, 생산성도 오를지 몰라요.)
3. Maya (you): "In theory, yes. But it’s a compressed schedule — four ten-hour days. The downside is that workers might have to work longer days." (이론상으론요. 근데 하루 10시간씩 나흘인 압축 근무예요. 단점은 하루 근무가 길어질 수 있다는 거예요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Ten hours a day? Hmm. I’d be tired by Thursday." (하루 열 시간이요? 음. 목요일쯤엔 지칠 것 같아요.)
5. Maya (you): "So would you vote yes or no? Tell me your real reasons." (그래서 찬성할 거예요, 반대할 거예요? 진짜 이유를 말해 줘요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Yes, I think. It’s worth trying. With a three-day weekend, I’d rest properly and come back with more energy. Honestly, the five-day week feels a little old-fashioned." (찬성할래요. 해 볼 만해요. 주말이 사흘이면 푹 쉬고 힘내서 올 거예요. 솔직히 주 5일은 좀 구식 같아요.)
7. Maya (you): "It depends on the type of business, though. Some businesses can’t afford it, and hospitals can’t just close on Fridays." (그래도 업종에 따라 달라요. 그럴 여유가 없는 회사도 있고, 병원은 금요일에 그냥 문을 닫을 수 없잖아요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "True. There’s no one-size-fits-all answer. I’ve heard it works well in some countries, but our team is different." (맞아요. 모두에게 맞는 정답은 없죠. 어떤 나라에서는 잘된다고 들었지만, 우리 팀은 사정이 달라요.)
9. Maya (you): "Exactly. We’d need to test it first. That’s why it’s only a two-month trial." (바로 그거예요. 먼저 시험해 봐야 해요. 그래서 두 달짜리 시범 운영인 거고요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Well, if it’s only a trial, we might as well try it." (음, 시범 운영일 뿐이라면 해 보는 게 낫겠네요.)
11. Maya (you): "Good answer. Now write that in the survey!" (좋은 대답이에요. 이제 그걸 설문에 쓰세요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: The pilot program would have four ten-hour days.
Maya thinks every business can afford a four-day week.
The trial would last two months.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: The downside is that ___. / It depends on the type of ___.
head: 상상 (It would be great if …)
단점 (The downside is that …)
조건 (It depends on …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It would be great if ___. / The downside is that ___. / It depends on the type of ___. Table (상상 (It would be great if …) → 단점 (The downside is that …)):
- we had Fridays off. → the days would be longer.
- we started at ten. → we’d finish late.
- we had longer lunches. → meetings would run late.
- we worked from home more. → it might get lonely.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It *would* be great if we *had* Fridays off. 금요일마다 쉬면 좋겠어요(지금은 안 쉬어요). 
If we *worked* four days, people *would* be happier. if + 과거형, would + 동사원형

If the trial *goes* well, they*’ll* keep it. 실제로 일어날 수 있는 일 
If I *ran* the company, I*’d* try it. 상상(사실이 아님) 
격식체 It *would appear* that … = ~인 것 같다
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- would + if — 상상하는 상황: It would be great if we had Fridays off. 금요일마다 쉬면 좋겠어요(지금은 안 쉬어요). / If we worked four days, people would be happier. if + 과거형, would + 동사원형
- will과 would: If the trial goes well, they’ll keep it. 실제로 일어날 수 있는 일 / If I ran the company, I’d try it. 상상(사실이 아님) / 격식체 It would appear that … = ~인 것 같다
Common mistakes on screen:
- If we would work less, … → If we worked less, … (if 부분에는 would를 쓰지 않아요.)
- The downside are long days. → The downside is long days. (downside는 하나라서 is.)
- It depends of the job. → It depends on the job. (depend 뒤에는 on.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: would + if — 상상하는 상황: It would be great if we had Fridays off. 금요일마다 쉬면 좋겠어요(지금은 안 쉬어요). If we worked four days, people would be happier. if + 과거형, would + 동사원형
will과 would: If the trial goes well, they’ll keep it. 실제로 일어날 수 있는 일 If I ran the company, I’d try it. 상상(사실이 아님) 격식체 It would appear that … = ~인 것 같다
mistakes: If we would work less, … → If we worked less, …
The downside are long days. → The downside is long days.
It depends of the job. → It depends on the job.

steps.note: 예) → It would be great if we had Fridays off. — The downside is that the days would be longer.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) → It would be great if we had Fridays off. — The downside is that the days would be longer. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: we had Fridays off → the days would be longer | we started at ten → we’d finish late | we had longer lunches → meetings would run late | we worked from home more → it might get lonely.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: It depends on the type of ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It would be great if we had Fridays off." (주 4일 근무); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It would be great if ___." / "The downside is that ___." / "It depends on the type of ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Workers might have to work longer days.
하루 일하는 시간이 길어질 수 있어요.
It works well in some countries.
We’d need to test it first.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 좋은 점: "People would be happier." (사람들이 더 행복할 거예요., 보통); "Productivity might go up." (생산성이 오를지도 몰라요., 보통); "It’s worth trying." (해 볼 만해요., 친근)
- 어려운 점: "Some businesses can’t afford it." (그럴 여유가 없는 회사도 있어요., 보통); "Workers might have to work longer days." (하루 일하는 시간이 길어질 수 있어요., 보통); "There’s no one-size-fits-all answer." (모두에게 맞는 정답은 없어요., 정중)
- 신중하게 말하기: "It works well in some countries." (어떤 나라에서는 잘돼요., 보통); "We’d need to test it first." (먼저 시험해 봐야 할 거예요., 정중); "In theory, ___." (이론상으로는 ~(실제로는 다를 수 있어요)., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 알아 두면 좋은 표현

feel a bit *old-fashioned* 좀 구식 같다(*old fashioned* 형태도 써요) 
We *might as well* try. (안 할 이유가 없으니) 해 보는 게 낫겠어요. 
customers *in need* 도움이 필요한 고객 · It *would appear* … ~인 것 같다
(참고) 숫자·시간 낱말

*compute* the hours 시간을 계산하다 · *exceed* 40 hours 40시간을 넘다 
*excess* work 지나치게 많은 일 · *regardless* of the day 요일과 상관없이 
설문과 시범 운영은 지어낸 이야기예요. 실제 결과는 직종과 지역에 따라 달라요.

B: The ___ is that the days would be longer.   A: Hmm. It depends ___ the job. 
B: Well, it’s only a trial. We might as ___ try it.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 알아 두면 좋은 표현: feel a bit old-fashioned 좀 구식 같다(old fashioned 형태도 써요) / We might as well try. (안 할 이유가 없으니) 해 보는 게 낫겠어요. / customers in need 도움이 필요한 고객 · It would appear … ~인 것 같다
- (참고) 숫자·시간 낱말: compute the hours 시간을 계산하다 · exceed 40 hours 40시간을 넘다 / excess work 지나치게 많은 일 · regardless of the day 요일과 상관없이 / 설문과 시범 운영은 지어낸 이야기예요. 실제 결과는 직종과 지역에 따라 달라요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: It would be great ___ we had Fridays off. / B: The ___ is that the days would be longer. A: Hmm. It depends ___ the job. / B: Well, it’s only a trial. We might as ___ try it. / 낱말 상자: if · downside · on · well
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 같은 근무 시간을 더 적은 날에 몰아 넣은

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: wage (임금, 급여), employer (고용주, 고용한 회사), employee (직원, 고용된 사람), trial (시범 운영, 시험), shift (교대 근무(시간)), efficiency (효율(성)), satisfaction (만족(감)), labor (노동), sector ((산업의) 부문, 분야), four-day week (주 4일 근무), compressed (같은 근무 시간을 더 적은 날에 몰아 넣은), pilot program (시범 프로그램).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: A long weekend is an incentive.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: afford ((돈·시간의) 여유가 있다) — "They can’t afford it."; implement (실행하다, 시행하다) — "Let’s implement it in August."; productivity (생산성) — "Productivity might go up."; industry (산업, 업계) — "the travel industry"; economy (경제) — "a strong economy"; schedule (일정) — "a new schedule"; policy (정책, 방침) — "a company policy"; incentive (동기가 되는 것, 장려책) — "A long weekend is an incentive."; motivate (의욕을 북돋우다) — "It could motivate the team.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Imagine a four-day week. What would be great?
Would a four-day week work for every job?
It depends on the type of ___. For example, ___.
If you had a free Friday every week, what would you do?
If I had a free Friday, I would ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Imagine a four-day week. What would be great?" (hint on screen: It would be great if ___.)
- "What’s one downside?" (hint on screen: The downside is that ___.)
- "Would a four-day week work for every job?" (hint on screen: It depends on the type of ___. For example, ___.)
- "If you had a free Friday every week, what would you do?" (hint on screen: If I had a free Friday, I would ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The Summer Survey
steps.text: The made-up survey asked employees about a two-month pilot program. Maya wrote an equation on the whiteboard and computed the total. Four ten-hour days still make forty hours, so the week won’t exceed the usual hours, and wages stay the same. It *would appear* that many people like the idea. But there is some uncertainty. The support desk must still help customers *in need* on Fridays, regardless of the new schedule, so a few people would work in shifts. For Maya, the trial has real significance, and a lot is at stake for the team. If it works, the company could subsequently plan a wider implementation. Jiwoo voted yes. “We *might as well* try,” she wrote.
steps.gloss: equation 식, 등식 · exceed 넘다 · would appear ~인 것 같다 · in need 도움이 필요한 · regardless of ~와 상관없이 · at stake 걸려 있는 · subsequently 그 뒤에 · implementation 실행, 시행
questions: How many hours would people work in a week?
Why would a few people work in shifts?

For Maya, the trial has real significance, and a lot is at stake for the team. If it works, the company could subsequently plan a wider implementation. steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "There should be a clear line." (퇴근 후 연락). Goal: 퇴근 후 연락을 두고 선을 긋는 의견 말하기. Today's scene: 7월 말 목요일 저녁 7시 30분, 동네 카페 안쪽 방. 이웃 여덟 명쯤이 둥글게 앉아 있고, 대니얼이 앞에서 진행하며 손을 들어 다음 사람을 가리킴. 벤이 휴대폰을 들어 보이며 말하고, 지우가 옆에서 고개를 끄덕임. 테이블 위 휴대폰 화면은 꺼져 있음(글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "There should be a clear line between ___ and ___.".

steps.en: There should be a clear line between ___ and ___.
steps.when: 바라는 규칙이나 경계를 말해요. *should be* = 그래야 맞다.
steps.extra: There should be a clear line between work and home.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "There should be a clear line between ___ and ___." (~와 ~ 사이에 분명한 선이 있어야 해요.). When to use it: 바라는 규칙이나 경계를 말해요. should be = 그래야 맞다. Note: There should be a clear line between work and home.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "It’s unfair to expect ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 요구가 공정하지 않다고 말해요. *expect + 사람 + to + 동사원형*.

steps.title: After-Hours Messages · 7월 말 목요일 저녁, 동네 카페 토론 모임에서

lines.en: OK, everyone. Tonight’s topic is after-hours work messages. Who’s first?
lines.ko: 자, 여러분. 오늘 주제는 퇴근 후 업무 메시지예요. 누가 먼저 할까요?

lines.en: I’ll start. Honestly, a quick reply isn’t a big deal.
lines.ko: 제가 할게요. 솔직히 짧게 답장하는 건 별일 아니에요.

lines.en: Once, maybe. But it adds up over time. Answering messages at night is exhausting.
lines.ko: 한 번이면 그렇죠. 하지만 시간이 지나면 쌓여요. 밤에 메시지에 답하는 건 정말 지쳐요.

lines.en: I agree with Ben. {{There should be a clear line between}} work {{and}} home. {{It’s unfair to expect}} people to reply at eleven p.m. Last month, our team group chat buzzed until midnight. No one asked us to reply, but we felt the pressure.
lines.ko: 벤 말에 동의해요. 일과 집 사이에는 분명한 선이 있어야 해요. 밤 11시에 답장을 바라는 건 불공평해요. 지난달 우리 팀 단톡방이 자정까지 울렸어요. 아무도 답하라고 하진 않았지만, 다들 부담을 느꼈어요.

lines.en: Sometimes it can’t be helped. It’s part of the job in some fields, like nursing.
lines.ko: 어쩔 수 없을 때도 있어요. 간호 일처럼 어떤 분야에서는 일의 한 부분이에요.

lines.en: Fair enough. But {{unless it’s an emergency,}} it can wait until morning. And bosses should set an example.
lines.ko: 일리 있어요. 그래도 급한 일이 아니면 아침까지 기다릴 수 있어요. 그리고 상사가 먼저 본보기를 보여야 해요.

lines.en: Some countries protect workers’ right to disconnect, I think.
lines.ko: 어떤 나라는 퇴근 후 연락을 거절할 권리를 법으로 보호한다고 들었어요.

lines.en: Maybe, but what’s your evidence? Let’s not guess about laws. Rules differ from place to place. So, where do you draw the line?
lines.ko: 그럴 수도 있지만, 근거가 뭐예요? 법은 짐작으로 말하지 말아요. 규칙은 곳마다 달라요. 그럼 여러분은 어디까지가 괜찮다고 봐요?

lines.en: For me, it’s about respect. Send it at night if you must, but don’t expect a reply before nine.
lines.ko: 저는 존중의 문제라고 봐요. 꼭 필요하면 밤에 보내도 되지만, 9시 전에 답장을 바라지는 마세요.

lines.en: Exactly. If it’s urgent, call. If it’s not, let it sleep — like me!
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 급하면 전화하고, 아니면 그냥 재워 두세요. 저처럼요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "After-Hours Messages · 7월 말 목요일 저녁, 동네 카페 토론 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "OK, everyone. Tonight’s topic is after-hours work messages. Who’s first?" (자, 여러분. 오늘 주제는 퇴근 후 업무 메시지예요. 누가 먼저 할까요?)
2. Neighbor: "I’ll start. Honestly, a quick reply isn’t a big deal." (제가 할게요. 솔직히 짧게 답장하는 건 별일 아니에요.)
3. Ben: "Once, maybe. But it adds up over time. Answering messages at night is exhausting." (한 번이면 그렇죠. 하지만 시간이 지나면 쌓여요. 밤에 메시지에 답하는 건 정말 지쳐요.)
4. Jiwoo: "I agree with Ben. There should be a clear line between work and home. It’s unfair to expect people to reply at eleven p.m. Last month, our team group chat buzzed until midnight. No one asked us to reply, but we felt the pressure." (벤 말에 동의해요. 일과 집 사이에는 분명한 선이 있어야 해요. 밤 11시에 답장을 바라는 건 불공평해요. 지난달 우리 팀 단톡방이 자정까지 울렸어요. 아무도 답하라고 하진 않았지만, 다들 부담을 느꼈어요.)
5. Neighbor: "Sometimes it can’t be helped. It’s part of the job in some fields, like nursing." (어쩔 수 없을 때도 있어요. 간호 일처럼 어떤 분야에서는 일의 한 부분이에요.)
6. Ben: "Fair enough. But unless it’s an emergency, it can wait until morning. And bosses should set an example." (일리 있어요. 그래도 급한 일이 아니면 아침까지 기다릴 수 있어요. 그리고 상사가 먼저 본보기를 보여야 해요.)
7. Neighbor: "Some countries protect workers’ right to disconnect, I think." (어떤 나라는 퇴근 후 연락을 거절할 권리를 법으로 보호한다고 들었어요.)
8. Daniel: "Maybe, but what’s your evidence? Let’s not guess about laws. Rules differ from place to place. So, where do you draw the line?" (그럴 수도 있지만, 근거가 뭐예요? 법은 짐작으로 말하지 말아요. 규칙은 곳마다 달라요. 그럼 여러분은 어디까지가 괜찮다고 봐요?)
9. Jiwoo: "For me, it’s about respect. Send it at night if you must, but don’t expect a reply before nine." (저는 존중의 문제라고 봐요. 꼭 필요하면 밤에 보내도 되지만, 9시 전에 답장을 바라지는 마세요.)
10. Ben: "Exactly. If it’s urgent, call. If it’s not, let it sleep — like me!" (바로 그거예요. 급하면 전화하고, 아니면 그냥 재워 두세요. 저처럼요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

items: The neighbor thinks a quick reply isn’t a big deal.
Jiwoo’s boss asked the team to reply at midnight.
Daniel says rules differ from place to place.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. The neighbor thinks a quick reply isn’t a big deal.
2. Jiwoo’s boss asked the team to reply at midnight.
3. Daniel says rules differ from place to place.
The scene they are about:
1. Daniel: "OK, everyone. Tonight’s topic is after-hours work messages. Who’s first?" (자, 여러분. 오늘 주제는 퇴근 후 업무 메시지예요. 누가 먼저 할까요?)
2. Neighbor: "I’ll start. Honestly, a quick reply isn’t a big deal." (제가 할게요. 솔직히 짧게 답장하는 건 별일 아니에요.)
3. Ben: "Once, maybe. But it adds up over time. Answering messages at night is exhausting." (한 번이면 그렇죠. 하지만 시간이 지나면 쌓여요. 밤에 메시지에 답하는 건 정말 지쳐요.)
4. Jiwoo: "I agree with Ben. There should be a clear line between work and home. It’s unfair to expect people to reply at eleven p.m. Last month, our team group chat buzzed until midnight. No one asked us to reply, but we felt the pressure." (벤 말에 동의해요. 일과 집 사이에는 분명한 선이 있어야 해요. 밤 11시에 답장을 바라는 건 불공평해요. 지난달 우리 팀 단톡방이 자정까지 울렸어요. 아무도 답하라고 하진 않았지만, 다들 부담을 느꼈어요.)
5. Neighbor: "Sometimes it can’t be helped. It’s part of the job in some fields, like nursing." (어쩔 수 없을 때도 있어요. 간호 일처럼 어떤 분야에서는 일의 한 부분이에요.)
6. Ben: "Fair enough. But unless it’s an emergency, it can wait until morning. And bosses should set an example." (일리 있어요. 그래도 급한 일이 아니면 아침까지 기다릴 수 있어요. 그리고 상사가 먼저 본보기를 보여야 해요.)
7. Neighbor: "Some countries protect workers’ right to disconnect, I think." (어떤 나라는 퇴근 후 연락을 거절할 권리를 법으로 보호한다고 들었어요.)
8. Daniel: "Maybe, but what’s your evidence? Let’s not guess about laws. Rules differ from place to place. So, where do you draw the line?" (그럴 수도 있지만, 근거가 뭐예요? 법은 짐작으로 말하지 말아요. 규칙은 곳마다 달라요. 그럼 여러분은 어디까지가 괜찮다고 봐요?)
9. Jiwoo: "For me, it’s about respect. Send it at night if you must, but don’t expect a reply before nine." (저는 존중의 문제라고 봐요. 꼭 필요하면 밤에 보내도 되지만, 9시 전에 답장을 바라지는 마세요.)
10. Ben: "Exactly. If it’s urgent, call. If it’s not, let it sleep — like me!" (바로 그거예요. 급하면 전화하고, 아니면 그냥 재워 두세요. 저처럼요!)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: There should be a clear line between ___ and ___.
It’s unfair to expect ___. / Unless it’s an emergency, ___.
head: 바라는 규칙 (There should be …)
예외 (Unless …)
대답
rows: it’s an emergency, it can wait.
Where do you draw the line?
you’re on call, turn it off.
a rule for the group chat.
A quick reply isn’t a big deal.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: There should be a clear line between ___ and ___. / It’s unfair to expect ___. / Unless it’s an emergency, ___. Table (바라는 규칙 (There should be …) → 예외 (Unless …)):
- a clear line. → it’s an emergency, it can wait.
- a quiet time after 9 p.m. → it’s urgent, don’t call.
- one work phone for nights. → you’re on call, turn it off.
- a rule for the group chat. → your boss asks, reply tomorrow.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: There should be + 명사 — 바라는 규칙

*There should be* a clear line. (하나) · *There should be* fewer messages. (여럿) 
질문: *Should there be* a rule? 규칙이 있어야 할까요?

*Unless* it’s an emergency, it can wait. = If it’s *not* an emergency, it can wait. 
미래 일이라도 unless 뒤에는 현재형: unless he calls
errors: There should be a clear line.
It’s unfair to expect us reply.
It’s unfair to expect us to reply.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- There should be + 명사 — 바라는 규칙: There should be a clear line. (하나) · There should be fewer messages. (여럿) / 질문: Should there be a rule? 규칙이 있어야 할까요?
- unless = if … not: Unless it’s an emergency, it can wait. = If it’s not an emergency, it can wait. / 미래 일이라도 unless 뒤에는 현재형: unless he calls
Common mistakes on screen:
- There should a clear line. → There should be a clear line. (should 뒤에 be를 빠뜨리지 마요.)
- It’s unfair to expect us reply. → It’s unfair to expect us to reply. (expect + 사람 + to + 동사원형.)
- Unless it will be urgent, … → Unless it’s urgent, … (unless 뒤에는 현재형(미래 뜻이라도).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: There should be + 명사 — 바라는 규칙: There should be a clear line. (하나) · There should be fewer messages. (여럿) 질문: Should there be a rule? 규칙이 있어야 할까요?
unless = if … not: Unless it’s an emergency, it can wait. = If it’s not an emergency, it can wait. 미래 일이라도 unless 뒤에는 현재형: unless he calls
mistakes: There should a clear line. → There should be a clear line.
It’s unfair to expect us reply. → It’s unfair to expect us to reply.
Unless it will be urgent, … → Unless it’s urgent, …

steps.note: 예) → There should be a clear line between work and home. Unless it’s an emergency, it can wait.
items: a clear line between work and home
a rule for the group chat
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) → There should be a clear line between work and home. Unless it’s an emergency, it can wait. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: a clear line between work and home → it’s an emergency | a quiet time after 9 p.m. → it’s urgent | a rule for the group chat → the boss calls | a separate work phone → you’re on call.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: There should be a clear line between ___ and ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "There should be a clear line." (퇴근 후 연락); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "There should be a clear line between ___ and ___." / "It’s unfair to expect ___." / "Unless it’s an emergency, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Answering messages at night is exhausting.
밤에 메시지에 답하는 건 정말 지쳐요.
Where do you draw the line?
It’s part of the job in some fields.
A quick reply isn’t a big deal.
Some countries protect workers’ right to disconnect.
퇴근 후 연락에 답하지 않을 권리를 보호하는 나라도 있어요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 문제점 말하기: "Answering messages at night is exhausting." (밤에 메시지에 답하는 건 정말 지쳐요., 보통); "It adds up over time." (시간이 지나면 쌓여요., 친근); "Where do you draw the line?" (어디까지가 괜찮다고 봐요?, 보통)
- 다른 쪽 의견: "Sometimes it can’t be helped." (어쩔 수 없을 때도 있어요., 보통); "It’s part of the job in some fields." (어떤 분야에서는 일의 한 부분이에요., 보통); "A quick reply isn’t a big deal." (짧은 답장은 별일 아니에요., 친근)
- 가치와 규칙: "Bosses should set an example." (상사가 먼저 본보기를 보여야 해요., 정중); "It’s about respect." (존중의 문제예요., 보통); "Some countries protect workers’ right to disconnect." (퇴근 후 연락에 답하지 않을 권리를 보호하는 나라도 있어요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 덩어리 표현

If you must message, *do so* early. 꼭 보내야 하면 일찍 그렇게 하세요. · keep it *up to date* 최신으로 유지하다 
*hand over* the phone 휴대폰을 (다음 사람에게) 넘겨주다 · not *for sale* 팔 물건이 아닌 
*In this respect*, … 이 점에서는 …
규칙에 관한 낱말 (참고)

a *clause* (계약서의) 조항 · a *penalty* 벌금 같은 처벌 
a *sanction* (공식적인) 제재 · *regulate* 규제하다 
예 — 프랑스(2017~)는 회사가 연락 규칙을 정하게 하고, 호주(2024~, 작은 회사 2025~)는 불합리한 경우가 아니면 근무 시간 밖 연락에 답하지 않을 권리를 줘요(연락 금지법 아님, 법률 조언 아님). Some countries have a law against it.은 운전 중 휴대폰을 손에 들고 쓰는 것처럼 금지된 일에.
steps.blank:
A: There should ___ a clear line between work and home. 
B: But sometimes it can’t be ___.   A: True. ___ it’s an emergency, it can wait. 
B: OK. So where do you ___ the line? 
낱말 상자: be · helped · Unless · draw
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 덩어리 표현: If you must message, do so early. 꼭 보내야 하면 일찍 그렇게 하세요. · keep it up to date 최신으로 유지하다 / hand over the phone 휴대폰을 (다음 사람에게) 넘겨주다 · not for sale 팔 물건이 아닌 / In this respect, … 이 점에서는 …
- 규칙에 관한 낱말 (참고): a clause (계약서의) 조항 · a penalty 벌금 같은 처벌 / a sanction (공식적인) 제재 · regulate 규제하다 / 예 — 프랑스(2017~)는 회사가 연락 규칙을 정하게 하고, 호주(2024~, 작은 회사 2025~)는 불합리한 경우가 아니면 근무 시간 밖 연락에 답하지 않을 권리를 줘요(연락 금지법 아님, 법률 조언 아님). Some countries have a law against it.은 운전 중 휴대폰을 손에 들고 쓰는 것처럼 금지된 일에.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: There should ___ a clear line between work and home. / B: But sometimes it can’t be ___. A: True. ___ it’s an emergency, it can wait. / B: OK. So where do you ___ the line? / 낱말 상자: be · helped · Unless · draw
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: emergency (비상, 급한 일), unfair (불공평한), exhausting (몹시 지치게 하는), law (법, 법률), disconnect (연결을 끊다), availability (연락이 되는 상태), after-hours (근무 시간 후의, 퇴근 후의), group chat (단체 대화방, 단톡방), work phone (업무용 휴대폰), on call ((부르면 일하도록) 대기 중인), message (메시지), reply (답장하다; 답장).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: expect (기대하다, 바라다) — "Don’t expect a reply."; respect (존중) — "It’s about respect."; right (권리(앞에서는 ‘맞는, 옳은’)) — "the right to disconnect"; urgent (급한) — "Is it urgent?"; contract (계약(서)) — "Read your contract."; culture ((한 집단의) 문화, 분위기) — "our team culture"; pressure (압박감, 부담) — "We felt the pressure."; boss (상사) — "My boss set an example."; react (반응하다) — "How did you react?".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Should there be a quiet time for work or study messages?
When is a night message OK?
A neighbor says, “A quick reply isn’t a big deal.” Answer.
That’s a fair point, but it adds up over time.
Where do you draw the line with phones at dinner?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Should there be a quiet time for work or study messages?" (hint on screen: There should be ___ between ___ and ___.)
- "When is a night message OK?" (hint on screen: Unless it’s ___, ___.)
- "A neighbor says, “A quick reply isn’t a big deal.” Answer." (hint on screen: That’s a fair point, but it adds up over time.)
- "Where do you draw the line with phones at dinner?" (hint on screen: For me, there should be ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: After the Debate
steps.text: When a neighbor said, “My time isn’t *for sale* after six,” the room burst into laughter. Daniel kept everyone on track: “We’re not opponents. Just react to the idea.” A small night message can trigger stress, someone added. Ben shared his school’s idea: one teacher is on call with the work phone, then *hands over* the phone to the next person each week. “If you must message after hours, *do so* with ‘no reply needed,’” he said. Work chats have had a boom, so some teams make their own rules. *In this respect*, everyone agreed: availability rules should be clear and *up to date*. At the rear of the room, Jiwoo suspended her notifications. “I swear I’ll check them at nine,” she laughed.
steps.gloss: for sale 팔려고 내놓은 · burst into 갑자기 ~하기 시작하다 · opponent 상대편 · trigger 일으키다 · hand over 넘겨주다 · boom 급증 · suspend 잠시 멈추다 · swear 맹세하다
questions: What did Ben’s school do with the work phone?
What did Jiwoo do at the rear of the room?

Reading on screen: "After the Debate". Text: "When a neighbor said, “My time isn’t for sale after six,” the room burst into laughter. Daniel kept everyone on track: “We’re not opponents. Just react to the idea.” A small night message can trigger stress, someone added. Ben shared his school’s idea: one teacher is on call with the work phone, then hands over the phone to the next person each week. “If you must message after hours, do so with ‘no reply needed,’” he said. Work chats have had a boom, so some teams make their own rules. In this respect, everyone agreed: availability rules should be clear and up to date. At the rear of the room, Jiwoo suspended her notifications. “I swear I’ll check them at nine,” she laughed." Words: for sale 팔려고 내놓은 · burst into 갑자기 ~하기 시작하다 · opponent 상대편 · trigger 일으키다 · hand over 넘겨주다 · boom 급증 · suspend 잠시 멈추다 · swear 맹세하다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Ben’s school do with the work phone?" / "What did Jiwoo do at the rear of the room?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘There should be a clear line between ___ and ___.’로 바라는 규칙을 말할 수 있어요.
‘It’s unfair to expect ___.’로 어떤 요구가 불공평하다고 말할 수 있어요.

steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘There should be a clear line between ___ and ___.’로 바라는 규칙을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s unfair to expect ___.’로 어떤 요구가 불공평하다고 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘Unless it’s an emergency, ___.’로 규칙의 예외를 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 평생 직장
steps.title_en: These days, it’s common to change jobs.
steps.scene_desc: 8월 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실. 선풍기가 돌아가고, 낮은 탁자 위에 수박 접시와 보리차 잔 두 개. 그레이스가 오래된 여행 사진첩을 펼쳐 보이며 이야기하고, 지우가 소파에 앉아 사진을 들여다봄(사진·책에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "These days, it’s common to change jobs." (평생 직장). Goal: 예전과 비교하며 길게 보고 말하기. Today's scene: 8월 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실. 선풍기가 돌아가고, 낮은 탁자 위에 수박 접시와 보리차 잔 두 개. 그레이스가 오래된 여행 사진첩을 펼쳐 보이며 이야기하고, 지우가 소파에 앉아 사진을 들여다봄(사진·책에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "These days, it’s common to ___.".

steps.when: 요즘 사정을 말해요. 흔히 예전과 비교할 때 써요.
steps.extra: These days, it’s common to change jobs every few years.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "These days, it’s common to ___." (요즘은 ~하는 게 흔해요.). When to use it: 요즘 사정을 말해요. 흔히 예전과 비교할 때 써요. Note: These days, it’s common to change jobs every few years.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Compared to ___, ___.".

steps.title: One Job for Life? · 8월 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실에서

lines.en: Grace, my old classmate just changed jobs again. That’s her fourth company in six years!
lines.ko: 그레이스, 제 동창이 또 이직했어요. 6년 동안 벌써 네 번째 회사예요!

lines.en: {{These days, it’s common to}} change jobs every few years. Job security isn’t what it used to be.
lines.ko: 요즘은 몇 년마다 직장을 옮기는 게 흔해요. 고용 안정은 예전 같지 않죠.

lines.en: {{Compared to}} my parents’ generation, it’s a big change. Back then, many people stayed with one employer until they retired.
lines.ko: 부모님 세대와 비교하면 큰 변화예요. 그때는 많은 사람이 은퇴할 때까지 한 회사에 다녔어요.

lines.en: Right. A permanent job and a pension. But now, loyalty isn’t always rewarded.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 평생 직장에 연금까지요. 그런데 지금은 회사에 충실해도 늘 보상받지는 못해요.

lines.en: And changing jobs can boost your salary. My classmate got a raise each time.
lines.ko: 그리고 이직하면 연봉이 오를 수도 있어요. 제 동창은 옮길 때마다 연봉이 올랐어요.

lines.en: True. But some managers think it looks bad on your résumé. Experience at one company counts too.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 하지만 이력서에 안 좋아 보인다고 생각하는 관리자도 있어요. 한 회사에서 쌓은 경험도 중요하고요.

lines.en: Maybe, but some younger workers want growth more. I changed jobs last year, and I’ve learned so much on Maya’s team.
lines.ko: 그럴 수도 있지만, 성장을 더 원하는 젊은 직장인도 있어요. 저도 작년에 이직했는데, 마야 팀에서 정말 많이 배웠어요.

lines.en: So, you mean growth is more important than stability?
lines.ko: 그러니까 안정보다 성장이 더 중요하다는 거예요?

lines.en: For me, right now, yes. But stability may matter more for me later in life.
lines.ko: 지금 저한테는 그래요. 나중에는 저도 안정이 더 중요해질지 모르죠.

lines.en: Look at me. I worked in travel for years, then moved to Seoul and became a teacher. It was a risk.
lines.ko: 저를 봐요. 여행 업계에서 몇 년 일하다가 서울로 와서 선생님이 됐잖아요. 모험이었죠.

lines.en: Do you ever miss your old job?
lines.ko: 예전 일이 그리울 때도 있어요?

lines.en: Sometimes. But {{in the long run}}, it was the right choice for me. There’s no right answer, though. It’s a personal choice.
lines.ko: 가끔요. 그래도 길게 보면 저한테는 옳은 선택이었어요. 하지만 정답은 없어요. 각자 고를 일이에요.

frame: Compared to ___, ___. / In the long run, ___.
head: 비교 대상 (Compared to …,)
달라진 점
길게 보면 (In the long run, …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: These days, it’s common to ___. / Compared to ___, ___. / In the long run, ___. Table (비교 대상 (Compared to …,) → 달라진 점):
- the past, → people change jobs more often.
- my parents’ generation, → people work from home more.
- ten years ago, → people use more online tools.
- big firms, → small firms decide faster.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Compared to* the past, people change jobs *more often*. 
뒤 문장에 비교하는 말을 써요: more · less · higher · -er 
compared with도 같은 뜻이에요.
in the long run / in the short run

*In the short run*, changing jobs is stressful. (당장은) 
*In the long run*, it can help your career. (오랜 시간 뒤에는) 
These days, it’s common *to* + 동사원형.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Compared to + 명사: Compared to the past, people change jobs more often. / 뒤 문장에 비교하는 말을 써요: more · less · higher · -er / compared with도 같은 뜻이에요.
- in the long run / in the short run: In the short run, changing jobs is stressful. (당장은) / In the long run, it can help your career. (오랜 시간 뒤에는) / These days, it’s common to + 동사원형.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Compare to the past, … → Compared to the past, … (Compared(-ed 형태)로 써요.)
- It’s common changing jobs. → It’s common to change jobs. (common 뒤에는 to + 동사원형.)
- In the long running, … → In the long run, … (in the long run으로 굳어진 표현이에요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: Compared to + 명사: Compared to the past, people change jobs more often. 뒤 문장에 비교하는 말을 써요: more · less · higher · -er compared with도 같은 뜻이에요.

steps.note: 예) → Compared to the past, people change jobs more often. In the long run, it’s a personal choice.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) → Compared to the past, people change jobs more often. In the long run, it’s a personal choice. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: the past → people change jobs more often | my first job → I have more skills now | big firms → small firms decide faster | ten years ago → more people work remotely.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "These days, it’s common to change jobs." (평생 직장); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "These days, it’s common to ___." / "Compared to ___, ___." / "In the long run, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Job security isn’t what it used to be.
Changing jobs can boost your salary.
It looks bad on your résumé.

나이가 들면 안정이 더 중요해질 수도 있어요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 그때와 지금: "Job security isn’t what it used to be." (고용 안정은 예전 같지 않아요., 보통); "Loyalty isn’t always rewarded." (회사에 충실해도 늘 보상받지는 못해요., 보통); "Changing jobs can boost your salary." (이직하면 연봉이 오를 수 있어요., 보통)
- 양쪽 의견: "It looks bad on your résumé." (이력서에 안 좋아 보여요., 친근); "Experience at one company counts too." (한 회사에서 쌓은 경험도 중요해요., 정중); "Some younger workers want growth." (성장을 원하는 젊은 직원들도 있어요., 보통)
- 결론을 열어 두기: "Stability may matter more later in life." (나이가 들면 안정이 더 중요해질 수도 있어요., 보통); "There’s no right answer." (정답은 없어요., 친근); "It’s a personal choice." (각자 고를 일이에요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Picture words on screen. New: résumé (이력서), pension (연금), fund (기금, 자금), salary (급여, 연봉), promotion (승진), generation (세대), reward (보상; 보상하다), stable (안정된, 변하지 않는), permanent (영구적인, 정규직의). Review words: retire (은퇴하다), retirement (은퇴, 은퇴 뒤의 생활), employer (고용주, 회사).

Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

items: What is common at work or school these days?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What is common at work or school these days?" (hint on screen: These days, it’s common to ___.)
- "Compare work today with work thirty years ago." (hint on screen: Compared to ___, ___.)
- "Stay at one company, or change jobs for growth? What’s your opinion?" (hint on screen: In the long run, I think ___.)
- "A friend says, “Changing jobs looks bad.” Answer politely." (hint on screen: That’s a fair point, but ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Grace’s Path
steps.text: *Long before* she moved to Seoul, Grace worked as a travel consultant at a large enterprise. Her company had a partnership with hotels in three countries, and her team handled one segment of the market: family trips. The job was stable, but its scope was small. Then the travel business began to undergo structural changes. Grace asked an older coworker for counsel. “Would you *care to* guess what she said?” Grace laughs. “Do what you love.” So Grace took a risk and *settled down* in Seoul as a teacher. Today, she’s a holder of two teaching certificates. “Compared to my old job, my salary is reasonably good, and I can *provide for* myself. Potentially, I could even teach teachers one day.”
steps.gloss: partnership 제휴, 협력 관계 · segment 부분, 영역 · scope 범위 · undergo 겪다 · structural 구조적인 · counsel 조언 · holder 가진 사람 · reasonably 꽤, 적당히 · potentially 어쩌면, 앞으로
questions: What did Grace’s team handle?
What advice did Grace’s coworker give?

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Grace’s team handle?" / "What advice did Grace’s coworker give?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

steps.scene_desc: 8월 말 목요일 저녁 7시 30분, 동네 카페 안쪽 방의 토론 모임. 이웃 8~9명이 둥글게 앉아 있고, 대니얼이 서서 진행하며, 지우가 번역 앱이 켜진 휴대폰(화면 글자 없이)을 들어 보이며 말하고, 옆의 이웃 한 명이 고개를 갸웃함. 글자·간판 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What matters most?" (AI 시대의 외국어). Goal: 가장 중요한 것을 강조하고 의심 말하기. Today's scene: 8월 말 목요일 저녁 7시 30분, 동네 카페 안쪽 방의 토론 모임. 이웃 8~9명이 둥글게 앉아 있고, 대니얼이 서서 진행하며, 지우가 번역 앱이 켜진 휴대폰(화면 글자 없이)을 들어 보이며 말하고, 옆의 이웃 한 명이 고개를 갸웃함. 글자·간판 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Even with ___, we still need ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 것이 쓸모 있다고 인정하고, 그래도 여전히 중요한 것을 말해요.
steps.extra: Even with AI translation, we still need teachers.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Even with ___, we still need ___." (~가 있어도 여전히 ~가 필요해요.). When to use it: 어떤 것이 쓸모 있다고 인정하고, 그래도 여전히 중요한 것을 말해요. Note: Even with AI translation, we still need teachers.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "What matters most is ___.".

steps.when: 핵심을 앞에 내세워요. *What … is*로 말하면 더 힘이 있어요.
steps.extra: What matters most is connection.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "What matters most is ___." (가장 중요한 건 ~예요.). When to use it: 핵심을 앞에 내세워요. What … is로 말하면 더 힘이 있어요. Note: What matters most is connection.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’m not convinced that ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 생각에 정중하게 의문을 나타내요.
steps.extra: I’m not convinced that apps are enough.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m not convinced that ___." (~라는 데는 확신이 안 서요.). When to use it: 어떤 생각에 정중하게 의문을 나타내요. Note: I’m not convinced that apps are enough.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Still Worth Learning? · 8월 말 목요일 저녁, 카페 안쪽 방 토론 모임에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Still Worth Learning? · 8월 말 목요일 저녁, 카페 안쪽 방 토론 모임에서

lines.en: OK, everyone, tonight’s question: with AI translation, do we still need to learn foreign languages? Jiwoo, you’re learning English. What’s your view?
lines.ko: 자, 여러분, 오늘의 질문이에요. AI 번역이 있는데도 외국어를 배워야 할까요? 지우 씨는 영어를 배우고 있죠. 어떻게 생각해요?

lines.en: Well, translation apps are getting better every year. I use one at work. But {{even with}} AI, {{we still need}} real language skills.
lines.ko: 음, 번역 앱은 해마다 좋아지고 있어요. 저도 회사에서 써요. 그래도 AI가 있어도 진짜 언어 실력은 여전히 필요해요.

lines.en: I’m not so sure. My app is fast and pretty accurate. Maybe kids won’t need to learn grammar.
lines.ko: 글쎄요. 제 앱은 빠르고 꽤 정확해요. 아이들은 문법을 안 배워도 될지 몰라요.

lines.en: Interesting. Jiwoo, what’s your evidence?
lines.ko: 흥미롭네요. 지우 씨, 근거가 뭐예요?

lines.en: In video calls with the Vancouver team, apps often miss the nuance. A polite “maybe” can sound like a “yes.”
lines.ko: 밴쿠버 팀과 화상 회의를 하면 앱이 미묘한 뜻을 자주 놓쳐요. 정중한 ‘글쎄요’가 ‘네’처럼 들리기도 해요.

lines.en: Sure, but that’s work. For travel, an app is enough.
lines.ko: 그렇긴 한데, 그건 일이잖아요. 여행할 때는 앱이면 충분해요.

lines.en: That’s a fair point. But for me, {{what matters most is}} connection. AI can’t build friendships.
lines.ko: 일리 있어요. 하지만 저한테 가장 중요한 건 사람과의 연결이에요. AI는 우정을 쌓아 주지 못해요.

lines.en: So it’s about connecting with people?
lines.ko: 그러니까 사람과 이어지는 게 핵심이라는 거죠?

lines.en: Exactly. Culture comes with language, too. And it’s still useful for jobs.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 언어를 배우면 문화도 따라와요. 그리고 일할 때도 여전히 쓸모 있어요.

lines.en: {{I’m not convinced that}} everyone needs it, though. Learning takes years.
lines.ko: 그래도 모두에게 필요한지는 확신이 안 서요. 배우는 데 몇 년이 걸리잖아요.

lines.en: True. I see it as a tool, not a replacement. And learning a language opens your mind.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 저는 앱을 대체물이 아니라 도구로 봐요. 그리고 언어를 배우면 생각이 넓어져요.

lines.en: Two different views, and both are fair. Let’s hear from the others.
lines.ko: 서로 다른 두 의견이 다 일리 있네요. 다른 분들 얘기도 들어 봐요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Still Worth Learning? · 8월 말 목요일 저녁, 카페 안쪽 방 토론 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "OK, everyone, tonight’s question: with AI translation, do we still need to learn foreign languages? Jiwoo, you’re learning English. What’s your view?" (자, 여러분, 오늘의 질문이에요. AI 번역이 있는데도 외국어를 배워야 할까요? 지우 씨는 영어를 배우고 있죠. 어떻게 생각해요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Well, translation apps are getting better every year. I use one at work. But even with AI, we still need real language skills." (음, 번역 앱은 해마다 좋아지고 있어요. 저도 회사에서 써요. 그래도 AI가 있어도 진짜 언어 실력은 여전히 필요해요.)
3. Neighbor: "I’m not so sure. My app is fast and pretty accurate. Maybe kids won’t need to learn grammar." (글쎄요. 제 앱은 빠르고 꽤 정확해요. 아이들은 문법을 안 배워도 될지 몰라요.)
4. Daniel: "Interesting. Jiwoo, what’s your evidence?" (흥미롭네요. 지우 씨, 근거가 뭐예요?)

8. Daniel: "So it’s about connecting with people?" (그러니까 사람과 이어지는 게 핵심이라는 거죠?)

10. Neighbor: "I’m not convinced that everyone needs it, though. Learning takes years." (그래도 모두에게 필요한지는 확신이 안 서요. 배우는 데 몇 년이 걸리잖아요.)
11. Jiwoo: "True. I see it as a tool, not a replacement. And learning a language opens your mind." (맞아요. 저는 앱을 대체물이 아니라 도구로 봐요. 그리고 언어를 배우면 생각이 넓어져요.)

Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 주제
What matters most is …
I’m not convinced that …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: I’m not convinced that ___. / What matters most is ___. Table (주제 → What matters most is …):
- learning English → connection.
- travel → being safe.
- a job interview → being clear.
- reading a novel → the nuance.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*What matters most is* connection. = Connection matters most. 
*What I need is* practice. 내게 필요한 건 연습이에요. 
What이 주어(What matters) / What + 주어 + 동사(What I need) — 둘 다 ‘~하는 것’

*Even with* AI, we still need teachers. (with + 명사) 
I’m *not convinced that* apps are enough. 앱으로 충분한지 확신이 안 서요.
errors: Even with AI is good, we still need it.
Even though AI is good, we still need it.
I’m not convince that it works.
I’m not convinced that it works.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- What matters most is …: What matters most is connection. = Connection matters most. / What I need is practice. 내게 필요한 건 연습이에요. / What이 주어(What matters) / What + 주어 + 동사(What I need) — 둘 다 ‘~하는 것’
- Even with / I’m not convinced: Even with AI, we still need teachers. (with + 명사) / I’m not convinced that apps are enough. 앱으로 충분한지 확신이 안 서요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- What matters most are connection. → What matters most is connection. (하나를 말하니까 is.)
- Even with AI is good, we still need it. → Even though AI is good, we still need it. (with + 명사 · though + 문장.)
- I’m not convince that it works. → I’m not convinced that it works. (convinced(-ed 형태)로 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: What matters most is …: What matters most is connection. = Connection matters most. What I need is practice. 내게 필요한 건 연습이에요. What이 주어(What matters) / What + 주어 + 동사(What I need) — 둘 다 ‘~하는 것’
Even with / I’m not convinced: Even with AI, we still need teachers. (with + 명사) I’m not convinced that apps are enough. 앱으로 충분한지 확신이 안 서요.
mistakes: What matters most are connection. → What matters most is connection.
Even with AI is good, we still need it. → Even though AI is good, we still need it.
I’m not convince that it works. → I’m not convinced that it works.

steps.note: 예) travel / safety → Even with AI, what matters most for travel is safety.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) travel / safety → Even with AI, what matters most for travel is safety. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: learning a language → connection | travel → safety | a work email → accuracy | a novel → the nuance.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "What matters most?" (AI 시대의 외국어); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Even with ___, we still need ___." / "What matters most is ___." / "I’m not convinced that ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Translation apps are getting better every year.
I see it as a tool, not a replacement.
Learning a language opens your mind.
Maybe kids won’t need to learn grammar.
아이들은 문법을 안 배워도 될지 몰라요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- AI 번역에 대해: "Translation apps are getting better every year." (번역 앱은 해마다 좋아지고 있어요., 보통); "They still miss the nuance." (여전히 미묘한 뜻을 놓쳐요., 보통); "I see it as a tool, not a replacement." (대체물이 아니라 도구라고 봐요., 보통)
- 언어를 배우는 이유: "Learning a language opens your mind." (언어를 배우면 생각이 넓어져요., 보통); "It’s about connecting with people." (사람과 이어지는 게 핵심이에요., 보통); "AI can’t build friendships." (AI는 우정을 쌓아 주지 못해요., 친근); "Culture comes with language." (언어를 배우면 문화도 따라와요., 보통)
- 다른 쪽 의견: "Maybe kids won’t need to learn grammar." (아이들은 문법을 안 배워도 될지 몰라요., 보통); "It’s still useful for jobs." (일할 때 여전히 쓸모 있어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 글에 관한 낱말

*literary* 문학의 · *poetry* 시(詩) 
a *publisher* 출판사 · *compose* (공들여) 쓰다, 짓다 
a *paragraph* 문단 · the *dialog* (책·영화 속) 대화, 대사
(참고) 모임에서 나온 낱말

a *scholar* 학자 · an *insight* 통찰, 새로운 깨달음 
a *composition* (한 편의) 글, 작문 · an *illustration* 삽화 
모임과 손님은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
steps.blank:
A: Do we still need to learn languages?   B: Yes. Even ___ AI, we still need them. What ___ most is connection. 
A: I’m not ___ that everyone needs it.   B: Fair point. I see it as a ___, not a replacement. 
낱말 상자: with · matters · convinced · tool
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 글에 관한 낱말: literary 문학의 · poetry 시(詩) / a publisher 출판사 · compose (공들여) 쓰다, 짓다 / a paragraph 문단 · the dialog (책·영화 속) 대화, 대사
- (참고) 모임에서 나온 낱말: a scholar 학자 · an insight 통찰, 새로운 깨달음 / a composition (한 편의) 글, 작문 · an illustration 삽화 / 모임과 손님은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Do we still need to learn languages? B: Yes. Even ___ AI, we still need them. What ___ most is connection. / A: I’m not ___ that everyone needs it. B: Fair point. I see it as a ___, not a replacement. / 낱말 상자: with · matters · convinced · tool
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: translation (번역), translator (번역가; 번역기), brain (뇌), tool (도구), global (세계적인, 전 세계의), native (그곳 태생의; 모국어로 하는), connection (연결, (사람 사이의) 유대), accuracy (정확성), fluency (유창함), nuance (미묘한 차이, 뉘앙스), rely ((on) ~에 의지하다), intelligence (지능).

items: It’s a tool, not a replacement.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: communication (의사소통) — "Good communication takes time."; culture (문화) — "Culture comes with language."; replacement (대신하는 것, 대체물) — "It’s a tool, not a replacement."; benefit (이점, 혜택) — "One benefit is new friends."; skill ((배워서 익힌) 기술, 능력) — "real language skills"; technology ((과학) 기술) — "Technology changes fast."; poet (시인) — "a famous poet"; precise (정확한, 정밀한) — "a precise translation".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

items: Do you use translation apps? When?
I use one when ___. / I don’t, because ___.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Do you use translation apps? When?" (hint on screen: I use one when ___. / I don’t, because ___.)
- "Even with AI, what do we still need?" (hint on screen: Even with AI, we still need ___.)
- "When you learn a language, what matters most?" (hint on screen: What matters most is ___.)
- "Is there an idea about AI you doubt?" (hint on screen: I’m not convinced that ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: A Translator’s View
steps.text: After the break, Daniel introduced a guest, a neighbor who translates poetry and literary books. She had *put together* a short list of points. “AI helps me a lot,” she said. “It gives me a first draft in seconds. *Mind you*, it often misses jokes and feelings.” She showed one paragraph from a novel. The app’s version was accurate, but the warm tone didn’t *come through*. “*Bear in mind* that a language is not only words. It carries a culture,” she said. Jiwoo agreed. Since she started learning English, she has understood her Vancouver teammates much better. Still, two neighbors felt that apps are enough for travel. Daniel thanked everyone. “Both views make sense,” he said.
steps.gloss: put together 모아서 만들다 · mind you 그렇긴 해도, 다만 · paragraph 문단 · tone 어조, 말투 · come through (느낌이) 전해지다 · bear in mind 명심하다

What didn’t come through in the app’s version?

steps.goal: 근거를 들어 찬반을 말하고 조건을 붙이기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 평일 저녁, 어학원 건물 앞 인도. 수업을 마친 그레이스가 가방과 책을 안고 나오고, 퇴근길의 지우가 반갑게 손을 흔듦. 그레이스는 생각에 잠긴 표정. 간판·글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "The earlier, the better?" (영어 조기 교육). Goal: 근거를 들어 찬반을 말하고 조건을 붙이기. Today's scene: 9월 평일 저녁, 어학원 건물 앞 인도. 수업을 마친 그레이스가 가방과 책을 안고 나오고, 퇴근길의 지우가 반갑게 손을 흔듦. 그레이스는 생각에 잠긴 표정. 간판·글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "The earlier, the better.".

steps.when: 흔히 하는 말을 짧게 해요: *the + -er, the + -er*(~할수록 더 ~).
steps.extra: The earlier, the better? Not always.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "The earlier, the better." (빠를수록 좋아요.). When to use it: 흔히 하는 말을 짧게 해요: the + -er, the + -er(~할수록 더 ~). Note: The earlier, the better? Not always.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "There’s no evidence that ___.".

steps.when: 근거를 확인했을 때 써요. 확실하지 않으면 “I haven’t seen good evidence that …”이라고 해요.
steps.extra: I haven’t seen good evidence that one class makes a big difference.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "There’s no evidence that ___." (~라는 증거는 없어요.). When to use it: 근거를 확인했을 때 써요. 확실하지 않으면 “I haven’t seen good evidence that …”이라고 해요. Note: I haven’t seen good evidence that one class makes a big difference.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "What really matters is ___.".

steps.when: 이야기를 다시 핵심으로 가져와요.
steps.extra: What really matters is that kids enjoy it.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "What really matters is ___." (정말 중요한 건 ~예요.). When to use it: 이야기를 다시 핵심으로 가져와요. Note: What really matters is that kids enjoy it.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Start Early? · 9월 평일 저녁, 어학원 건물 앞에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Start Early? · 9월 평일 저녁, 어학원 건물 앞에서

lines.en: Jiwoo! Perfect timing. A parent asked me a tricky question today.
lines.ko: 지우 씨! 마침 잘 만났어요. 오늘 한 학부모가 어려운 질문을 했어요.

lines.en: Oh? What was it?
lines.ko: 그래요? 뭐였는데요?

lines.en: Should her four-year-old start English classes now?
lines.ko: 네 살 아이가 지금 영어 수업을 시작해야 하냐고요.

lines.en: Well, people always say, “{{The earlier, the better.}}” Kids pick up languages naturally, right?
lines.ko: 음, 다들 ‘빠를수록 좋다’고 하잖아요. 아이들은 언어를 자연스럽게 익히잖아요, 그렇죠?

lines.en: Up to a point. Exposure is the key. But {{there’s no evidence that}} one expensive class makes a big difference. At least, I haven’t seen any.
lines.ko: 어느 정도까지는요. 많이 접하는 게 핵심이에요. 하지만 비싼 수업 하나가 큰 차이를 만든다는 증거는 없어요. 적어도 저는 못 봤어요.

lines.en: Parents spend a fortune on it, though.
lines.ko: 그래도 부모들은 거기에 큰돈을 쓰잖아요.

lines.en: I know. And kids shouldn’t be pushed too hard. It can be a lot of pressure.
lines.ko: 그러게요. 그리고 아이들을 너무 몰아붙이면 안 돼요. 큰 부담이 될 수 있거든요.

lines.en: My cousin’s son goes to an English academy. He’s six, and he loves it.
lines.ko: 제 사촌의 아들이 영어 학원에 다녀요. 여섯 살인데 정말 좋아해요.

lines.en: So, you mean he has fun there?
lines.ko: 그러니까 거기서 재미있게 지낸다는 거죠?

lines.en: Yes! He sings songs and plays games. I think play is more important at that age.
lines.ko: 네! 노래도 부르고 게임도 해요. 그 나이에는 노는 게 더 중요한 것 같아요.

lines.en: Then that’s great. {{What really matters is}} that he enjoys it. Make it fun, not stressful.
lines.ko: 그럼 아주 좋네요. 정말 중요한 건 아이가 즐기는 거예요. 스트레스 말고 재미있게 해야 해요.

lines.en: That makes sense. And it shouldn’t replace the mother tongue. Every child is different.
lines.ko: 맞는 말이에요. 그리고 모국어를 밀어내면 안 되겠죠. 아이마다 다 다르고요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Start Early? · 9월 평일 저녁, 어학원 건물 앞에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Grace: "Jiwoo! Perfect timing. A parent asked me a tricky question today." (지우 씨! 마침 잘 만났어요. 오늘 한 학부모가 어려운 질문을 했어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Oh? What was it?" (그래요? 뭐였는데요?)
3. Grace: "Should her four-year-old start English classes now?" (네 살 아이가 지금 영어 수업을 시작해야 하냐고요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Well, people always say, “The earlier, the better.” Kids pick up languages naturally, right?" (음, 다들 ‘빠를수록 좋다’고 하잖아요. 아이들은 언어를 자연스럽게 익히잖아요, 그렇죠?)
5. Grace: "Up to a point. Exposure is the key. But there’s no evidence that one expensive class makes a big difference. At least, I haven’t seen any." (어느 정도까지는요. 많이 접하는 게 핵심이에요. 하지만 비싼 수업 하나가 큰 차이를 만든다는 증거는 없어요. 적어도 저는 못 봤어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Parents spend a fortune on it, though." (그래도 부모들은 거기에 큰돈을 쓰잖아요.)
7. Grace: "I know. And kids shouldn’t be pushed too hard. It can be a lot of pressure." (그러게요. 그리고 아이들을 너무 몰아붙이면 안 돼요. 큰 부담이 될 수 있거든요.)
8. Jiwoo: "My cousin’s son goes to an English academy. He’s six, and he loves it." (제 사촌의 아들이 영어 학원에 다녀요. 여섯 살인데 정말 좋아해요.)
9. Grace: "So, you mean he has fun there?" (그러니까 거기서 재미있게 지낸다는 거죠?)
10. Jiwoo: "Yes! He sings songs and plays games. I think play is more important at that age." (네! 노래도 부르고 게임도 해요. 그 나이에는 노는 게 더 중요한 것 같아요.)
11. Grace: "Then that’s great. What really matters is that he enjoys it. Make it fun, not stressful." (그럼 아주 좋네요. 정말 중요한 건 아이가 즐기는 거예요. 스트레스 말고 재미있게 해야 해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "That makes sense. And it shouldn’t replace the mother tongue. Every child is different." (맞는 말이에요. 그리고 모국어를 밀어내면 안 되겠죠. 아이마다 다 다르고요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.
