Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: The parent’s child is four years old.
Grace says one expensive class makes a big difference.
Jiwoo’s cousin’s son doesn’t like his English academy.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. The parent’s child is four years old.
2. Grace says one expensive class makes a big difference.
3. Jiwoo’s cousin’s son doesn’t like his English academy.
The scene they are about:
1. Grace: "Jiwoo! Perfect timing. A parent asked me a tricky question today." (지우 씨! 마침 잘 만났어요. 오늘 한 학부모가 어려운 질문을 했어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Oh? What was it?" (그래요? 뭐였는데요?)
3. Grace: "Should her four-year-old start English classes now?" (네 살 아이가 지금 영어 수업을 시작해야 하냐고요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Well, people always say, “The earlier, the better.” Kids pick up languages naturally, right?" (음, 다들 ‘빠를수록 좋다’고 하잖아요. 아이들은 언어를 자연스럽게 익히잖아요, 그렇죠?)
5. Grace: "Up to a point. Exposure is the key. But there’s no evidence that one expensive class makes a big difference. At least, I haven’t seen any." (어느 정도까지는요. 많이 접하는 게 핵심이에요. 하지만 비싼 수업 하나가 큰 차이를 만든다는 증거는 없어요. 적어도 저는 못 봤어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Parents spend a fortune on it, though." (그래도 부모들은 거기에 큰돈을 쓰잖아요.)
7. Grace: "I know. And kids shouldn’t be pushed too hard. It can be a lot of pressure." (그러게요. 그리고 아이들을 너무 몰아붙이면 안 돼요. 큰 부담이 될 수 있거든요.)
8. Jiwoo: "My cousin’s son goes to an English academy. He’s six, and he loves it." (제 사촌의 아들이 영어 학원에 다녀요. 여섯 살인데 정말 좋아해요.)
9. Grace: "So, you mean he has fun there?" (그러니까 거기서 재미있게 지낸다는 거죠?)
10. Jiwoo: "Yes! He sings songs and plays games. I think play is more important at that age." (네! 노래도 부르고 게임도 해요. 그 나이에는 노는 게 더 중요한 것 같아요.)
11. Grace: "Then that’s great. What really matters is that he enjoys it. Make it fun, not stressful." (그럼 아주 좋네요. 정말 중요한 건 아이가 즐기는 거예요. 스트레스 말고 재미있게 해야 해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "That makes sense. And it shouldn’t replace the mother tongue. Every child is different." (맞는 말이에요. 그리고 모국어를 밀어내면 안 되겠죠. 아이마다 다 다르고요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: The earlier, the better? There’s no evidence that ___.
head: 흔한 생각
I haven’t seen good evidence that …
What really matters is …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: The earlier, the better? There’s no evidence that ___. / What really matters is ___. Table (흔한 생각 → I haven’t seen good evidence that …):
- The earlier, the better. → one class makes kids fluent.
- Expensive is better. → price is everything.
- More hours, more learning. → long hours help small kids.
- Grammar first. → grammar rules help infants.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*The earlier, the better.* 일찍 시작할수록 좋아요. 
*The more* you listen, *the more* you understand. 많이 들을수록 더 많이 이해해요. 
*The sooner, the better.* (자주 쓰는 짧은 말)

*What really matters is* practice. (+ 명사) 
What really matters is *that* kids enjoy it. (+ that + 문장) 
*There’s no evidence that* … ~라는 근거는 없어요(확인한 근거가 있을 때만).
errors: There’s no evidences that it works.
There’s no evidence that it works.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- The + -er, the + -er: The earlier, the better. 일찍 시작할수록 좋아요. / The more you listen, the more you understand. 많이 들을수록 더 많이 이해해요. / The sooner, the better. (자주 쓰는 짧은 말)
- What really matters is …: What really matters is practice. (+ 명사) / What really matters is that kids enjoy it. (+ that + 문장) / There’s no evidence that … ~라는 근거는 없어요(확인한 근거가 있을 때만).
Common mistakes on screen:
- The more early, the better. → The earlier, the better. (early는 earlier로 바꿔요.)
- Earlier, better. → The earlier, the better. (두 부분 앞에 모두 the.)
- There’s no evidences that it works. → There’s no evidence that it works. (evidence에는 -s를 붙이지 않아요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: The + -er, the + -er: The earlier, the better. 일찍 시작할수록 좋아요. The more you listen, the more you understand. 많이 들을수록 더 많이 이해해요. The sooner, the better. (자주 쓰는 짧은 말)
What really matters is …: What really matters is practice. (+ 명사) What really matters is that kids enjoy it. (+ that + 문장) There’s no evidence that … ~라는 근거는 없어요(확인한 근거가 있을 때만).
mistakes: The more early, the better. → The earlier, the better.
Earlier, better. → The earlier, the better.
There’s no evidences that it works. → There’s no evidence that it works.

steps.note: 예) early English / having fun → Early English? What really matters is having fun.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) early English / having fun → Early English? What really matters is having fun. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: early English → having fun | learning grammar → using it | reading books → enjoying them | school grades → effort.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "The earlier, the better?" (영어 조기 교육); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "The earlier, the better." / "There’s no evidence that ___." / "What really matters is ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: They shouldn’t be pushed too hard.
It can be a lot of pressure.
Parents spend a fortune on it.
It shouldn’t replace the mother tongue.
Play is more important at that age.
그 나이에는 노는 게 더 중요해요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 일찍 시작하자는 쪽: "Kids pick up languages naturally." (아이들은 언어를 자연스럽게 익혀요., 보통); "Exposure is the key." (많이 접하는 게 핵심이에요., 보통)
- 조심할 점: "They shouldn’t be pushed too hard." (너무 몰아붙이면 안 돼요., 보통); "It can be a lot of pressure." (큰 부담이 될 수 있어요., 보통); "Parents spend a fortune on it." (부모들이 거기에 큰돈을 써요., 친근); "It shouldn’t replace the mother tongue." (모국어를 밀어내면 안 돼요., 보통)
- 도움이 되는 것: "Play is more important at that age." (그 나이에는 노는 게 더 중요해요., 보통); "Every child is different." (아이마다 달라요., 보통); "Make it fun, not stressful." (스트레스 말고 재미있게 해요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 아이·교육에 관한 낱말

*educate* children 아이들을 교육하다 · *educational* toys 교육용 장난감 
fine *motor* skills (그림 그리기 같은) 손의 섬세한 움직임 
a toy *maker* 장난감 회사 
연구 — 학교 수업만으로 비교하면 일찍 시작한 아이가 늘 더 빨리 늘지는 않았어요(Muñoz 편, 2006). 전문가 조언이 아니에요.
(참고) 정중한 말 · 무례한 말

*Shut up!*은 무례한 말이에요. Could you be quiet, please?라고 해요. 
an *innocent* question 나쁜 뜻 없는 질문 
She’s *keen* to learn. 정말 배우고 싶어 해요. · *fortunate* 운이 좋은
steps.blank:
A: Should kids start English early?   B: Well, the ___, the better? I haven’t seen good ___ that one class makes a big difference. 
A: Kids pick up languages ___, though.   B: True. What really ___ is that they enjoy it. 
낱말 상자: earlier · evidence · naturally · matters
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 아이·교육에 관한 낱말: educate children 아이들을 교육하다 · educational toys 교육용 장난감 / fine motor skills (그림 그리기 같은) 손의 섬세한 움직임 / a toy maker 장난감 회사 / 연구 — 학교 수업만으로 비교하면 일찍 시작한 아이가 늘 더 빨리 늘지는 않았어요(Muñoz 편, 2006). 전문가 조언이 아니에요.
- (참고) 정중한 말 · 무례한 말: Shut up!은 무례한 말이에요. Could you be quiet, please?라고 해요. / an innocent question 나쁜 뜻 없는 질문 / She’s keen to learn. 정말 배우고 싶어 해요. · fortunate 운이 좋은
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Should kids start English early? B: Well, the ___, the better? I haven’t seen good ___ that one class makes a big difference. / A: Kids pick up languages ___, though. B: True. What really ___ is that they enjoy it. / 낱말 상자: earlier · evidence · naturally · matters
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: academy (학원), infant (아기, 젖먹이), pupil ((주로 어린) 학생), principal (교장), tongue (혀), bilingual (두 언어를 쓰는), exposure ((자주) 접함, 노출), fortune (큰돈; 운), development (발달, 성장), education (교육), natural (자연스러운), educational (교육적인, 교육용의).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: There’s no evidence that it works.
It can be a lot of pressure.
Too much stress isn’t good for kids.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: early (일찍; 이른) — "start English early"; evidence (증거, 근거) — "There’s no evidence that it works."; pressure (압박감, 부담) — "It can be a lot of pressure."; mother ((mother tongue) 모국어(앞에서는 ‘엄마, 어머니’)) — "Korean is my mother tongue."; develop (발달하다, 자라다) — "Kids develop at different speeds."; brain (뇌) — "A child’s brain grows fast."; stress (스트레스) — "Too much stress isn’t good for kids."; play (놀다; 놀이(앞에서는 ‘(운동·악기를) 하다’)) — "Kids learn when they play.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Do you agree with “The earlier, the better”? Why?
Yes, because ___. / Not always. I haven’t seen good evidence that ___.
When you learn something new, what really matters?
What’s an easy way to get exposure to English?
You can watch ___. / You can listen to ___.
How can learning be fun, not stressful?
Make it fun, not stressful. For example, ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Do you agree with “The earlier, the better”? Why?" (hint on screen: Yes, because ___. / Not always. I haven’t seen good evidence that ___.)
- "When you learn something new, what really matters?" (hint on screen: What really matters is ___.)
- "What’s an easy way to get exposure to English?" (hint on screen: You can watch ___. / You can listen to ___.)
- "How can learning be fun, not stressful?" (hint on screen: Make it fun, not stressful. For example, ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Do you agree with “The earlier, the better”? Why?
When you learn something new, what really matters?
What’s an easy way to get exposure to English?
How can learning be fun, not stressful?

steps.title: Grace’s Reply
steps.text: That night, Grace wrote a short reply to the parent. *Firstly*, she said, there’s no single right age. Children are keen to play, and play is universal. Kids invent games and songs in any language. Secondly, small kids learn best from *day to day* life, so families can *make use of* simple things: picture books, songs, or a walk in the park. “You don’t have to pump a fortune into classes,” she wrote. She gave one concrete example: a five-minute English song at bedtime. Language skills evolve slowly. “It’s an evolution, not a race,” she added. “Don’t worry about mistakes.” She ended with a note: this was her opinion as a teacher, not expert advice.
steps.gloss: firstly 첫째로 · keen 몹시 하고 싶어 하는 · universal 어디에나 있는 · invent 지어내다 · day to day 매일의, 일상의 · make use of 잘 활용하다 · pump … into ~에 쏟아붓다 · concrete 구체적인 · evolve 서서히 발전하다 · evolution 서서히 일어나는 변화
questions: What was Grace’s concrete example?
According to Grace, where do small kids learn best?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Grace’s Reply". Text: "That night, Grace wrote a short reply to the parent. Firstly, she said, there’s no single right age. Children are keen to play, and play is universal. Kids invent games and songs in any language. Secondly, small kids learn best from day to day life, so families can make use of simple things: picture books, songs, or a walk in the park. “You don’t have to pump a fortune into classes,” she wrote. She gave one concrete example: a five-minute English song at bedtime. Language skills evolve slowly. “It’s an evolution, not a race,” she added. “Don’t worry about mistakes.” She ended with a note: this was her opinion as a teacher, not expert advice." Words: firstly 첫째로 · keen 몹시 하고 싶어 하는 · universal 어디에나 있는 · invent 지어내다 · day to day 매일의, 일상의 · make use of 잘 활용하다 · pump … into ~에 쏟아붓다 · concrete 구체적인 · evolve 서서히 발전하다 · evolution 서서히 일어나는 변화.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was Grace’s concrete example?" / "According to Grace, where do small kids learn best?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘The earlier, the better?’로 흔한 생각에 의문을 던질 수 있어요.
‘There’s no evidence that ___.’나 ‘I haven’t seen good evidence that ___.’로 주장을 조심스럽게 따져 볼 수 있어요.
‘What really matters is ___.’로 핵심을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘The earlier, the better?’로 흔한 생각에 의문을 던질 수 있어요.
- ‘There’s no evidence that ___.’나 ‘I haven’t seen good evidence that ___.’로 주장을 조심스럽게 따져 볼 수 있어요.
- ‘What really matters is ___.’로 핵심을 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 아이와 스마트폰
lessons.title_en: It’s up to them.

steps.title: 아이와 스마트폰
steps.title_en: It’s up to them.
steps.scene_desc: 9월 말 퇴근 후, 회사 근처 카페 창가 자리. 마야가 휴대폰(화면 글자 없이)을 탁자에 내려놓고 쓴웃음을 지으며 말하고, 지우가 커피잔을 들고 귀 기울임. 창밖은 저녁 거리. 글자·간판 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s up to them." (아이와 스마트폰). Goal: 규칙을 제안하고 책임을 말하기. Today's scene: 9월 말 퇴근 후, 회사 근처 카페 창가 자리. 마야가 휴대폰(화면 글자 없이)을 탁자에 내려놓고 쓴웃음을 지으며 말하고, 지우가 커피잔을 들고 귀 기울임. 창밖은 저녁 거리. 글자·간판 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "There should be a rule that ___.".

steps.en: There should be a rule that ___.
steps.when: 가족·학교·모임에 필요한 규칙을 제안해요.
steps.extra: There should be a rule that phones stay in the living room at night.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "There should be a rule that ___." (~라는 규칙이 있어야 해요.). When to use it: 가족·학교·모임에 필요한 규칙을 제안해요. Note: There should be a rule that phones stay in the living room at night.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "On the whole, ___.".

steps.when: 양쪽을 다 생각해 본 뒤 전체적인 의견을 말해요.
steps.extra: On the whole, phones are useful for kids.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "On the whole, ___." (대체로, ~.). When to use it: 양쪽을 다 생각해 본 뒤 전체적인 의견을 말해요. Note: On the whole, phones are useful for kids.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: There should be a rule that ___. / It’s up to ___ to ___. Table (문제 → There should be a rule that …):
- phones at night → phones stay in the living room.
- phones in class → phones are off in class.
- online games → kids play one hour a day.
- group chats → people don’t send messages after 10 p.m.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It’s *up to* you. 네가 정해. 
It’s *up to* parents *to* set limits. 한도를 정하는 건 부모가 할 일이에요. 
It *was up to* me. (과거) 내가 정할 일이었어요.
There should be / On the whole

*There should be a rule that* … (+ 문장) 
*On the whole*, phones are useful. 대체로 휴대폰은 쓸모 있어요.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- be up to: It’s up to you. 네가 정해. / It’s up to parents to set limits. 한도를 정하는 건 부모가 할 일이에요. / It was up to me. (과거) 내가 정할 일이었어요.
- There should be / On the whole: There should be a rule that … (+ 문장) / On the whole, phones are useful. 대체로 휴대폰은 쓸모 있어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s up to parents set limits. → It’s up to parents to set limits. (동사 앞에 to를 써요.)
- It’s up for you. → It’s up to you. (up to로 굳어진 표현이에요.)
- We need a rule what phones stay out. → We need a rule that phones stay out. (문장 앞에는 that을 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). - 걱정: "Screens are addictive." (화면은 중독성이 있어요., 보통); "Banning them doesn’t work." (금지해도 소용없어요., 보통)
- 도움이 되는 것: "Parents should set limits." (부모가 한도를 정해야 해요., 보통); "They need to learn to use them wisely." (현명하게 쓰는 법을 배워야 해요., 보통); "Schools can help too." (학교도 도울 수 있어요., 보통); "It’s about balance." (균형이 중요해요., 친근); "Lead by example." (먼저 본보기를 보여요., 보통)

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:

steps.title: The Family Phone Rules
steps.text: A week later, Maya told Jiwoo the news. Her sister and niece sat down together and *set down* some family rules on paper. *As of* October, the phone stays in the living room at the stroke of nine. Her niece helped *fill in* the details: one hour of games on weekends, and no phones at dinner, even for adults. “Kids resist rules from above,” Maya said, “but they follow rules they help make.” Her sister also turned on parental controls to block harmful content. Of course, every plan has its limits. Some days, homework is neglected and someone snaps. “I wouldn’t dare tell my sister what to do,” Maya laughed. “But hopefully, it works.”

questions: As of October, where does the phone stay at night?
Why does Maya think her niece will follow the rules?

steps.scene_desc: 10월 초 목요일 저녁, 동네 카페 안쪽 방의 토론 모임. 대니얼이 진행하며 손짓하고, 중년 이웃 한 명이 손을 들어 말하며, 지우가 듣고 고개를 끄덕임. 탁자 위 찻잔과 메모지(글자 없이). 간판·글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Not necessarily." (대학은 꼭 가야 할까). Goal: 일반론과 예외를 나눠 말하기. Today's scene: 10월 초 목요일 저녁, 동네 카페 안쪽 방의 토론 모임. 대니얼이 진행하며 손짓하고, 중년 이웃 한 명이 손을 들어 말하며, 지우가 듣고 고개를 끄덕임. 탁자 위 찻잔과 메모지(글자 없이). 간판·글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Not necessarily.".

steps.when: 일반적인 생각에 *부드럽게* 반대할 때 써요. No보다 부드러워요.
steps.extra: A: You need a degree to succeed. B: Not necessarily.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Not necessarily." (꼭 그렇지는 않아요.). When to use it: 일반적인 생각에 부드럽게 반대할 때 써요. No보다 부드러워요. Note: A: You need a degree to succeed. B: Not necessarily.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "For some people, ___, but for others ___.".

steps.en: For some people, ___, but for others ___.
steps.when: 답이 사람마다 다르다고 말해요. others = other people.
steps.extra: For some people, college is great, but for others, it isn’t.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "For some people, ___, but for others ___." (어떤 사람에게는 ~지만, 다른 사람에게는 ~.). When to use it: 답이 사람마다 다르다고 말해요. others = other people. Note: For some people, college is great, but for others, it isn’t.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s more about ___ than ___.".

steps.when: 둘 중 무엇이 더 중요한지 말해요. *about* 뒤에 더 중요한 것.
steps.extra: It’s more about skills than diplomas.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s more about ___ than ___." (~보다 ~가 더 중요해요.). When to use it: 둘 중 무엇이 더 중요한지 말해요. about 뒤에 더 중요한 것. Note: It’s more about skills than diplomas.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). steps.title: Is a Degree a Must? · 10월 초, 동네 카페 토론 모임에서

lines.en: Welcome back, everyone. Tonight’s question: does everyone need to go to university?
lines.ko: 여러분, 다시 오신 걸 환영해요. 오늘 질문은 ‘모든 사람이 대학에 가야 할까?’예요.

lines.en: I think so. A degree opens doors. Employers still check degrees.
lines.ko: 저는 그렇다고 봐요. 학위가 있으면 기회가 열려요. 회사들은 아직도 학위를 봐요.

lines.en: {{Not necessarily.}} {{For some people}}, a degree is the right path, {{but for others}}, it isn’t.
lines.ko: 꼭 그렇지는 않아요. 어떤 사람에게는 학위가 맞는 길이지만, 다른 사람에게는 아니에요.

lines.en: Can you give us an example, Jiwoo?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 예를 하나 들어 줄래요?

lines.en: Me! I went to college, but I studied something else. I learned design mostly at work and online. You can learn online for free these days.
lines.ko: 저요! 대학 전공은 달랐고, 디자인은 주로 일하며 온라인으로 배웠어요. 요즘은 무료로 배울 수 있죠.

lines.en: Some people say many successful people dropped out. But that’s the exception, not the rule.
lines.ko: 성공한 사람 중에 중퇴한 사람이 많다고들 하죠. 하지만 그건 예외지, 흔한 경우가 아니에요.

lines.en: That’s a fair point. Still, in my field, skills matter more than diplomas.
lines.ko: 일리 있는 말씀이에요. 그래도 제 분야에서는 졸업장보다 실력이 더 중요해요.

lines.en: So it depends on the field?
lines.ko: 그럼 분야에 따라 다르다는 건가요?

lines.en: Exactly. In many fields, you need a qualification.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 많은 분야에서는 자격이 필요하죠.

lines.en: True. But tuition is so expensive. Some students graduate with a lot of debt.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그런데 등록금이 너무 비싸요. 빚을 많이 진 채 졸업하는 학생도 있어요.

lines.en: Sure, but university is about more than jobs. You meet people and learn to think.
lines.ko: 그렇죠. 하지만 대학이 취업만을 위한 곳은 아니에요. 사람을 만나고 생각하는 법을 배우잖아요.

lines.en: Great points on both sides. Maybe {{it’s more about}} the person {{than}} the path.
lines.ko: 양쪽 다 좋은 의견이에요. 어쩌면 어떤 길이냐보다 어떤 사람이냐가 더 중요한가 봐요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Is a Degree a Must? · 10월 초, 동네 카페 토론 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "Welcome back, everyone. Tonight’s question: does everyone need to go to university?" (여러분, 다시 오신 걸 환영해요. 오늘 질문은 ‘모든 사람이 대학에 가야 할까?’예요.)
2. Neighbor: "I think so. A degree opens doors. Employers still check degrees." (저는 그렇다고 봐요. 학위가 있으면 기회가 열려요. 회사들은 아직도 학위를 봐요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Not necessarily. For some people, a degree is the right path, but for others, it isn’t." (꼭 그렇지는 않아요. 어떤 사람에게는 학위가 맞는 길이지만, 다른 사람에게는 아니에요.)
4. Daniel: "Can you give us an example, Jiwoo?" (지우 씨, 예를 하나 들어 줄래요?)
5. Jiwoo: "Me! I went to college, but I studied something else. I learned design mostly at work and online. You can learn online for free these days." (저요! 대학 전공은 달랐고, 디자인은 주로 일하며 온라인으로 배웠어요. 요즘은 무료로 배울 수 있죠.)
6. Neighbor: "Some people say many successful people dropped out. But that’s the exception, not the rule." (성공한 사람 중에 중퇴한 사람이 많다고들 하죠. 하지만 그건 예외지, 흔한 경우가 아니에요.)
7. Jiwoo: "That’s a fair point. Still, in my field, skills matter more than diplomas." (일리 있는 말씀이에요. 그래도 제 분야에서는 졸업장보다 실력이 더 중요해요.)
8. Daniel: "So it depends on the field?" (그럼 분야에 따라 다르다는 건가요?)
9. Neighbor: "Exactly. In many fields, you need a qualification." (바로 그거예요. 많은 분야에서는 자격이 필요하죠.)
10. Jiwoo: "True. But tuition is so expensive. Some students graduate with a lot of debt." (맞아요. 그런데 등록금이 너무 비싸요. 빚을 많이 진 채 졸업하는 학생도 있어요.)
11. Neighbor: "Sure, but university is about more than jobs. You meet people and learn to think." (그렇죠. 하지만 대학이 취업만을 위한 곳은 아니에요. 사람을 만나고 생각하는 법을 배우잖아요.)
12. Daniel: "Great points on both sides. Maybe it’s more about the person than the path." (양쪽 다 좋은 의견이에요. 어쩌면 어떤 길이냐보다 어떤 사람이냐가 더 중요한가 봐요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Daniel, Neighbor exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Daniel (you): "Welcome back, everyone. Tonight’s question: does everyone need to go to university?" (여러분, 다시 오신 걸 환영해요. 오늘 질문은 ‘모든 사람이 대학에 가야 할까?’예요.)
2. Neighbor (you): "I think so. A degree opens doors. Employers still check degrees." (저는 그렇다고 봐요. 학위가 있으면 기회가 열려요. 회사들은 아직도 학위를 봐요.)
3. Jiwoo (learner): "Not necessarily. For some people, a degree is the right path, but for others, it isn’t." (꼭 그렇지는 않아요. 어떤 사람에게는 학위가 맞는 길이지만, 다른 사람에게는 아니에요.)
4. Daniel (you): "Can you give us an example, Jiwoo?" (지우 씨, 예를 하나 들어 줄래요?)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "Me! I went to college, but I studied something else. I learned design mostly at work and online. You can learn online for free these days." (저요! 대학 전공은 달랐고, 디자인은 주로 일하며 온라인으로 배웠어요. 요즘은 무료로 배울 수 있죠.)
6. Neighbor (you): "Some people say many successful people dropped out. But that’s the exception, not the rule." (성공한 사람 중에 중퇴한 사람이 많다고들 하죠. 하지만 그건 예외지, 흔한 경우가 아니에요.)
7. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s a fair point. Still, in my field, skills matter more than diplomas." (일리 있는 말씀이에요. 그래도 제 분야에서는 졸업장보다 실력이 더 중요해요.)
8. Daniel (you): "So it depends on the field?" (그럼 분야에 따라 다르다는 건가요?)
9. Neighbor (you): "Exactly. In many fields, you need a qualification." (바로 그거예요. 많은 분야에서는 자격이 필요하죠.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "True. But tuition is so expensive. Some students graduate with a lot of debt." (맞아요. 그런데 등록금이 너무 비싸요. 빚을 많이 진 채 졸업하는 학생도 있어요.)
11. Neighbor (you): "Sure, but university is about more than jobs. You meet people and learn to think." (그렇죠. 하지만 대학이 취업만을 위한 곳은 아니에요. 사람을 만나고 생각하는 법을 배우잖아요.)
12. Daniel (you): "Great points on both sides. Maybe it’s more about the person than the path." (양쪽 다 좋은 의견이에요. 어쩌면 어떤 길이냐보다 어떤 사람이냐가 더 중요한가 봐요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Daniel and Neighbor. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

frame: Not necessarily. For some people, ___, but for others ___.
head: 일반적인 생각
Not necessarily. For some people, …
but for others, …
rows: a degree is the right path,
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Not necessarily. For some people, ___, but for others ___. / It’s more about ___ than ___. Table (일반적인 생각 → Not necessarily. For some people, …):
- Everyone needs a degree. → a degree is the right path,
- Online classes are enough. → they work well,
- Big cities are best. → city life is fun,
- Expensive is better. → it’s worth it,
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Not necessarily.* 꼭 그렇지는 않아요(No보다 부드러움). 
Expensive classes aren’t *necessarily* better.

*For some people*, college is great, *but for others*, it isn’t. 
It’s *more about* skills *than* diplomas. = 실력이 더 중요해요.
errors: For some, it’s good, but for other, it isn’t.
For some, it’s good, but for others, it isn’t.
It’s more about skills that diplomas.
It’s more about skills than diplomas.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Not necessarily: Not necessarily. 꼭 그렇지는 않아요(No보다 부드러움). / Expensive classes aren’t necessarily better.
- For some … / more about … than: For some people, college is great, but for others, it isn’t. / It’s more about skills than diplomas. = 실력이 더 중요해요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It isn’t necessary better. → It isn’t necessarily better. (부사 necessarily를 써요.)
- For some, it’s good, but for other, it isn’t. → For some, it’s good, but for others, it isn’t. (‘다른 사람들’은 others.)
- It’s more about skills that diplomas. → It’s more about skills than diplomas. (비교는 than.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

For some … / more about … than: For some people, college is great, but for others, it isn’t. It’s more about skills than diplomas. = 실력이 더 중요해요.

For some, it’s good, but for other, it isn’t. → For some, it’s good, but for others, it isn’t.
It’s more about skills that diplomas. → It’s more about skills than diplomas.

steps.note: 예) college / the right path → For some people, college is the right path, but for others, it isn’t.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) college / the right path → For some people, college is the right path, but for others, it isn’t. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: college → the right path | online classes → enough | a big company → the best place | studying abroad → worth it.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: For some people, ___, but for others ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Not necessarily." (대학은 꼭 가야 할까); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Not necessarily." / "For some people, ___, but for others ___." / "It’s more about ___ than ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: University is about more than jobs.
You can learn online for free.
성공한 사람 중에 중퇴한 사람이 많아요.
That’s the exception, not the rule.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 대학이 필요하다는 쪽: "A degree opens doors." (학위가 있으면 기회가 열려요., 보통); "Employers still check degrees." (회사들은 아직도 학위를 봐요., 보통); "University is about more than jobs." (대학이 취업만을 위한 곳은 아니에요., 보통)
- 다른 길도 있다는 쪽: "Skills matter more than diplomas." (졸업장보다 실력이 더 중요해요., 보통); "You can learn online for free." (온라인에서 무료로 배울 수 있어요., 친근); "Many successful people dropped out." (성공한 사람 중에 중퇴한 사람이 많아요., 보통)
- 따져 보기: "Tuition is so expensive." (등록금이 너무 비싸요., 친근); "That’s the exception, not the rule." (그건 예외지, 흔한 경우가 아니에요., 보통); "It depends on the field." (분야에 따라 달라요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 학교·공부 낱말: an essay 에세이, (한 주제로 쓰는) 짧은 글 · an examination 시험(= exam) / attendance 출석 · a grant (갚지 않는) 학비 지원금 / an institution (대학 같은) 기관 · academic 학업의, 학문의 / 모임과 보고서는 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요. 누구에게나 가장 좋은 길은 없어요.
- (참고) 대니얼의 조사에 나온 낱말: the mayor 시장(시의 대표) · govern (나라·도시를) 다스리다 / the council chamber 의회 회의장 · found a school 학교를 세우다 / a fragment 조각, 파편
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Does everyone need a degree? B: Not ___. For some people, it’s useful, but for ___, it isn’t. / A: Tuition is so ___. B: True. And it’s more ___ skills than diplomas. / 낱말 상자: necessarily · others · expensive · about
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: university (대학교, 종합대학), college (대학, 단과대학), diploma (졸업장), tuition (등록금, 수업료), debt (빚), graduate (졸업하다), professor (교수), literature (문학), exception (예외), success (성공), drop ((drop out) 학교를 그만두다, 중퇴하다), vocational (직업 교육의).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: My major didn’t correspond to my job.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: degree (학위) — "a degree in design"; employer (고용주, 회사) — "Employers still check degrees."; skill (기술, 실력) — "Skills matter more."; field (분야) — "It depends on the field."; education (교육) — "a good education"; qualification (자격, 자격증) — "You need a qualification."; possess (가지다, 소유하다) — "He possesses real skills."; correspond ((to) ~와 일치하다, 들어맞다) — "My major didn’t correspond to my job.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Not necessarily. For some people, ___, but for others ___.
In a field you like, what matters more?
What can people learn online for free?
You can learn ___ online for free.
Is a famous school always better?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Does everyone need a degree?" (hint on screen: Not necessarily. For some people, ___, but for others ___.)
- "In a field you like, what matters more?" (hint on screen: In ___, it’s more about ___ than ___.)
- "What can people learn online for free?" (hint on screen: You can learn ___ online for free.)
- "Is a famous school always better?" (hint on screen: Not necessarily. It depends on ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: After the Meeting
steps.text: After the meeting, Daniel stayed to chat with Jiwoo and Grace. *The other day*, he said, he read a short report about a cluster of new job-training schools. One indication of their success: most graduates found work quickly. “*For all* the talk about degrees, people want skills,” he said. Grace agreed, *except that* she valued her own university years. “My major didn’t correspond to my later jobs, but it taught me to think.” Jiwoo said both views made sense. The complexity of the topic surprised her. “You can’t extract one simple answer from it,” she said. “It’s more about the person than the path.” Daniel smiled. “That’s why we talk.”
steps.gloss: the other day 며칠 전에 · cluster (가까이 모인) 무리 · indication 조짐, 표시 · for all ~에도 불구하고 · except that ~라는 점만 빼면 · correspond to ~와 맞다 · complexity 복잡함 · extract 뽑아내다
questions: What did Daniel read about the other day?
What surprised Jiwoo?

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Daniel read about the other day?" / "What surprised Jiwoo?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘For some people, ___, but for others ___.’로 사람마다 다르다고 말할 수 있어요.
‘It’s more about ___ than ___.’로 무엇이 더 중요한지 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Not necessarily.’로 부드럽게 반대할 수 있어요.
- ‘For some people, ___, but for others ___.’로 사람마다 다르다고 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s more about ___ than ___.’로 무엇이 더 중요한지 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 현금 없는 생활
steps.title_en: Card or phone only?
steps.scene_desc: 10월 중순 토요일 오후, 동네 새 베이커리 카페 계산대 앞. 대니얼이 지폐를 내밀다가 멈칫하고 놀란 표정, 직원이 미안한 얼굴로 카드 단말기를 가리킴, 옆에서 지우가 휴대폰을 단말기에 갖다 대며 웃음. 진열대에 빵, 창밖은 가을 거리(간판·화면·안내판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Card or phone only?" (현금 없는 생활). Goal: 가능성을 말하고 일반화에 반박하기. Today's scene: 10월 중순 토요일 오후, 동네 새 베이커리 카페 계산대 앞. 대니얼이 지폐를 내밀다가 멈칫하고 놀란 표정, 직원이 미안한 얼굴로 카드 단말기를 가리킴, 옆에서 지우가 휴대폰을 단말기에 갖다 대며 웃음. 진열대에 빵, 창밖은 가을 거리(간판·화면·안내판에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s likely that ___.".

steps.when: 앞으로 아마 일어날 일을 예상해요. 더 확실하면 *most likely*, 반대는 *unlikely*.
steps.extra: It’s likely that most shops will go cashless.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It’s likely that ___." (~할 가능성이 커요. 아마 ~할 거예요.). When to use it: 앞으로 아마 일어날 일을 예상해요. 더 확실하면 most likely, 반대는 unlikely. Note: It’s likely that most shops will go cashless.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I can’t imagine ___ing.".

steps.when: 아주 놀랍거나 나에게는 불가능하게 느껴질 때 써요. imagine 뒤에는 *-ing*.
steps.extra: I can’t imagine running a shop without cash.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I can’t imagine ___ing." (~하는 건 상상이 안 돼요.). When to use it: 아주 놀랍거나 나에게는 불가능하게 느껴질 때 써요. imagine 뒤에는 -ing. Note: I can’t imagine running a shop without cash.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That’s not always the case.".

steps.when: 일반적인 생각에 부드럽게 반박해요. 뒤에 예를 들어요.
steps.extra: That’s not always the case. Some markets still only take cash.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That’s not always the case." (꼭 그렇지만은 않아요.). When to use it: 일반적인 생각에 부드럽게 반박해요. 뒤에 예를 들어요. Note: That’s not always the case. Some markets still only take cash.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("No Cash, Please · 10월 중순 토요일 오후, 새로 생긴 베이커리 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: No Cash, Please · 10월 중순 토요일 오후, 새로 생긴 베이커리 카페에서

lines.en: Two lattes, please. Here’s twenty thousand won.
lines.ko: 라테 두 잔 주세요. 여기 2만 원이요.

lines.en: Sorry, we’re a cashless store. Card or phone only.
lines.ko: 죄송해요, 저희는 현금 없는 매장이에요. 카드나 휴대폰 결제만 돼요.

lines.en: Really? {{I can’t imagine}} running a shop without cash!
lines.ko: 정말요? 현금 없이 가게를 운영한다니 상상이 안 되네요!

lines.en: Don’t worry, I’ve got it. {{Most people pay by phone now.}} See? Done.
lines.ko: 걱정 마요, 제가 낼게요. 요즘은 대부분 휴대폰으로 내요. 봐요, 끝!

lines.en: Thanks. But {{what if the system goes down?}} And {{every payment leaves a record.}}
lines.ko: 고마워요. 그런데 시스템이 멈추면 어떡해요? 게다가 결제할 때마다 기록이 남잖아요.

lines.en: The system rarely goes down. Besides, {{it’s faster and cleaner.}}
lines.ko: 시스템이 멈추는 일은 거의 없어요. 게다가 더 빠르고 깔끔하잖아요.

lines.en: Maybe. But {{I still carry some cash just in case.}} And {{cash is easier to budget with.}}
lines.ko: 그럴지도요. 그래도 저는 혹시 몰라 현금을 좀 들고 다녀요. 그리고 현금이 돈 관리하기가 더 쉬워요.

lines.en: {{That’s not always the case.}} My bank app shows my spending every week.
lines.ko: 꼭 그렇지만은 않아요. 제 은행 앱은 매주 지출을 보여 줘요.

lines.en: Fair enough. But {{older people might be left behind.}} My elderly neighbor pays with coins.
lines.ko: 그건 인정해요. 하지만 어르신들은 뒤처질 수도 있어요. 제 이웃 어르신은 동전으로 내세요.

lines.en: Good point. Still, {{it’s likely that}} most shops will go cashless. {{It’s already happening.}}
lines.ko: 좋은 지적이에요. 그래도 대부분의 가게가 현금을 안 받게 될 가능성이 커요. 벌써 그렇게 되고 있어요.

lines.en: Hmm. What’s your evidence?
lines.ko: 음. 근거가 뭐예요?

lines.en: Three cafés on this street stopped taking cash this year. {{It’s only a matter of time.}}
lines.ko: 이 거리 카페 세 곳이 올해 현금을 안 받기 시작했어요. 시간문제예요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "No Cash, Please · 10월 중순 토요일 오후, 새로 생긴 베이커리 카페에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "Two lattes, please. Here’s twenty thousand won." (라테 두 잔 주세요. 여기 2만 원이요.)
2. Barista: "Sorry, we’re a cashless store. Card or phone only." (죄송해요, 저희는 현금 없는 매장이에요. 카드나 휴대폰 결제만 돼요.)
3. Daniel: "Really? I can’t imagine running a shop without cash!" (정말요? 현금 없이 가게를 운영한다니 상상이 안 되네요!)
4. Jiwoo: "Don’t worry, I’ve got it. Most people pay by phone now. See? Done." (걱정 마요, 제가 낼게요. 요즘은 대부분 휴대폰으로 내요. 봐요, 끝!)
5. Daniel: "Thanks. But what if the system goes down? And every payment leaves a record." (고마워요. 그런데 시스템이 멈추면 어떡해요? 게다가 결제할 때마다 기록이 남잖아요.)
6. Jiwoo: "The system rarely goes down. Besides, it’s faster and cleaner." (시스템이 멈추는 일은 거의 없어요. 게다가 더 빠르고 깔끔하잖아요.)
7. Daniel: "Maybe. But I still carry some cash just in case. And cash is easier to budget with." (그럴지도요. 그래도 저는 혹시 몰라 현금을 좀 들고 다녀요. 그리고 현금이 돈 관리하기가 더 쉬워요.)
8. Jiwoo: "That’s not always the case. My bank app shows my spending every week." (꼭 그렇지만은 않아요. 제 은행 앱은 매주 지출을 보여 줘요.)
9. Daniel: "Fair enough. But older people might be left behind. My elderly neighbor pays with coins." (그건 인정해요. 하지만 어르신들은 뒤처질 수도 있어요. 제 이웃 어르신은 동전으로 내세요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Good point. Still, it’s likely that most shops will go cashless. It’s already happening." (좋은 지적이에요. 그래도 대부분의 가게가 현금을 안 받게 될 가능성이 커요. 벌써 그렇게 되고 있어요.)
11. Daniel: "Hmm. What’s your evidence?" (음. 근거가 뭐예요?)
12. Jiwoo: "Three cafés on this street stopped taking cash this year. It’s only a matter of time." (이 거리 카페 세 곳이 올해 현금을 안 받기 시작했어요. 시간문제예요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Daniel and Barista. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

frame: It’s likely that ___. / ___ is unlikely to ___.
head: It’s likely that …
반박하기
예
rows: Kids still use coins for snacks.
My bank just opened a new one.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It’s likely that ___. / ___ is unlikely to ___. / That’s not always the case. ___. Table (It’s likely that … → 반박하기):
- most shops will go cashless. → That’s not always the case.
- coins will disappear. → I’m not so sure.
- everyone will pay by phone. → Not necessarily.
- banks will close more branches. → That’s not always the case.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*It’s likely that* shops will go cashless. = 아마 그렇게 될 거예요. 
Shops are *likely to* go cashless. (+ 동사원형) 
Cash is *unlikely to* disappear soon. = 아마 안 그럴 거예요.

I *can’t imagine* liv*ing* without my phone. 휴대폰 없이 사는 건 상상이 안 돼요. (imagine + -ing) 
I *can’t imagine* a world without cash. (imagine + 명사)
errors: It’s likely to shops will close.
It’s likely that shops will close.
I can’t imagine to live without cash.
I can’t imagine living without cash.
Cash is unlikely to disappear soon.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- likely · unlikely: It’s likely that shops will go cashless. = 아마 그렇게 될 거예요. / Shops are likely to go cashless. (+ 동사원형) / Cash is unlikely to disappear soon. = 아마 안 그럴 거예요.
- I can’t imagine + -ing: I can’t imagine living without my phone. 휴대폰 없이 사는 건 상상이 안 돼요. (imagine + -ing) / I can’t imagine a world without cash. (imagine + 명사)
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s likely to shops will close. → It’s likely that shops will close. (문장을 이을 때는 that + 주어·동사.)
- I can’t imagine to live without cash. → I can’t imagine living without cash. (imagine 뒤에는 -ing(to ×).)
- Cash is unlikely disappear soon. → Cash is unlikely to disappear soon. (be unlikely to + 동사원형.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: likely · unlikely: It’s likely that shops will go cashless. = 아마 그렇게 될 거예요. Shops are likely to go cashless. (+ 동사원형) Cash is unlikely to disappear soon. = 아마 안 그럴 거예요.
I can’t imagine + -ing: I can’t imagine living without my phone. 휴대폰 없이 사는 건 상상이 안 돼요. (imagine + -ing) I can’t imagine a world without cash. (imagine + 명사)

I can’t imagine to live without cash. → I can’t imagine living without cash.
Cash is unlikely disappear soon. → Cash is unlikely to disappear soon.

steps.note: 예) shops / go cashless → It’s likely that shops will go cashless.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) shops / go cashless → It’s likely that shops will go cashless. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: shops → go cashless | coins → disappear | banks → close more branches | people → carry less cash.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Card or phone only?" (현금 없는 생활); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s likely that ___." / "I can’t imagine ___ing." / "That’s not always the case.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Most people pay by phone now.
It’s only a matter of time.
Older people might be left behind.
What if the system goes down?
Cash is easier to budget with.
I still carry some cash just in case.
혹시 몰라 아직 현금을 좀 들고 다녀요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 현금 없는 쪽: "Most people pay by phone now." (요즘은 대부분 휴대폰으로 내요., 보통); "It’s faster and cleaner." (더 빠르고 깔끔해요., 보통); "It’s already happening." (벌써 그렇게 되고 있어요., 보통); "It’s only a matter of time." (시간문제예요., 친근)
- 현금도 필요하다는 쪽: "Older people might be left behind." (어르신들은 뒤처질 수도 있어요., 보통); "What if the system goes down?" (시스템이 멈추면 어떡해요?, 보통); "Cash is easier to budget with." (현금이 돈 관리하기 더 쉬워요., 보통); "Every payment leaves a record." (결제할 때마다 기록이 남아요., 보통); "I still carry some cash just in case." (혹시 몰라 아직 현금을 좀 들고 다녀요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

낱말 상자: likely · case · living
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 결제 낱말: tap your card 카드를 (단말기에) 대다 / pay in cash / by card 현금으로 / 카드로 내다 · The system is down. 시스템이 멈췄어요.
- (참고) 낱말 더 보기: unite 하나로 뭉치다 · embrace 기꺼이 받아들이다 / greatly 크게, 매우 · altogether 완전히 / a civilian 민간인(군인이 아닌 사람) · ethnic 민족의(문화·뿌리가 같은)
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Will shops stop taking cash? B: Yes. It’s ___ that most shops will go cashless. / A: That’s not always the ___. Some markets only take cash. B: True. But I can’t imagine ___ without my phone. / 낱말 상자: likely · case · living
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: cashless (현금 없는, 현금을 안 받는), payment (결제, 지불), coin (동전), account ((은행) 계좌), withdraw ((돈을) 찾다, 인출하다), hacking (해킹), elderly (연세 드신, 고령의), stock (주식), secure (안전한), privacy (사생활, 개인 정보 보호), transaction (거래), digital (디지털의).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: A home is a big asset.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: system (시스템, 체계) — "The payment system went down."; asset (자산) — "A home is a big asset."; inflation (물가 상승, 인플레이션) — "Inflation made coffee more expensive."; access (이용, 접근) — "easy access to a bank"; bank (은행) — "I went to the bank."; fee (수수료, 요금) — "a small card fee"; budget (예산) — "a weekly budget"; record (기록) — "a record of every payment"; security (보안, 안전) — "online security".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: How do most people pay for small things, like coffee, where you live?
Most people pay by ___. / It’s likely that ___.
Do you think cash will disappear one day?
It’s likely that ___. / I don’t think so. ___.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "How do most people pay for small things, like coffee, where you live?" (hint on screen: Most people pay by ___. / It’s likely that ___.)
- "Do you think cash will disappear one day?" (hint on screen: It’s likely that ___. / I don’t think so. ___.)
- "What’s something you can’t imagine living without?" (hint on screen: I can’t imagine living without ___.)
- "Someone says, “Everyone pays by phone.” How do you push back?" (hint on screen: That’s not always the case. ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Cash or No Cash?
steps.text: At the next discussion group, Daniel asked, “Will we stop using cash altogether?” One neighbor said cash would *most likely* disappear within ten years. “Years ago, I had to *fill in* a form at the bank to withdraw money. Now I just tap my phone.” Another neighbor disagreed. “I use my card *in conjunction with* cash. If there’s a power cut or a hacking problem, *something like that*, I can still pay.” Jiwoo said, “I can’t imagine going back to cash. But shops shouldn’t turn away people who only have coins.” Daniel summed up. “So most of us embrace digital payment, but we want an option for everyone.” For once, the whole group felt greatly united.
steps.gloss: altogether 완전히 · most likely 십중팔구, 아마 · fill in (서류를) 작성하다 · in conjunction with ~와 함께 · something like that 그런 것 · embrace 기꺼이 받아들이다 · united 하나로 뭉친
questions: Why does one neighbor carry cash with a card?
What did most of the group want in the end?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Cash or No Cash?". Text: "At the next discussion group, Daniel asked, “Will we stop using cash altogether?” One neighbor said cash would most likely disappear within ten years. “Years ago, I had to fill in a form at the bank to withdraw money. Now I just tap my phone.” Another neighbor disagreed. “I use my card in conjunction with cash. If there’s a power cut or a hacking problem, something like that, I can still pay.” Jiwoo said, “I can’t imagine going back to cash. But shops shouldn’t turn away people who only have coins.” Daniel summed up. “So most of us embrace digital payment, but we want an option for everyone.” For once, the whole group felt greatly united." Words: altogether 완전히 · most likely 십중팔구, 아마 · fill in (서류를) 작성하다 · in conjunction with ~와 함께 · something like that 그런 것 · embrace 기꺼이 받아들이다 · united 하나로 뭉친.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why does one neighbor carry cash with a card?" / "What did most of the group want in the end?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. steps.title: SNS와 행복
steps.title_en: It makes people feel left out.
steps.scene_desc: 10월 말 늦은 오후, 단풍 든 공원 벤치. 촬영을 막 마친 클로이가 카메라 가방을 옆에 두고 휴대폰 화면을 보며 사진을 고르고, 옆에 앉은 지우가 고개를 기울여 웃으며 이야기함. 바닥에 노란 은행잎, 멀리 삼각대를 접는 사람(화면·간판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It makes people feel left out." (SNS와 행복). Goal: 영향을 말하고 반대쪽도 함께 보기. Today's scene: 10월 말 늦은 오후, 단풍 든 공원 벤치. 촬영을 막 마친 클로이가 카메라 가방을 옆에 두고 휴대폰 화면을 보며 사진을 고르고, 옆에 앉은 지우가 고개를 기울여 웃으며 이야기함. 바닥에 노란 은행잎, 멀리 삼각대를 접는 사람(화면·간판에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It makes people feel ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 것이 사람들의 기분을 어떻게 바꾸는지 말해요. *make + 사람 + 동사원형*(to 없이).
steps.extra: Seeing perfect photos makes people feel left out.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It makes people feel ___." (사람들이 ~하게 느끼게 만들어요.). When to use it: 어떤 것이 사람들의 기분을 어떻게 바꾸는지 말해요. make + 사람 + 동사원형(to 없이). Note: Seeing perfect photos makes people feel left out.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "There’s no doubt that ___.".

steps.when: 아주 확실하다고 생각하는 것을 말해요. 흔히 뒤에 but이 이어져요.
steps.extra: There’s no doubt that social media helps people stay in touch.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "There’s no doubt that ___." (~인 건 확실해요.). When to use it: 아주 확실하다고 생각하는 것을 말해요. 흔히 뒤에 but이 이어져요. Note: There’s no doubt that social media helps people stay in touch.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "At the same time, ___.".

steps.when: 한쪽 이야기를 한 뒤 다른 면을 덧붙여요.
steps.extra: It’s fun. At the same time, it takes a lot of time.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "At the same time, ___." (한편으로는 ~. 동시에 ~.). When to use it: 한쪽 이야기를 한 뒤 다른 면을 덧붙여요. Note: It’s fun. At the same time, it takes a lot of time.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The Real Me · 10월 말, 클로이의 촬영이 끝난 뒤 공원 벤치에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: The Real Me · 10월 말, 클로이의 촬영이 끝난 뒤 공원 벤치에서

lines.en: Sorry, Jiwoo. Let me post one photo from the shoot. Hmm, which filter?
lines.ko: 미안해요, 지우 씨. 촬영 사진 하나만 올릴게요. 음, 필터는 뭘로 하지?

lines.en: Take your time. Can I ask you something? Does social media make you happy?
lines.ko: 천천히 해요. 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? SNS를 하면 행복해요?

lines.en: Good question. {{There’s no doubt that}} {{it helps people stay in touch.}} My parents in Toronto see my life every week.
lines.ko: 좋은 질문이에요. SNS가 연락에 도움 되는 건 확실해요. 토론토의 부모님이 매주 제 생활을 보시거든요.

lines.en: True. {{At the same time,}} {{everyone shows only their best moments.}}
lines.ko: 맞아요. 한편으로는 다들 가장 좋은 순간만 보여 주잖아요.

lines.en: Right. It’s like a drama trailer. Only the best scenes, never the boring ones.
lines.ko: 그렇죠. 드라마 예고편 같아요. 제일 좋은 장면만 나오고, 지루한 장면은 절대 안 나와요.

lines.en: Exactly. And {{it’s easy to compare yourself.}} Sometimes {{it makes people feel}} left out.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 그리고 나를 남과 비교하기 쉬워요. 가끔은 사람들이 소외감을 느끼게 돼요.

lines.en: I know. To be honest, {{I spend too much time scrolling.}}
lines.ko: 알아요. 솔직히 저는 화면을 넘기면서 시간을 너무 많이 써요.

lines.en: Me too. {{It’s designed to be addictive.}} As a designer, I know the tricks!
lines.ko: 저도요. 중독되게 설계돼 있거든요. 디자이너라서 그 수법을 알아요!

lines.en: Ha! But {{you can find your community,}} too. I found a great group of video makers.
lines.ko: 하하! 그래도 나랑 맞는 모임을 찾을 수도 있어요. 저는 영상 만드는 사람들의 좋은 모임을 찾았어요.

lines.en: Fair. {{I took a break from it once.}} For a week, I deleted the app, and I felt calmer.
lines.ko: 인정해요. 저는 한 번 SNS를 쉬어 본 적이 있어요. 일주일 동안 앱을 지웠더니 마음이 더 차분해졌어요.

lines.en: So it’s not all good or bad. {{It’s how you use it.}} {{It has its uses.}} And no filter today. Just the real me!
lines.ko: 다 좋지도 다 나쁘지도 않네요. 쓰기 나름이고, 쓸모도 있어요. 오늘은 필터 없이, 있는 그대로의 나로!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Real Me · 10월 말, 클로이의 촬영이 끝난 뒤 공원 벤치에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Sorry, Jiwoo. Let me post one photo from the shoot. Hmm, which filter?" (미안해요, 지우 씨. 촬영 사진 하나만 올릴게요. 음, 필터는 뭘로 하지?)
2. Jiwoo: "Take your time. Can I ask you something? Does social media make you happy?" (천천히 해요. 뭐 하나 물어봐도 돼요? SNS를 하면 행복해요?)
3. Chloe: "Good question. There’s no doubt that it helps people stay in touch. My parents in Toronto see my life every week." (좋은 질문이에요. SNS가 연락에 도움 되는 건 확실해요. 토론토의 부모님이 매주 제 생활을 보시거든요.)
4. Jiwoo: "True. At the same time, everyone shows only their best moments." (맞아요. 한편으로는 다들 가장 좋은 순간만 보여 주잖아요.)

6. Jiwoo: "Exactly. And it’s easy to compare yourself. Sometimes it makes people feel left out." (바로 그거예요. 그리고 나를 남과 비교하기 쉬워요. 가끔은 사람들이 소외감을 느끼게 돼요.)
7. Chloe: "I know. To be honest, I spend too much time scrolling." (알아요. 솔직히 저는 화면을 넘기면서 시간을 너무 많이 써요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Me too. It’s designed to be addictive. As a designer, I know the tricks!" (저도요. 중독되게 설계돼 있거든요. 디자이너라서 그 수법을 알아요!)
9. Chloe: "Ha! But you can find your community, too. I found a great group of video makers." (하하! 그래도 나랑 맞는 모임을 찾을 수도 있어요. 저는 영상 만드는 사람들의 좋은 모임을 찾았어요.)

11. Chloe: "So it’s not all good or bad. It’s how you use it. It has its uses. And no filter today. Just the real me!" (다 좋지도 다 나쁘지도 않네요. 쓰기 나름이고, 쓸모도 있어요. 오늘은 필터 없이, 있는 그대로의 나로!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. frame: There’s no doubt that ___. / It makes people feel ___.
head: Social media …
make(s) people …
At the same time, …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: There’s no doubt that ___. / It makes people feel ___. / At the same time, ___. Table (Social media … → make(s) people …):
- Perfect photos → feel left out.
- Long videos → stay up late.
- Old friends’ posts → feel close again.
- Endless scrolling → lose track of time.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
It *makes* people *feel* lonely. 사람들을 외롭게 만들어요. (to 없이) 
Short videos *make* me *stay up* late. 짧은 영상 때문에 늦게까지 안 자요. 
Her post *made* me *laugh*. (과거: made)
no doubt · at the same time

*There’s no doubt that* it’s useful. 유용한 건 확실해요. 
It’s useful. *At the same time*, it takes time. 유용해요. 한편으로는 시간이 많이 들어요.
errors: It makes me to feel tired.
At the same time, it’s risky.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- make + 사람 + 동사원형: It makes people feel lonely. 사람들을 외롭게 만들어요. (to 없이) / Short videos make me stay up late. 짧은 영상 때문에 늦게까지 안 자요. / Her post made me laugh. (과거: made)
- no doubt · at the same time: There’s no doubt that it’s useful. 유용한 건 확실해요. / It’s useful. At the same time, it takes time. 유용해요. 한편으로는 시간이 많이 들어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It makes me to feel tired. → It makes me feel tired. (make + 사람 뒤에는 to 없이 동사원형.)
- It makes people feeling bad. → It makes people feel bad. (-ing가 아니라 동사원형 feel.)
- At same time, it’s risky. → At the same time, it’s risky. (the same time이라고 해요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: make + 사람 + 동사원형: It makes people feel lonely. 사람들을 외롭게 만들어요. (to 없이) Short videos make me stay up late. 짧은 영상 때문에 늦게까지 안 자요. Her post made me laugh. (과거: made)
no doubt · at the same time: There’s no doubt that it’s useful. 유용한 건 확실해요. It’s useful. At the same time, it takes time. 유용해요. 한편으로는 시간이 많이 들어요.
mistakes: It makes me to feel tired. → It makes me feel tired.
It makes people feeling bad. → It makes people feel bad.
At same time, it’s risky. → At the same time, it’s risky.

steps.note: 예) perfect photos / feel left out → Perfect photos make people feel left out.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) perfect photos / feel left out → Perfect photos make people feel left out. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: perfect photos → feel left out | funny videos → laugh | long videos → stay up late | kind comments → feel good.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "It makes people feel left out." (SNS와 행복); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It makes people feel ___." / "There’s no doubt that ___." / "At the same time, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.
